Gyurov has the support of the country’s pro-Western opposition and signed a security cooperation agreement with Ukraine as prime minister.

He said on Sunday that he wanted “a Bulgaria that looks forward, a country that is European, free, and proud”.

“Next week, Bulgaria must choose between two personalities, two directions,” he said after the vote, and invited Iotova to a debate before the next round.

Although the role of president is largely ceremonial, the president leads the armed forces, can veto legislation and sign treaties.

World.title: Real Madrid beat Barcelona 2-1 at Camp Nou to halve gap to La Liga leaders
World.content:
French superstar Kylian Mbappe scores a brace for Madrid to inflict Barcelona’s first domestic defeat of the campaign.

Share Real Madrid beat Barcelona 2-1 at Camp Nou to halve gap to La Liga leaders on social media

Kylian Mbappe struck twice to earn Jose Mourinho’s Real Madrid a 2-1 El Clasico victory over La Liga leaders Barcelona at Camp Nou, cutting the gap to three points.

French superstar Mbappe opened the scoring before half-time on Sunday, then slotted home late on to inflict Barca’s first domestic defeat of the campaign after Raphinha had equalised for the champions.

Real Madrid remain third, behind Atletico Madrid and Hansi Flick’s Barca, who had won their first nine games before a chastening week.

The Catalans suffered a second straight defeat after losing against Paris Saint-Germain on Tuesday in the Champions League.

Barca won six of the seven previous Clasicos since the German arrived, but were surprisingly subdued against Mourinho’s side.

“In general, we didn’t have a great game. In the first half, we weren’t ourselves; there were a lot of things we could have done better,” Barcelona midfielder Pedri told DAZN.

“We wanted to win the Clasico in front of our fans, but the season is very long… a league is not won here.”

Los Blancos, without suspended winger Vinicius Junior, won their fifth straight game across all competitions, and are finding their footing under veteran Portuguese coach Mourinho.

After two trophyless seasons, Madrid turned back to Mourinho to try to stop Barca’s dominance, and this result will give them hope they are on the right track.

The opening period of the game was cagey, with few opportunities.

Barca defender Pau Cubarsi twice reacted well to shut down Mbappe, while Real Madrid’s Marc Cucurella took a rapid liking to Lamine Yamal’s shirt, constantly grabbing at the 19-year-old winger.



Anthony Gordon, playing in his first Clasico since joining Barcelona from Newcastle, back-heeled the ball to Raphinha, who fired narrowly wide as Barca threatened.

The hosts were dealt a setback when young defender Xavi Espart pulled up hurt and needed to be replaced by Alejandro Balde before the half-hour mark.

Andriy Lunin, playing in goal for Madrid after Thibaut Courtois pulled out of the squad with flu, saved at his near post from Gordon before the visitors took the lead.

Mbappe scored his 10th league goal of the season and also his easiest, with Barca’s Gerard Martin clearing a cross straight at the Frenchman, who deflected it into the net.

Barca responded by carving out a glorious chance for an equaliser, but teenage sensation Yamal, for once, miscued in front of goal, firing wide when poised to level.

The game opened up, and Yan Diomande came close to doubling Madrid’s lead before half-time, drilling into the side netting.

Martin redeemed himself early in the second half as he held off Jude Bellingham, who could neither beat the defender nor find a free Mbappe.

Raphinha, who had a quiet first half, pulled Barcelona level just after the hour mark.

Pedri fed the Brazilian, La Liga’s top goalscorer with 13, who fired through Bellingham’s legs, and Lunin could not keep the shot out.

The Ukrainian goalkeeper did make a superb save to deny Martin a corner as Barcelona flowed forward with the wind finally in their sails.

Yamal bent an effort wide with Lunin at full stretch, and Barca substitute Frenkie de Jong had a shot desperately blocked by Dean Huijsen.

There was a sting in the tail for the Catalans, though, as substitute Gabriel Jesus lost possession and Madrid raced through on goal.

Eduardo Camavinga beat Cubarsi and unselfishly cut the ball back for Mbappe to tuck home his second of the night into an empty net, with Joan Garcia drawn out of position.

World.title: Elon Musk Says Ukraine Violated Starlink’s Rules
World.content:
In Washington, the issue deepened divides between Congress and the Trump administration over the U.S. approach to Russia. A group of Republican and Democratic senators warned the White House this past week that they would block Mr. Trump’s pending nominations if Ukraine’s full Starshield capabilities were not restored.

Mr. Trump was said to have called Mr. Musk earlier in the week and asked him to restore Ukraine’s full access to the communication systems.

The episode has highlighted the geopolitical influence Mr. Musk wields through SpaceX. While Starlink now has over 13 million subscribers including in some homes as an internet provider, Starshield is increasingly seen as the backbone for U.S. military communications.

Ukraine feared that the unexplained changes in its satellite service, which came as President Trump eased sanctions on Russia and demanded Ukraine stop attacking oil refineries, were part of an attempt to force it to capitulate to Moscow. The slowdown in the service did not affect strikes inside Russia, where the technology does not work.



“I thank all Americans and all our partners who took this seriously and truly helped — members of Congress, senators, all the media, the State Department and the president,” Mr. Zelensky said. “Protecting lives matters.”



Ukraine’s defense minister, Yevhen Khmara, announced earlier Saturday that drones connected to Starshield had flown at speeds near 250 miles an hour for the first time since the initial disruptions.

“This is another example when direct dialogue and the persistent position of the president of Ukraine at the highest level produce results,” Mr. Khmara said in a statement.

World.title: Serbia's veteran ruler Vučić concedes election to student-led protest movement
World.content:
VuÄiÄ had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.

The Student List's lead candidate Ilija SrdanoviÄ told BBC Serbian: "This will be a free state."

He said the anti-corruption movement, which had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia, hoped to "free the country from tyranny".

VuÄiÄ made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade.

There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off. "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle."

The centre of Novi Sad - the northern city that triggered the student-led protests - was crowded. "Everything is going to get better now," David VasiÄ, one of those celebrating, told the BBC Serbian.

The Student List - which has no obvious leaders and whose members are not used to politics - had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.

It decided to field candidates to the 250-member parliament from across Serbian society including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities.

World.title: Deeply divided Israel braces for pivotal election
World.content:
The prime minister has traditionally relied on a stable base of right-wing voters, but is projected to see a thinning of support in this election. Some voters may be slipping away to opposition parties like Eisenkot's. Others, including some die-hard Likud voters we spoke to, said the 7 October attacks had pushed them towards parties further on the right.

Lt Col (Res) Eyal Hajbi, head of the regional civil defence unit in the Netanyahu stronghold of Sderot, right on the Gaza border, lost several friends and colleagues in the attacks. He lights candles for them every day in his office, and told me he would be thinking about them when he cast his ballot on Tuesday.

Standing on a ridge overlooking the ruins of northern Gaza, he gestured to the wasteland where Israel's army has completely flattened the neighbourhoods of Beit Lahia and Beit Hanoun.

"As far as I'm concerned, after 7 October, we should wipe them all out," he said. "I've changed my understanding of Gaza. Before, I wouldn't have said we should destroy it."

He told me he and his family had always voted Likud, but that now he was voting for the far-right party of Itamar Ben Gvir, Jewish Power.

"My family has become more extreme than it ever was before," he said. "If once we deliberated over it, today we don't think twice; we vote."

Polls suggest that less than 10% of Israelis are undecided and that very few of those are considering switching between government parties and opposition ones.

Ben Gvir, National Security minister in Netanyahu's coalition, has been reaching out to younger voters through headline-grabbing social media campaigns.

A poll for one of Israel's leading newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth, published on 9 October, suggested that more than 16% of first-time voters in Israel would choose far-right parties like his.

In Sderot, a group of 18 year olds from a nearby Jewish religious college told me their political views had been affected by the 7 October attacks far more than their parents. All four teenagers were planning to vote for another far-right party, Religious Zionism, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

"Today, the whole younger generation understands that peaceful paths will not work," Aviad Elmahach, one of the teenagers, told me. "Older adults, who are set in a fixed mindset, find [it] harder to change, but the youth understand that we need to be here with strength and an iron fist, which is the only way to win."

The lesson of 7 October, he said, was that Israel needed to be as forceful as possible in its relations with the Palestinians, more than 74,000 of whom have been killed by Israel in Gaza since then, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

"The youth have a fresh new perspective that has not yet become entrenched in politics, and they understand very well why we're voting for Smotrich - it means holding the land with strength and giving [the Palestinians] nothing through peaceful gestures."

World.title: Venezuelan opposition leader María Machado returns after months in exile
World.content:
Venezuelan opposition leader MarÃ­a Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after more than 10 months in exile.

"I am here. With you," Machado wrote on X on Sunday. Her return comes after repeated prior efforts to re-enter the country came to no avail.

In January, a month after Machado left Venezuela on a speedboat under cover of darkness to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, the US seized her opponent, President NicolÃ¡s Maduro.

The Trump administration then backed his deputy, Delcy RodrÃ­guez, as leader and she was sworn in as interim president, later signing an oil deal which granted very favourable terms to the US.

Machado was photographed on Sunday attending Mass at a church in the Venezuelan state of Lara, surrounded by supporters hugging her and clasping her hands.

She then began travelling to the capital Caracas in a caravan of cheering supporters. More supporters have lined the route of her journey to the capital.

Her ally, former presidential candidate Edmundo GonzÃ¡lez, confirmed her arrival, writing in a statement: "I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear MarÃ­a Corina, is on Venezuelan soil."

"Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!" GonzÃ¡lez said.

He added that he will soon join Machado in Venezuela to advance the country "toward freedom".

An advisor to Machado said in September that over the previous few weeks Machado had attempted seven times to return to Venezuela, but was denied each time. There have been reports that the US was involved in delaying her return, which it has denied.

It's unclear what Machado plans to do next now that she's back, but she has previously said she would run for president again if an election were held. Her ability to return to her country was always contingent on approval from the Trump administration, which it appears has now been granted.

World.title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
World.content:
Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.

The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.

Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".

Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week.

The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday.

"Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."

He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."

Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov said that drones operating via Starlink in Ukraine had a speed restriction of 70-90km/h (43-56mph) and did not work on Russian territory.

"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he wrote on Telegram.

"It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine's defence ministry.

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.

Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.

Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h. Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h.

"The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram.

World.title: Suspect in deadly Paris suburb shooting sent for psychiatric observation
World.content:
The lawyer for Pengo Bossio Wangi, the one person killed during the attack, told French media the move to place the suspect under observation was "very rare".

He alleged that it was being used to portray the suspect as criminally irresponsible rather than having acted deliberately.

Wangi, a 26-year-old French-Congolese martial artist, was named as the one fatality on Saturday.

The mixed martial arts club where he trained paid tribute to him, saying: "On the mats as off them, he was one of those who lead by example: present, respectful, always ready to lift others up.

"His smile, his energy and his generosity will remain etched in our walls and in our hearts."

Three of those injured in the attack were taken to hospital in a serious condition - including a 12-year-old girl who remains in a critical condition.

The mayor of La VerriÃ¨re, Nicolas Dainville, told French radio network France Info on Sunday that he had spoken to the girl's mother over the phone and confirmed she was "doing better".

Another injured resident was recovering while a third remained in a critical condition, he said.

The suspect had been known to police prior to the attack but not to France's intelligence services, local media report. PNAT previously said he had four previous convictions that had been "automatically expunged".

He is thought to have used an old semi-automatic weapon during the attack, firing in bursts from his car window.

World.title: Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates
World.content:
All West Bank land crossings will be closed during Tuesday's election in Israel, the country's military says, and Palestinian workers will be barred from entering all settlements.

The restrictions come amid a crackdown in the occupied West Bank after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the territory.

The Israel Defense Forces announced a "ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers throughout Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings" on Tuesday.

It said most workers would also be barred from settlements from Sunday, with the exception of industrial zones and a limited number of other areas.

Before the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, more than 100,000 Palestinian workers were permitted to enter Israel. Since then only a small fraction have had their permits restored.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a major operation on Friday in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.

The Israeli military have been demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron, with hundreds of families having been displaced.

World.title: Gabon says access to social media restored after eight-month ban
World.content:
Gabon says it has lifted a ban on social media imposed eight months ago - a move that triggered widespread criticism at the time.

The High Communication Authority (HAC) announced the U-turn on Saturday in a televised statement. The BBC has approached the country's media regulator for comment.

The ban had been introduced on 17 February, with the HAC saying that online content was fuelling conflict and deepening divisions in the country.

The move came as a shock to the central African nation of about 2.5 million people, where social media platforms such as Facebook, TikTok, YouTube and Instagram have been particularly popular with younger people who use it for business as well as pleasure.

Many turned to VPNs in order to continue accessing social media sites following the ban.

The ban had been imposed at a time when the Gabonese President Brice Oligui Nguema was facing a wave of social unrest less than a year after his election.

Teachers and civil servants had staged strikes over what they said were low pay and poor working conditions.

The opposition said the suspension was an abuse of power.

Nguema won last year's elections with more than 90% of the vote, two years after his coup had ended more than five decades of rule by the Bongo family.

At the time he pledged to reform Gabon, a small, oil- and timber-rich country, where digital blackouts were used by the previous governments to control information.

World.title: El Salvador president says bodies found in Haiti are not those of hostages
World.content:
Four bodies handed over to special forces on a mission to Haiti to recover Salvadoran hostages are "not our men", El Salvador's president has said.

Nayib Bukele said a nongovernmental organisation delivered the human remains to one of Haiti's airports claiming they were four El Salvadoran air technicians, but that one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's army uniform.

He had dispatched a military contingent, reportedly of hundreds of soldiers, on Thursday after the four men vanished after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups".

The hostages had been part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), which is tasked with tackling worsening gang violence in Haiti.

The men had been travelling back to their camp in an armoured vehicle when they were attacked in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets. No gang has so far claimed responsibility.

Bukele previously said the Salvadoran military operation in Haiti had the sole purpose of returning the four men alive. Approximately 450 soldiers had so far been deployed, according to Haitian newspaper Le Nouvelliste.

Bukele said the bodies the mission had received included one of a man of "considerably greater height than that of our air technicians", a person "who was wearing part of a uniform from an army that is not ours", and that among the remains were identification cards and uniforms from other countries.

He posted pictures showing the ID card of a GSF member and a corresponding national ID card from Chad in Africa.

Bukele's comments poured skepticism on an earlier report in the New York Times, citing people close to the Salvadoran mission, that the bodies found on the outskirts of the Haitian capital, Port-au-Prince, on Saturday were thought to belong to the missing men.

The newspaper reported that the bodies delivered to the military contingent had been badly burned, meaning a medical examination would be required to identify them.

It cited one unnamed source briefed on the situation as saying the ID posted by Bukele in fact belonged to a soldier who had lost it when he had been injured.

Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of its president in 2021.

The multinational force dispatched to quell the violence and push back the armed gangs has struggled to penetrate areas where they hold sway.

More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September this year, the UN said at the start of October.

Bukele said the four GSF members had primarily been there to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".

When they were abducted, helicopters were deployed and multiple attempts were made to reach the location, but these efforts were hampered by fighting in the area, the Salvadoran armed forces said.

World.title: Does Nigeria truly have over 103 million voters?, By Chidi Anselm Odinkalu
World.content:
Ahead of Nigeria’s general elections in January and February 2027, Africa Confidential warns that “turnout in the elections is likely to be even lower than the average 26.7% four years ago. Nigerian voters are among the least enthusiastic in the world…. Out of more than 93.4 million registered voters, 24.9 million total votes were cast. This represented an 8.03-point decline from the 2019 elections and was the lowest voter turnout since Nigeria’s return to civilian rule in 1999.”

Complaints about “voter apathy” are the staple of Nigeria’s electoral commentariat. The numbers and patterns seem to bear this out. In 1999, turnout was 52.3 per cent. Officially, it grew to 69 per cent in 2003; and has fallen since then to 57.5 per cent in 2007; 53.7 per cent in 2011; 43.7 per cent in 2015; and 34.8 per cent in 2019, before cratering to 26.7 per cent in 2023.

These claims require us to accord credibility to the underlying numbers from the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). That begins with belief in the baseline of INEC’s electoral register against which turnout is judged. If that register is flawed, then all calculations hinged on it also suffer.

Yet, the foundational affliction underlying of Nigeria’s elections is not in INEC’s numbers. Rather, it is an absence of credible demographic management system against which to verify INEC’s claims.

The National Population Commission (NPoPC) claims 53 per cent of births in the country are registered and only 10 per cent of deaths are. The implications of this for the credibility of the electoral register should worry everyone.

To be sure, electoral rolls are ambulatory. People are not static: we move; relocate, and die too. This is why a demographic management system is essential. In Nigeria, this does not exist.

A register of voters does not automatically change because a person whose name is on it has died. But a person should also not be on the register one decade after their death. In Nigeria, there is no way of stopping this.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

These define the many curiosities about Nigeria’s voting numbers. First, they bear no rational relationship to wider demographic trends. Nigeria’s pattern of supposedly precipitous collapse in voter turnout, for instance, is inversely proportional to both baseline population and civic gripe.

In 1999, Nigeria’s population was estimated to be 115,766,000. Nigeria’s current population is estimated at 244 million. That means the country has more than doubled its population since 1999 by 128,234,000 or 110.77 per cent.

Over the same period, the voting roll has grown by 81.4 per cent, even as life expectancy in the intervening quarter century has increased by about nine years. If life expectancy is growing with the population and crude death rates falling, then the rate of growth in the voting population should ordinarily outstrip the underlying population growth rate.

In 20 years from 1999 to 2023, Nigeria’s population rose by about 87 per cent but the register of voters grew by 36,530,063 or 63.05 per cent. The mis-match between the two trendlines is significant.

In 1999, Nigeria had 57.94 million registered voters. This rose by 2.88 million or 4.97 per cent to 60.82 million in 2003 and then by a mere three-quarters of a million or 1.23 per cent to 61.57 million in 2007. By 2011, the number of registered voters climbed by over 12 million (20.5 per cent) to 73.53 million, representing an average yearly growth rate of nearly 5.12 per cent, where previously it had grown by 1.24 per cent in 1999-2003 and 0.3 per cent between 2003 and 2007.

By 2015, the population of registered voters fell to 68.83 million, a deficit of 4.7 million voters or 6.39 per cent, representing an annualised rate of reversal of 1.6 per cent. Yet, over the same period, Nigeria, a country with a median age of just under 18 years, had grown in population from an estimated 162.9 million to 181.2 million, an increase of 15.174 million or 11.23 per cent, representing an annual growth rate of 2.8 per cent.

The patterns from these numbers do not lend themselves to easy explanations. It is possible to speculate about what may explain this significant delta in growth between the general population and register of voters. Rational factors such as migration; agency dysfunctions in INEC; civic inertia or disaffection; or high transaction costs may be relevant. But there remain worrying patterns that are not easily accounted for even by all these.

As the Justice Uwais presidential committee on electoral reform pointed out in its 2008 report, much of what passed for electoral numbers in Nigeria before 2011 was voodoo. Just to illustrate this point, the INEC does not have a breakdown of official results for the 2007 presidential elections yet there are turnout figures for that election.

This leads to a second issue: Nigeria’s register of voters has always had invalid voters. The current register of voters in Nigeria dates back to November 2010 when the Attahiru Jega-led INEC set about establishing a credible register of voters for the country. The Commission had limited time to authenticate the raw data before the 2011 general election.

When the Automatic Fingerprint Identification System (AFIS) finished its work on the 2011 register nearly four years later, INEC invalidated 4.7 million entries, which reduced the number of registered voters from 73.53 in 2011 to 68.83 in 2015 but not before these invalid 4.7 million were eligible to vote in 2011.

Third, the biggest problem may be dead voters. That’s an oxymoron because the dead should not vote. In 2022, INEC explained that it could not expunge the dead from the register because “the country does not have reliable data of births and deaths and the commission cannot engage in arbitrary removal of the names of individuals it suspects are deceased.”

This has not changed. It means we have no way of knowing how many ghosts there are among the 103.4 million on INEC’s current register. By failing to display the register as required by law, the Commission does not even care to disabuse suspicions that its register may be bloated. Its response to non-compliance is institutional insouciance.

Nigeria’s register of voters is the classic Hotel California: it is “programmed to receive” and, for anyone with their name on it, “you can check out any time you like but you can never leave.” The implications of this for electoral integrity are staggering.

An illustrative exercise may help. Nigerian law allows adults alone to vote. The World Bank estimates the country’s crude mortality rate at 11.64 per 1000. Applied to a baseline from 2011, that is about 34,748,845 dead in 15 years.

But not all these will be adults. Mortality rate for under-5s is 117 per 1000 live births. That’s 700,000 to 855,000 under-five child deaths yearly. To 2025, that could be about 12 million dead under-fives since 2011.

The country also reported an estimated median of 111,425 deaths among 5–14-year-olds from 1990 to 2016. Applied again to a 2011 baseline, that’s another 1,671,375. In total, there could be up to 13.67 million infants, children, and adolescent deaths since 2011.

Adjusting the crude death rates for mortality among infants, children, and adolescents, there could be about 18-20 million people liable to be lanced from the electoral register since 2011. Applying the same methodology to a baseline of the 2023 register, that could be up to five million dead people alone on the register since the last election.

In its latest announcement, however, INEC said it captured a total of 10,772,421 new voters. It has not accounted for deaths or natural attrition.

Separately, at the end of 2025, the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre, (IDMC) reported that Nigeria had at least 3.7 million in internal displacement. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees adds up to 478,000 Nigerian refugees outside the country. Admittedly not all of these are adults of voting age.

Almost assuredly, INEC’s 103.4 million voters is corpulent. When you look at the numbers on INEC’s register and account for the fact that the baseline data goes back to 2011, there is a reasonable likelihood that up to about 25 per cent on it could be dead or dud. That should put all the talk about voter apathy in perspective. But this story has a uniquely Nigerian sting: our diaspora on earth may not have a vote, but we may have a diaspora in Heaven with a veto.

Chidi Anselm Odinkalu, a lawyer, teaches at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy and can be reached through [email protected].

World.title: The odds against Tinubu, By Wole Olaoye
World.content:
…If major opposition figures (Obi, Atiku, Kwankwaso, Adebayo, or a broader coalition platform) successfully present a single consolidated ticket, they would have aggregated core voting blocs across the South-East, South-South, urban centres, and northern strongholds, creating a direct head-to-head race with a real possibility of an opposition victory or, at worst, triggering Nigeria’s first-ever presidential run-off.

Candidate Bola Ahmed Tinubu is formidable enough without the presidential halo. Now, with all presidential powers at his command, he has to be considered a frontrunner in the forthcoming elections. But there are headwinds signalling the fact that although he is redoubtable, he is not unbeatable.

The problem with many of his opponents over the years is that they took him for granted. Part of that mindset is demonstrated when the opposition relies on rehashed stories of Tinubu’s failings to sway the electorate, instead of presenting alternative programmes to some of his manifestly unpopular policies.

Dream Ticket

The way things stand at the moment, none of the other presidential candidates has enough gravitas to unseat Tinubu. The ruling APC is the only party that has unveiled its campaign structure and rolled out its vote-catching machine. All the opposition parties have barely 83 days to overtake the current order.

Where the game will begin to appear interesting is if, as I argue later in this piece, Atiku Abubakar of the ADC and Peter Obi of the NDC team up to present what Anti-Tinubu elements have described as a dream ticket.

In 2023, the opposition vote was split among the PDP, Labour Party (LP), and NNPP. A unified ticket between Obi and Atiku could pool their substantial voting bases — bringing together Obi’s strong momentum in the South-East, South-South, and urban youth demographics alongside Atiku’s established political machinery and influence across parts of the North.

Under the Nigerian Constitution, a winning candidate must secure a plurality of votes and at least 25 per cent of the votes in two-thirds of the states (24 out of 36) plus the Federal Capital Territory. A dispassionate assessment of the current state of affairs shows that neither Obi nor Atiku can singlehandedly attain this threshold.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The most significant hurdle in any merger would be deciding who takes the presidential slot. If Atiku heads the ticket, it might alienate Obi’s supporters in the South-East and many reform-minded voters who view Obi as a symbol of structural political change. If Obi heads the ticket, it could face friction from impatient traditional northern political elites who can’t wait for power to return to the North.

The accepted wisdom in political circles is that 80-year-old Atiku cannot conceivably accept being vice president to Obi, while Kwankwaso will rue being left out in the cold in the event of an Atiku/Obi ticket. It’s all about self-interest. Until the elections come and go, you cannot vouch for where some of the major players will eventually cast their lot.

The looming ghost of tribal/geopolitical manoeuvres cannot be discountenanced in the calculus. If the wishes of many northern opposition elements were horses, Peter Obi will subordinate his ambition to Atiku and agree to play second fiddle. As already stated, an alliance of the two leaders would fundamentally reshape the political landscape, presenting a formidable challenge to President Tinubu and the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC).

The recent gathering of anti-Tinubu elements in the G-100 is a significant development. The coalition has tried to bypass direct ego clashes by setting up joint legal and media committees to manage expectations, but individual loyalists often pressure their preferred principals not to compromise.

Local Firefights

While national opposition leaders negotiate a mega-coalition in Abuja, local state chapters operate under entirely different survival tensions. In many states, opposition parties (such as factions of the PDP, SDP, and ADC) are fierce rivals at the local level. If a national coalition mandates that a specific party yield its structure in a particular state to accommodate another coalition partner, local party executives often rebel, leading to localised anti-coalition friction or secret parallel alignments.

An example of how local politics and personal ambition affect loyalty can be seen in the case of the former deputy senate president, Ovie Omo-Agege, who defected to the National Democratic Congress (NDC) after he officially quit the All Progressives Congress (APC) in May. Internal friction and ticket rivalries within the APC played a central role in his defection to NDC, whose flag he will be flying in the race for the Delta Central Senatorial District in 2027.

The looming ghost of tribal/geopolitical manoeuvres cannot be discountenanced in the calculus. If the wishes of many northern opposition elements were horses, Peter Obi will subordinate his ambition to Atiku and agree to play second fiddle. As already stated, an alliance of the two leaders would fundamentally reshape the political landscape, presenting a formidable challenge to President Tinubu and the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC).

But diehard Obi supporters will not be receptive to their hero reverting to the role of a spare tyre. Obi is the most credible face of the South-East in the current electoral race. The South-West has multiple notable aspirants, including President Bola Tinubu, Prince Adewole Adebayo and Governor Seyi Makinde, while the North-East features figures such as Atiku Abubakar and Mohammed Hayatuddeen. The South-South has Rotimi Amaechi. The North-Central and North-West regions are yet to produce strong frontline contenders.

Perhaps the three regions in the North are strategically avoiding multiple aspirants to prevent vote splitting?

Northern Wind

There are other strategic machinations in the mix. If you have your ears to the ground, you will hear the whispering campaign in the North of a plan to encourage political attrition between the South-West and South-East, so that while the Yoruba and Igbo Turks of the South are at each other’s throats, the Northern elite can perfect their plan of installing one of their own in power.

It sounds so childishly pedestrian at first until you re-analyse the verbal effusions of one of the perennial appointees whose definition of the ‘North’ is “I, Me and Myself”.

…If the election were contested under the existing multi-candidate dynamic (APC, PDP, LP, NNPP), despite economic headwinds, President Tinubu and the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) can secure a national plurality, even with a reduced vote share, dependent on state spread requirements.

The Northern Elders’ Forum and other such bodies who could have led the way in campaigning for their elected governors to banish the almajiri system (which hides under the cloak of religion to legitimise destitution), and other social drawbacks in the region are suddenly awake in this season of political horse-trading. Their critics are asking where they were when Buhari was running for a second term after his uneventful first leg.

There will always be jostling for elbow room between various ethnic nationalities, but I think the Yoruba and Igbo wouldn’t be foolish enough to swallow the bait of seasoned provocateurs determined to drive a wedge between them. Elections will come and go. People will remain.

The same admonition goes to the fake reprisalists in the north, who are always ready to justify ethnic cleansing and forceful takeover of other people’s ancestral lands in the name of revenging some ancient indeterminate wrongs done by the routed victims. In this season of electioneering, we are seeing how some people are digging up their demons from infernal depths in the name of political strategy.

Difficult as it may seem, the opposition should either come together to put their best combination forward or be prepared to lick their wounds as disparate vanquished wannabes.

Outcome

There are two possible outcomes:

(a) If the election were contested under the existing multi-candidate dynamic (APC, PDP, LP, NNPP), despite economic headwinds, President Tinubu and the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) can secure a national plurality, even with a reduced vote share, dependent on state spread requirements.

(b) If major opposition figures (Obi, Atiku, Kwankwaso, Adebayo, or a broader coalition platform) successfully present a single consolidated ticket, they would have aggregated core voting blocs across the South-East, South-South, urban centres, and northern strongholds, creating a direct head-to-head race with a real possibility of an opposition victory or, at worst, triggering Nigeria’s first-ever presidential run-off.

Wole Olaoye is a Public Relations consultant and veteran journalist. He can be reached on [email protected], Twitter: @wole_olaoye; Instagram: woleola2021

World.title: Ebola: Day pandemic killed an Aláàfin, By Festus Adedayo
World.content:
Nigeria is treating the reported Ebola case discovered in Abuja with its usual levity. Authorities should remember that if you fail to cut the sapling of an Iroko tree while it is young and allow it to grow rotund in size, it will someday demand unbearable ẹbọ (spiritual sacrifices) in its adulthood. Since 20 October, when a 42-year-old Ugandan, confirmed to be the wife of a Swiss diplomat living in the Federal Capital Territory, tested positive for the dreaded disease, Nigeria has literally been carelessly caressing the nozzle of a loaded rifle and holding the head of a deadly rattlesnake with tentative hands.

Our forefathers warned against this posture of dangerous complacency. In both the careless handling of firearms and the timid caressing of venomous reptiles, they frowned at such folly in two graphic proverbs, warning that: “A kì í fi ọwọ tẹtẹrẹ mú ìbọn; a kì í fi ọwọ rọrọ mú ejo” – you do not handle a gun carelessly, nor do you grasp a snake with soft, hesitant hands.

History provides a stern warning about what happens when public health complacency meets administrative lethargy. Between 1827 and 1831, in Ọyọ-Ilé, the majestic capital of the Old Oyo Empire, the people tried to ignore the subtle signs of danger. But as the Yoruba say, bullets eventually escaped, the gun boomed, and the snake’s bite led to documented catastrophe.

A strange, debilitating disease called Pẹhẹ had suddenly sprouted from nowhere. It was an infectious, highly contagious disease that waged a deadly, relentless war on the human respiratory system. Pẹhẹ ravaged the capital of the Empire, a tragic chapter meticulously recorded by the legendary historian Samuel Johnson on page 254 of his monumental work, History of the Yoruba.

Because it is only the beginning of a war that human beings can anticipate and never its ultimate ending, by 1831, Pẹhẹ had mutated from a localized health scare into an uncontrollable pestilence. In that fatal year, it breached the sacred palace walls and took away the highly revered supreme monarch of the Empire, Aláàfin Májòótú. When Májòótú succumbed to the breath-stealing plague, Aláàfin Amodo ascended a throne already sitting atop a crumbling nation.

The tragic death of Aláàfin Májòótú’s in the hands of an ordinary pandemic stands as an eternal reminder that not even the most sacred grove or exalted royal court is spared when pestilence wages war. Plagues are fiercely democratic; they respect neither crown nor stool.

This tragic historical truth brings to mind one of my favorite musical lines by Kelani Yesufu, the legendary Egba-born Yoruba Sakara music singer and social poet. It was in a masterwork track that the bard titled “Ikú ò Mo Olówó”. It is a profound philosophical treatise asserting that death is no respecter of wealth, crown, or social status.

Yesufu composed the track as a grieving tribute to Shittu Shitta Alabi, his master lead drummer, who suddenly slumped and died on stage at Sokenu Village, Abeokuta, during a live performance in 1972. In a haunting symbol of lifelong devotion to craft, Alabi passed into eternity with his Sakara drum still clutched tightly in his lifeless hands.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Kelani Yesufu’s musical prowess and cultural prominence reached its zenith during the mid-to-late 20th century. Standing tall alongside contemporaries like S. Aka (Sanusi Ayinde Aka, Baba Wahidi, a.k.a. Omo Lawale), the legendary Sakara genre lord Yusuff Olatunji, Haruna Ishola, and Lefty Salami, Yesufu combined traditional Yoruba instrumentation, specifically the solemn, melancholic goje violin and rhythmic Sakara hand drums, to attack public decay and social vices.

Kelani became renowned as an against-the-grain musician due to his unorthodox, cutting poetry. He deployed his storytelling craft in fighting well-known social crusades, manifested in tracks like “Emu Ògùrò” (where he mercilessly attacked reckless drunkenness) and “April Fool,” another of his sharp, satirical social commentaries.

Yesufu was the courageous bard who first dared to break the ancient cultural taboo surrounding venereal diseases with his famous track “Àtòsí” (Gonorrhea). Before Yesufu’s bold intervention, Yoruba society was conditioned to mask the disease under the deceptive, romanticised label Àrùn Gbajúmò — an infection reserved for notables and men of means. In his track, Yesufu urged society to face hard epidemiological facts, dismantling the hypocritical contradictions inherent in romanticising a disgraceful affliction simply because it affected the elite.

While lamenting the death of his master drummer in a grief-encrusted voice, Kelani sermonized on the absolute inevitability and impartiality of death. The track eventually became a sacred document frequently cited by cultural historians, a poignant testament to the profound, lifelong spiritual bond developed between traditional Yoruba vocalists and their lead drummers. It was that exact same symbiotic bond that existed between Yusuff Olatunji and his lead drummer, Kasumu Ishola Sanni; between Haruna Ishola and Raufu Ojubanire; between Lefty Salami and Nosiru Akanmu; and between the fiery Ayinla Omowura and Adewole Alao, famously known as Onílù Olà, the drummer of fortune. Plagues, like death itself, sever these human bonds without mercy.

In Ọyọ-Ilé, Pẹhẹ claimed the lives of thousands of citizens in rapid succession. The pestilence was reported to be the devastating climax of a four-year cycle of recurrent epidemic outbreaks in the empire’s capital. It provoked a historic visit to Ọyọ-Ilé in 1827 by the famous Cornish explorer, Richard Lander. Lander had arrived in the Empire’s capital riding on the fame of his association with solving the mystery of the course and outlet of the River Niger, alongside the Scottish explorer Hugh Clapperton. After Clapperton and other members of the expedition succumbed to tropical illnesses, Lander was commissioned by the British government to return, sailing with his brother from Badagry to Bussa by canoe, where they were eventually captured and ransomed.

When Lander arrived at Ọyọ-Ilé, he recorded his astonishment at the crude yet organised quarantine structures implemented by the empire’s authorities. The traditional council had taken victims of Pẹhẹ to an isolation centre, established inside a dense forest roughly half a mile outside the city walls. In his journal, Lander observed that the sick were placed systematically “underneath the branches of trees…”

The strict customary law of the empire dictated that the next of kin of Pẹhẹ victims were solely responsible for bringing food and water to the perimeter of the forest isolation grounds.

However, this outbreak severely crippled the empire because it arrived alongside a devastating combination of external and internal crises. A brutal drought had covertly walked into Ọyọ-Ilé that same year. Consequently, the metropolis suffered the double agony of severe famine and political instability, which had commenced a decade earlier due to internal rivalries. The Pẹhẹ pandemic was like rubbing coarse salt into an open, bleeding wound. Historical descriptions of Pẹhẹ paint it as a highly contagious respiratory illness that caused swift, terrifying fatalities across all social strata. Aláàfin Májòótú and Ọyọ-Ilé’s ancient political structures were completely overwhelmed.

In his notes, Lander helped preserve the oral memory of this tragedy. He recorded that the combination of acute famine and political turmoil severely worsened the plight of those confined to the forest isolation center. Because the victims were largely drawn from poor backgrounds, many ended up dying of sheer starvation rather than the viral load of Pẹhẹ itself.

It was recorded that although Pẹhẹ directly killed thousands in 1831, Ọyọ-Ilé was already suffocating from the loss of more than 100,000 of its inhabitants to famine, civil strife, and disease combined. This massive health disaster shattered Old Oyo’s demographic foundation and completely paralysed its military leadership. It dramatically accelerated the empire’s fall to Fulani invasions and internal rebellions, culminating in the total evacuation and permanent abandonment of Ọyọ-Ilé as the capital between 1835 and 1836. Plagues do not merely kill bodies; if mishandled, they topple empires.

If pre-colonial Nigeria was naive in curtailing the spread of infectious pathogens, centuries later, it is outright criminal for modern authorities to follow suit. Long before modern medicine, diseases like chickenpox and smallpox attacked the rich and the poor with equal, indiscriminate fury.

In response to their inability to comprehend or halt the ravages of smallpox, the ancient Yoruba deified the disease out of sheer terror. Smallpox was elevated to the pantheon of sacred deities as Ṣọnpọnná. Because of the mysterious way it struck from nowhere, the deity was given fearful, exalted appellations. One was Olóde, “The Owner of the Outside” or “Lord of the Open Space,” referencing how the contagion traveled invisibly through open air and wind; Ọbalúayé “The King Who is Lord of the World”; and Babalúayé “The Father Who is the Lord of the Earth.”

Till this day in ancient Ilé-Ifẹ, the annual Ìtàpá festival is celebrated to memorialise those ancient pox outbreaks. When you observe the intricate lesions of white chalk painted across the bodies of Ọbàtálá priests during the sacred festival, you are looking at a living artistic ritual depicting the skin pustules suffered by their ancestors.

Ṣọnpọnná priests were both deeply revered and terrifyingly feared as specialist medical practitioners. They presided over the containment of pox outbreaks, performing ritual sacrifices, administering botanical variolation (inoculation), caring for the afflicted, and executing strict, solitary burials for those killed by the disease to prevent further contamination.

Until its global eradication in the 20th century, no disease struck deeper dread into the Yoruba psyche than smallpox, owing to its high transmission rate, swift lethality, and unpredictable seasonality. The disease routinely peaked between January and February, the dry, dusty harmattan months, proving itself to be an opportunistic killer that exploited seasonal vulnerability.

Similarly, cholera has been an explosive, killer epidemic in Nigeria’s history. It struck water supplies and wiped out entire communities overnight. But no historical outbreak matched the terrifying speed of the 1918 Influenza Pandemic.

Originating in March 1918 in Kansas, USA, and carried across oceans by returning World War I troops, the “Spanish Flu” quickly earned the grim distinction of killing more people than any other pandemic in human history. It became the first truly nationwide pandemic to sweep through Nigeria, imported directly by maritime passengers and crew arriving at coastal ports.

Lagos was the epicentre of the tragedy. Public historian Oludamola Adebowale notes that passengers who contracted the virus in Accra, Gold Coast (modern Ghana), boarded ships bound for Lagos and seeded the contagion upon arrival. The spread was so violent that within the first two months, maritime quarantines completely collapsed. Lagos lost 1.5 per cent of its entire population of 81,941 people in a matter of weeks. Out of a national population estimated at 18 million in 1918, over 500,000 Nigerians died within six months, with between 50 per cent and 80 per cent of the entire population contracting the virus.

From Lagos, the flu followed trade routes like wildfire. In 1918 October, Abeokuta was to get its first index patient. Ibadan got its on October 5, 1918 and gradually, Oyo, Ilorin, Minna, Bida, Jebba, Zaria, Kano, and Bauchi got theirs. Calabar and Onitsha got theirs on October 14, 1918 while it was spread farther by ships through Forcados port to Warri and Asaba, Port Harcourt and Bonny. Traveling through passengers on River Niger, the Spanish flu pandemic spread to Lokoja, Sokoto, Maiduguri, as well as to other parts of the Northern Nigeria, so much that, by December 1918, the whole of the country had completely bowed to the Spanish flu.

Traveling via passengers along the River Niger, the Spanish flu penetrated Lokoja, Sokoto, and Maiduguri. By December 1918, the entire geographic entity of Nigeria had completely bowed to the devastating flu. With this mountain of historical tragedy, and our recent, painful experience during COVID-19, Nigeria’s current dilly-dallying on the reported Abuja Ebola case is utterly incomprehensible.

Ebola is not an abstract threat. Since its discovery in September 1976 along the Ebola River in Yambuku, (in the Democratic Republic of Congo, then Zaire) where it claimed its first victim, a local school headmaster named Mabalo Lokela, the virus has exhibited one of the highest case-fatality rates known to science. Historically, regional outbreaks in the DRC have claimed 4,690 lives out of 9,742 confirmed cases, representing a terrifying crude case fatality rate (CFR) of roughly 48 per cent.

Nigeria should know better because we have faced this monster before. In 2014, Nigeria admirably fought and won a decisive war against Ebola. When Patrick Sawyer, an index patient from Liberia, arrived at First Consultants Medical Centre in Lagos, the nation stood on the precipice of unimaginable catastrophe. It took the extraordinary courage of Dr Stella Ameyo Adadevoh, the timeless amazon who sacrificed her life so millions might live, alongside her medical director, Dr Benjamin Ohiaeri, and their heroic team, to halt the chain of transmission.

In a modern parallel to the strict isolation protocols of Ọyọ-Ilé two centuries prior, Dr Adadevoh and Dr Ohiaeri stood firm against intense diplomatic pressure from Liberian officials who demanded that Sawyer be discharged to attend an international conference in Calabar. Instead, they held him in a makeshift containment unit, locked down their hospital, and immediately alerted health authorities. Dr Adadevoh paid the ultimate price, contracting the virus and passing away on 19 August, 2014, alongside noble colleagues. But her brave stand kept Nigeria’s total casualty count to just 20 cases and eight deaths — a miraculous feat praised globally.

Look at how other nations manage this threat today. Consider Rwanda. Despite its proximity to the DRC and despite the busy border city of Gisenyi, sitting directly adjacent to DRC’s Lake Kivu region, Rwanda has consistently maintained zero recorded Ebola cases during major regional surges. This is not by luck; it is by design. The Rwandan Ministry of Health and the Rwanda Biomedical Center maintain active, continuous border screening, rigorous contact tracing protocols, and specialised containment facilities in sites like Rusizi, Rubavu, and Kigali. They understand that public health requires constant vigilance, not reactive panic.

Meanwhile, in Nigeria, when reports of a new Ebola threat surfaced, the government reacted with its typical bureaucratic fanfare: on 9 June, a ₦10 billion emergency intervention fund was approved, and a Presidential Task Force on Ebola Virus Disease Preparedness was constituted under the chairmanship of the Chief of Staff to the President. Months later, as reports of new cases trickle into the Federal Capital Territory, Nigerians are rightly asking: Where is the readiness? What tangible containment infrastructure has been built? How has the ₦10 billion emergency allocation been utilised?

We cannot afford to treat a deadly pathogen with administrative levity or political rhetoric. As our ancestors warned us through the sacred memory of Aláàfin Májòótú, when a government fails to cut the sapling of an epidemic early, it will eventually grow into an uncontainable beast that demands the ultimate sacrifice from the nation. Nigeria must wake up, stop caressing the nozzle of the rifle, put down the head of the rattlesnake, and act before history repeats its grim legacy once more.

Festus Adedayo is an Ibadan-based journalist.

World.title: Ebola: NCDC expands health declaration requirement for international travellers
World.content:
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has expanded its health declaration requirement for international travellers after confirming an Ebola case in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

The agency’s Director-General, Jide Idris, announced the decision during a media briefing in Abuja on Sunday.

Mr Idris said the requirement initially applied to international travellers but was later restricted to passengers arriving from selected countries linked to the Ebola outbreak, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda.

“But with this case, we have reversed that directive,” he said.

He said the NCDC had sent advisories to the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) and the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA), and expected further instructions to guide implementation in collaboration with airlines.

Airport screening

Mr Idris said Nigeria’s preparedness measures had focused on five international airports: Lagos, Abuja, Enugu, Kano and Port Harcourt.

He said Port Health Services was working with aviation personnel, immigration and customs officials to strengthen preparedness and screening at the country’s points of entry.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to Mr Idris, the NCDC needs to coordinate with aviation authorities because it does not independently control airport operations.

He said agencies were working together to implement the required measures, while immigration and customs officials were involved at land borders.

Mr Idris also acknowledged operational challenges at Lagos airport, where ongoing construction had created difficulties. He said the NCDC would engage FAAN and the NCAA to address issues affecting Port Health Services’ work.

He added that access to restricted airport areas must follow established security procedures.

Ebola response

The revised screening measures form part of Nigeria’s response to a confirmed case of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus in the FCT on 20 October.

As PREMIUM TIMES reported, the patient is a 42-year-old Ugandan woman who travelled to Nigeria from Uganda on 3 October. She developed symptoms on 6 October and sought medical attention before her infection was confirmed.

At Sunday’s briefing, Mr Idris said health authorities had identified 53 primary contacts linked to the patient. These comprise 44 people associated with the health facility where she received treatment and nine additional contacts, including household members. They attended to her at another facility and were members of the FCT team that collected samples.

He said contact tracing was ongoing and that officials were monitoring the identified contacts.

Health officials are following up with contacts for 21 days, the maximum incubation period for Ebola, to identify any symptoms that might indicate infection.

Mr Idris appealed to Nigerians identified as contacts to cooperate with public health officials, stressing that being identified as a contact does not mean a person has Ebola.

The NCDC is also strengthening infection prevention and control measures in healthcare facilities, supporting laboratory capacity and providing public health information to counter rumours and misinformation.

The agency urged Nigerians to rely on verified information from authorised public health sources and cooperate with response measures as investigations continue.

World.title: CBD COP17: Namibian Biosafety Expert Martha Kandawa-Schulz dies in Yerevan
World.content:
Martha Kandawa-Schulz, Namibia’s Cartagena Protocol National Focal Point, died in Yerevan, Armenia, while participating in the ongoing United Nations Biodiversity Conference (CBD COP17).

Ms Kandawa-Schulz, a professor, died on 23 October, according to a statement the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) Secretariat issued Sunday evening.

She was serving as Co-Chair of the Contact Group on Risk Assessment and Risk Management of Living Modified Organisms at the conference.

In a message to delegates, the Secretariat described her as a highly respected colleague whose dedication, expertise, and leadership contributed significantly to the Convention and its Protocols, as well as to the global biosafety community.

It said her commitment and collegiality had earned her the respect and appreciation of colleagues who had the privilege of working with her.

The Secretariat extended its condolences to her family, friends, colleagues, and the Government and people of Namibia.

It also expressed sympathy to the African Group and others mourning her death.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The Presidency and the Secretariat are working closely together to support her family and the Namibian delegation on site, and to facilitate the necessary arrangements,” the statement said.

The Secretariat also announced that a book of condolences would be available to delegates from 13:00 on Monday at Entrance 2, near the Asia-Pacific Room, for those wishing to pay their respects.

It urged delegates to honour Ms Kandawa-Schulz’s memory and recognise her contributions to the shared objectives of the Convention.

The circumstances surrounding her death were not stated, although reports indicate that she collapsed during her engagement in the working group meeting on Friday.

CBD COP17 is taking place in Yerevan, Armenia, bringing together governments and other stakeholders to deliberate on global biodiversity conservation and the implementation of the Convention and its associated protocols.

Government representatives, delegates, scientists, civil society representatives and researchers, among others, from nearly 196 countries are participating in the conference.

World.title: CBD COP17: Nigeria, six others each win $50,000 grant for biodiversity projects
World.content:
Nigeria and six other countries under the High Ambition Coalition (HAC) for Nature and People have won $50,000 seed grants each under the Rapid Deployment Mechanism (RDM) to execute projects aimed at accelerating progress towards their 30×30 conservation targets.

The grants were announced and awarded on the sidelines of the ongoing 17th session of the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17) in Armenia.

The beneficiary countries are Costa Rica, Mexico, Nigeria, Nepal, Zambia, Rwanda, and Kenya, each receiving a certificate confirming a $50,000 grant for its respective project.

Nigeria received the grant for its project proposal titled “Strengthening Nigeria’s 30×30 Progress through Ecological Connectivity, Terrestrial and Marine OECMs, and Protected Area Management Effectiveness”.

PREMIUM TIMES gathered that the project will be implemented by the Nigerian Conservation Foundation (NCF).

Costa Rica’s project, titled “From 30×30 Coverage to Effective Conservation: Developing an Acceptable Visitation Load Tool for Cocos Island National Park”, seeks to improve conservation management at the national park.

Mexico received the grant for its project, “Strengthening Mexico’s Marine 30×30 through Underwater Acoustic Baselines and Evidence-Based Protected Area Management”.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Nepal’s project, “Operationalising Nepal’s National OECM Guideline: Recognising New OECMs to Advance the 30×30 Target”, focuses on recognising other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs) to advance its conservation target.

Zambia’s project is titled “Strengthening Zambia’s 30×30 Progress through the Busanga Swamps Wetland Inventory and Management Effectiveness Assessment”.

Rwanda’s project, “Advancing Rwanda’s 30×30 Commitments through Community-Based Terrestrial OECMs and Ecological Connectivity”, seeks to strengthen community-based conservation and ecological connectivity.

Kenya’s project, “Advancing Kenya’s Marine 30×30 through Community-Led OECMs, Indigenous and Local Knowledge, and Effective Marine Protected Area Management”, focuses on marine conservation.

Nigeria receives award

Nigeria’s award was presented to Sikeade Egbuwalo, the country’s focal point to the Convention on Biological Diversity.

Representatives of the other beneficiary countries also took turns receiving their awards, except Kenya, whose representative was unavoidably absent.

In her remarks, Mrs Egbuwalo appreciated the HAC secretariat and the RDM for the recognition and support.

“This support will not only help us to achieve the 30×30 targets but also help us to address the issue of fragmented habitat, which has been a big issue in Nigeria,” she said.

The RDM is an initiative of the HAC for Nature and People designed to address funding gaps by providing small-scale financing to catalyse broader conservation impacts.

“By providing fast, flexible seed grants, the RDM bridges the gap between early-stage requirements and larger funding sources, helping countries accelerate actions to achieve their 30×30 goals,” the organisers said.

During the gala, some recipients of the 2025 RDM grants shared their experiences and highlighted the funding’s importance to biodiversity conservation efforts in their respective countries.

In his closing remarks, Labaran Ahmed, Nigeria’s Chief Scientific Officer at the Federal Department of Forestry and HAC for Nature and People Co-Chair, expressed the Nigerian government’s appreciation to the HAC secretariat for its deliberations.

“We look forward to seeing your projects move forward and contribute to your country’s effort to achieve the 30×30 targets,” he said.

Significance

In his reaction to the award, Director-General of the Nigerian Conservation Foundation (NCF), Joseph Onoja, said the award represents a significant milestone in Nigeria’s conservation journey and reinforces NCF’s leadership in advancing biodiversity conservation, ecological connectivity, and sustainable natural resource management.

“Working in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Environment, NCF will provide scientific and technical support to the Federal Government of Nigeria in advancing the country’s commitment to the global 30×30 target of conserving at least 30% of land and sea by 2030,” he said.

Mr Onoja explained that the project will identify, map, and profile priority terrestrial and marine Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures (OECMs); assess protected area management effectiveness; and develop a national Management Effectiveness Framework.

These interventions, he said, will generate critical evidence and recommendations to strengthen Nigeria’s protected and conserved area network, improve conservation governance, and support the implementation of Target 3 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

He said the award underscores the importance of strategic partnerships between government and conservation organisations in translating global biodiversity commitments into measurable national outcomes.

“NCF remains committed to working closely with the Federal Ministry of Environment, relevant government agencies, research institutions, conservation partners, and local communities to strengthen ecological connectivity, improve protected area management, and advance Nigeria’s 30×30 ambition,” he said.

Mr Onoja said the initiative represents an important investment in Nigeria’s ecological future, safeguarding biodiversity, strengthening ecosystem resilience, and ensuring that nature continues to support the wellbeing and livelihoods of present and future generations.

World.title: Uneven petrol prices, lingering hardship as Zaria residents question NNPC discount
World.content:
Residents of Zaria Local Government Area in Kaduna State have expressed dissatisfaction with the impact of the federal government’s petrol price reduction at Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) retail stations, saying the intervention has done little to ease the rising cost of living.

In interviews with PREMIUM TIMES Hausa, commercial drivers, motorcycle and tricycle operators, traders and other residents said the reduction had yet to translate into meaningful relief for households and businesses struggling with high transportation costs, expensive food items and declining purchasing power.

While some residents acknowledged the reduction in petrol prices, others complained that the price difference was too small to affect their daily expenses significantly.

Some also questioned whether the relief was being implemented uniformly across filling stations.

The complaints highlight the challenges of translating a temporary reduction in fuel costs into broader economic relief, particularly for low-income households and small businesses that depend heavily on petrol-powered transportation and generators.

Commercial drivers say the relief is yet to reach them

For commercial drivers, who spend a significant portion of their daily earnings on petrol, even a modest price reduction can make a difference.

However, Danlami Garba-Dan Kabo, a commercial driver in Zaria, said he has yet to see any meaningful benefit despite buying petrol at an NNPC station in Dakatsalle.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Garba-Dan Kabo said he preferred buying fuel from privately owned filling stations because he saw little difference between their prices and those offered at NNPC outlets.

“The price reduction is supposed to help the poor, but we are yet to benefit from this relief, especially those of us who are drivers,” he said.

He explained that the high cost of petrol had made it increasingly difficult for commercial drivers to earn enough to support their families.

According to him, some drivers could go two or three days without working because they could not afford to operate their vehicles.

“Some drivers have two or three wives and children to cater for, yet they spend two to three days without work because of the high cost of petrol in the country,” he said.

Motorcycle and tricycle operators seek further cuts

Commercial motorcycle and tricycle operators also said petrol prices remained a major burden on their businesses.

Idris, a commercial motorcycle rider in Zaria, called on the government to further reduce petrol prices, arguing that the existing reduction had not provided enough relief for operators who depend on daily earnings to sustain themselves and their families.

Sanin Mallan, a commercial tricycle operator popularly known as a Keke NAPEP rider, said he regularly bought petrol from NNPC stations because he considered the fuel good quality.

However, he said the price remained high and appealed to the government to introduce further reductions.

Transport operators’ accounts show how fuel prices affect not only petrol buyers but also commuters who depend on commercial vehicles to travel to work, schools, and markets.

Traders say high fuel costs are squeezing household budgets

Beyond the transport sector, traders in Zaria said the high cost of living had weakened consumer demand, making it increasingly difficult for businesses to sell their goods.

Alhaji Dahiru, a retailer at Sabon Kasuwa market, said high petrol prices contributed to rising commodity prices and reduced his customers’ purchasing power.

He illustrated the pressure by comparing parboiled rice prices over the past five years.

According to him, a tier of parboiled rice that sold for between ₦450 and ₦500 about five years ago later rose to ₦7,500 before dropping to ₦3,500.

He said the price had recently increased again to ₦4,500 per tier, while local rice sold for between ₦3,800 and ₦4,000 per tier.

Mr Dahiru said the high cost of essential commodities had left many customers unable to buy food in the quantities they could previously afford.

He added that on some days, he spent more than 24 hours in his shop without selling a single bag of parboiled rice.

His account reflects the wider pressure facing small retailers when customers cut back on purchases because their incomes cannot keep pace with the prices of essential goods.

Some residents welcome the reduction, but want more

Not all residents were dissatisfied with the petrol price reduction.

Hamisu Sani, chairman of a cooperative car wash in Zaria, welcomed the reduction, saying petrol prices at NNPC stations had fallen from ₦1,423 to ₦1,379 per litre.

He expressed hope that the government would sustain policies that improve the economic conditions of low-income earners.

However, Suleman Abba-GT, a mobile phone dealer at PZ in Zaria, said the reduction had not brought the relief many Nigerians needed.

He argued that a meaningful reduction should substantially lower the amount consumers spend on petrol.

“The reduction in petrol prices should be significant enough to make a real difference. For instance, if it costs ₦50,000 to fill your tank, the cost should be reduced to at least ₦40,000 or ₦30,000,” he said.

His position reflects the expectations of consumers who believe a modest reduction in fuel prices may not offset the cumulative increases in transportation, food, and other household expenses.

Varying prices at filling stations

To examine the implementation of the price reduction, we visited several NNPC and privately owned filling stations in Zaria to check petrol availability and compare prices.

The visits revealed varying pump prices across the stations inspected, raising questions about how far the reduction had been implemented at the time of the visits.

At the former NNPC station at Danmagaji Market, now operated by Eterna, petrol sold for ₦1,410 per litre. Customers, including commercial drivers, tricycle operators, and motorcycle riders, bought fuel there. Some said they considered the petrol good quality.

At Shafa Filling Station near the Kwangila flyover, a staff member, who requested anonymity, said petrol sold for ₦1,430 per litre. He said customers frequently complained about the price and hoped it would be reduced.

At the NNPC station in Randan Kano, Zaria, petrol sold for ₦1,379 per litre. A staff member at the station said he was unaware of the government’s price-reduction arrangement and could not confirm whether the station was selling fuel under the new terms.

At the NNPC station in Silver, Samaru, petrol sold for ₦1,414 per litre.

A staff member there, who also spoke on condition of anonymity, said he knew about the price-reduction initiative but claimed it had not been fully implemented at the station.

“Some time ago, some people came to the station, took photographs and conducted inspections intending to implement the reduced petrol price. However, the reduction has yet to be implemented at this station,” he said.

However, Samuel Omata, manager of the NNPC station in PZ, Zaria, said his station had implemented the reduced price since 8 October.

Mr Omata explained that customers could access the discount by downloading an application developed by NNPC and transferring money from their bank accounts into its wallet to pay for petrol.

According to him, customers received a discount of ₦66 per litre, which increased with the quantity of petrol purchased.

The differences in prices recorded at the stations visited, along with the varying accounts of implementation, suggest consumers may not have experienced the same level of relief across the outlets inspected.

However, the visits capture prices at the time of reporting and, on their own, do not establish the extent of nationwide compliance with the policy.

Why the federal government introduced the reduction

The petrol price intervention followed a federal government announcement that NNPC Retail would forgo its retail profit margin and sell petrol at cost for 30 days to cushion Nigerians against rising international crude oil and refined petroleum product prices.

PREMIUM TIMES previously reported that Bayo Onanuga, spokesperson to President Bola Tinubu, announced the arrangement, which was backed by the president.

Under the arrangement, NNPC Retail was expected to sell petrol at its landing cost rather than add its usual retail profit margin. For example, if the landing cost were ₦1,300 per litre, the company would sell the product at that price under the stated arrangement.

The Presidency said the intervention was among measures announced by the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, to mitigate the effects of rising international oil prices on Nigerians, particularly vulnerable households.

The policy was intended to provide temporary relief by reducing the amount consumers paid for petrol at participating NNPC outlets.

However, residents in Zaria point to the limits of a temporary fuel-price intervention when household incomes remain under pressure and food and other essential goods remain expensive.

Residents want relief that reaches households

The residents interviewed said they wanted further reductions in petrol prices and more consistent implementation across filling stations.

Their accounts also point to a broader concern: reducing the pump price of petrol does not automatically translate into lower food prices, cheaper transport fares, or improved household purchasing power.

For residents already struggling to meet basic needs, the intervention’s impact will ultimately depend on the size and duration of the savings, how consistently the policy is implemented, and whether lower fuel costs translate into reduced expenses elsewhere in the economy.

In Zaria, many interviewees said the reduction had yet to make a substantial difference in their daily lives.

World.title: Ebola: NCDC urges hospitals to act before laboratory confirmation
World.content:
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has urged public and private healthcare facilities nationwide to strengthen infection prevention measures and isolate suspected Ebola cases before laboratory results are available.

The NCDC Director-General, Jide Idris, issued the directive during a media briefing in Abuja on Sunday, stressing that healthcare workers must promptly identify and report suspected cases without waiting for laboratory confirmation.

The call comes five days after Nigeria confirmed its first Ebola case in more than a decade, involving a 42-year-old Ugandan-born woman living in Abuja who recently travelled to Uganda.

Officials confirmed her infection on 20 October, prompting the federal government to activate a coordinated public health response.

‘Strengthen infection control’
