Speaking further on the response, Mr Idris called on leaders of all public and private healthcare facilities in Nigeria to review and strengthen infection prevention and control measures.

He said hospitals must consistently implement screening and triage procedures, ensure appropriate personal protective equipment is available, and train healthcare workers to use it correctly.

“Any suspected case must be promptly separated from other patients and reported to the relevant public health authorities,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Healthcare workers should not wait for laboratory confirmation before taking appropriate precautions.”

Mr Idris also emphasised the importance of standard precautions, including regular hand hygiene, environmental cleaning, injection safety, safe handling of sharps and proper waste management.

Mr Idris said the NCDC was working with FCT health authorities to strengthen screening, triage, isolation readiness and healthcare worker protection.

The agency was also assessing priority facilities and deploying trained infection prevention and control professionals to provide practical guidance and mentorship.

Strengthened response

The directive comes as health authorities continue investigating the circumstances surrounding the confirmed infection and work to prevent further transmission.

PREMIUM TIMES previously reported that the woman developed symptoms on 6 October, three days after returning to Nigeria, and initially sought treatment at a private hospital, believing she had malaria.

She later visited another private hospital, where she was admitted on 11 October after her condition failed to improve. Her infection was subsequently confirmed through laboratory testing.

Explaining how the case was detected, Mr Idris said healthcare workers attending to the patient recognised clinical features that raised concern. Their vigilance contributed to an alert being captured through the NCDC’s event-based surveillance system.

He said the development demonstrated the importance of surveillance systems and the role of healthcare workers in identifying unusual health events that require investigation.

According to him, the national response involves the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, the NCDC, FCT health authorities, other relevant government agencies and technical partners.

He said the response is being coordinated through a structured Incident Management System and the Emergency Operations Centre, under the national leadership of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare and the Presidential Task Force on Ebola virus disease.

‘Healthcare workers are central to containment efforts’

Mr Idris commended healthcare workers whose clinical judgement and vigilance helped identify the case, saying their role was critical in triggering the public health response.

He said the government was drawing on experienced clinicians and case managers, including professionals who participated in Nigeria’s previous Ebola response, to support clinical management and infection prevention efforts.

The NCDC is also maintaining heightened surveillance and strengthening laboratory capacity to ensure that suspected cases can be promptly investigated and tested.

Mr Idris said the response would prioritise the safety, health and welfare of healthcare workers, adding that the government would continue to review its plans as new information became available.

He said the immediate priorities remained protecting healthcare workers, providing appropriate clinical care and preventing transmission into the wider community.

World.title: Brazil’s Lula clinches victory over Flavio Bolsonaro to win fourth term
World.content:
Brazil President Lula

Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday as he clinched election victory against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who trounced him in the first round.

The leftist icon, who turns 81 on Tuesday, defied all projections to win an unprecedented fourth term at the helm of Latin America’s largest country.

According to official results, he won 51.75 percentof the votes to 48.25 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who had entered election day confident with his lead in the polls.

With Lula’s victory, Brazil staved off a conservative wave that has seen numerous countries — such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru — all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump.

After a campaign marred by scandal and mud-slinging, Sunday’s vote plunged into chaos after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extending voting by two hours, at the request of Lula who said buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.

Supporters of Brazil’s President and Workers’ Party (PT) re-election candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva react to the presidential runoff election results in the state of Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 25, 2026. Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on October 25, 2026, as he clinched election victory against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who trounced him in the first round. (Photo by NELSON ALMEIDA / AFP)

Flavio Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some parts of the country due to heavy rains, but his camp lashed out at the country-wide extension.

“Either we win. Or we win. Consider yourself warned,” pro-Bolsonaro lawmaker Nikolas Ferreira wrote on X as the votes streamed in.

The bitter campaign laid bare the deep divisions in the country of over 200 million people.

“It’s a disgrace. We’ve never had anything like this in Brazil, and now they’ve come up with the idea of extending the election period by two hours,” said Aurelio Junior, 45, a dentist in Brasilia.

Jacqueline Maria Lima de Franca, 34, a business owner in Rio de Janeiro backing Lula said it was “more than fair…everyone should have the right to vote, and that was being neglected.”

– Lula rises from the ashes, again –

Lula, a defining figure in Brazilian politics over four decades, was blindsided after his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro.

The left swung into action with massive rallies declaring “Never Again Bolsonaro,” where protesters recalled the former president’s chaotic handling of the Covid pandemic, devastation of the Amazon rainforest and cuts to public programs.

Lula also revamped his social media strategy, taking video selfies and even bought his first cellphone, while supporters carried out a feverish campaign to change the minds of family, friends and neighbors, and encourage them to vote after high levels of abstention.

His re-election marks another remarkable comeback for the man who grew up dirt poor in the northeast in a family of illiterate farmers.

Lula, revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months.

The charges, annulled on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him.

In his third term he has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but voters complain about the cost of living and a sense of insecurity.

Lula’s social policies became a point of tension as he expanded welfare programs during the campaign.

“Brazil needs more time with Lula, primarily because the country is on the verge of falling into the clutches of fascism,” Maria Fernanda Elisbao, a 21-year-old editorial assistant, told AFP.

– A tricky term ahead –

Lula heads into a fourth term with a country divided, with almost half of the nation voting against him and desperate for change.

“We’re in a deep hole, things are dire. People can barely afford to eat — buying meat is out of the question,” said Tereza Cristina Ramos, a 68-year-old retiree, who voted in Rio de Janeiro.

Already one of the world’s oldest leaders, Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030.

He will thus have spent 16 years in power, following his first stint as president from 2003 to 2010.

Lula is also facing a hostile Congress dominated by the right.

His options are also constrained by the economic outlook, with growth expected to slow.

He has also come under renewed pressure to confront rampant insecurity in a country plagued by criminal factions that sow terror in working-class neighborhoods.

The president’s campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Trump’s United States.

Voters must “choose a country where the flag is respected,” he said, his raspy voice more hoarse than ever after a tireless campaign. He accused his rival of wanting to “govern with the American flag.”

World.title: Justice, fairness, peace and Nigeria’s 2027 election
World.content:
By ANTHONY OGBEIFUN

As Nigeria approaches the 2027 general election, the country stands again at a familiar crossroads: the choice between narrow, sectional calculation and the broader national demand for justice, fairness and peace. Elections are not merely contests for power. In a plural society such as Nigeria, they are also referendums on whether citizens believe the state belongs to all of them.

Few Nigerian voices expressed this truth more memorably than the late elder statesman and Dan Masanin Kano, Alhaji Yusuf Maitama Sule. In May 2015, Sule led a delegation of the Northern Leaders Forum to congratulate then President-elect Muhammadu Buhari. His counsel on that occasion remains strikingly relevant today.

Sule told Buhari: “With justice, you can rule Nigeria well. Justice is the key.”

It was a simple statement, but one carrying the weight of Nigeria’s history. The country’s recurrent crises—ethnic suspicion, religious tension, electoral violence, insecurity, economic exclusion and the erosion of public trust—are not disconnected accidents. They are symptoms of a deeper disorder: the feeling among many citizens that fairness is selective, opportunity is unequal and power is used to reward loyalty rather than serve the common good.

Sule understood this. “Behind every crisis anywhere in the world is injustice,” he said. And the antidote, he insisted, is “justice.”

That insight should guide every political party, candidate, campaign organisation and voter ahead of 2027. A nation cannot be held together by slogans alone. Neither can it be governed successfully by force, intimidation or the temporary advantage of incumbency. Sule warned: “The world itself can never be governed by force, never by fear, even never by power. In the end, what governs is the mind. What conquers is the spirit and the weapons of governing the mind and conquering the spirit are justice and fair play.”

Nigeria’s 2027 election will therefore test not only the popularity of candidates, but the moral seriousness of the political class.

Justice, in the sense Sule meant it, is broader than court judgments or legal technicalities. It includes fair representation, equitable distribution of public resources, respect for the rule of law, protection of minorities, credible elections and equal treatment before public institutions.

It means that a farmer in Zamfara, a trader in Onitsha, a teacher in Lagos, a fisherman in Bayelsa and a herder in Sokoto should all be able to expect the state to protect their lives, respect their rights and respond to their needs without discrimination.

Sule put it plainly: “If you do justice to all and sundry — and I say all and sundry — because Allah says, ‘If you are going to judge between two people, do justice irrespective of the tribe, religion or even political inclination; justice must be done to whosoever deserves it.’”

That standard is demanding. It rejects the politics of “our turn” when it becomes a cover for exclusion. It also rejects the politics of revenge, where one group’s victory is treated as another group’s defeat. Nigeria needs leaders who can rise above such thinking.

The late Dan Masanin Kano was equally clear that justice must not be selective. “I am not asking you — and I know you will not — to discriminate against any part of Nigeria,” he told Buhari. “But I am asking you to do justice to all parts of Nigeria.”

For political parties preparing for 2027, fairness must begin before the first ballot is cast. It must be visible in candidate selection, zoning arrangements, internal party democracy, campaign financing and the treatment of aspirants.

When parties manipulate primaries, impose candidates, marginalise women and young people, or allow money to determine nomination, they weaken the legitimacy of the eventual winner. A flawed process produces a fragile mandate. And a fragile mandate makes governing harder, especially in a country where citizens are already sceptical of political promises.

Fairness also requires issue-based campaigns. Nigeria’s problems are real: insecurity, unemployment, inflation, poor infrastructure, weak public services, climate pressure on agriculture and widespread poverty. These challenges do not respect ethnicity or religion. Candidates should therefore be judged on their plans to secure communities, create jobs, reform institutions, expand opportunities and restore public confidence.

A campaign built on fear, sectional resentment or religious division may win attention, but it cannot build a nation. Sule’s warning remains urgent: force, fear and power cannot govern the mind or conquer the spirit. Only justice and fair play can.

Sule linked justice directly to peace and development. “Justice will bring about peace,” he said. “Peace and stability are the pre-requisites of development.”

No society develops sustainably in an atmosphere of fear. Investors hesitate where contracts are uncertain and violence is common. Farmers abandon land where insecurity prevails. Young people lose hope where merit is ignored and corruption rewards the connected. Communities retreat into distrust when they believe the state protects some citizens more than others.

Peace is not merely the absence of gunfire. It is the presence of confidence: confidence that elections will count, that courts will be impartial, that public offices will serve the public, and that no region, faith or class will be permanently shut out of opportunity.

The 2027 election offers Nigeria a chance to rebuild that confidence. But it will require more than campaign rhetoric. It will require electoral institutions that are visibly independent, security agencies that act professionally, political actors who accept results peacefully, and citizens who refuse to be used as instruments of violence.

Nigeria does not lack talent, resources or ideas. What it often lacks is the disciplined commitment to justice that turns diversity into strength rather than division. Maitama Sule’s message was not addressed to one president alone. It was addressed to every Nigerian leader, in every generation, and to every citizen who hopes for a better country.

As 2027 approaches, voters should ask hard questions: Which candidate will uphold the rule of law even when it is inconvenient? Which party will distribute opportunity fairly? Which leader will govern for all Nigerians, not merely for those who funded a campaign or share a regional identity?

The answer should not be based on sentiment, ethnicity or fear. It should be based on justice.

Sule’s counsel remains a compass: “With justice, you can rule Nigeria well. Justice is the key.” If Nigeria’s political class embraces that key, the 2027 election can become more than another contest for office. It can become a renewal of the national promise—a step towards a country at peace with itself, fair to all its people, and capable at last of fulfilling its vast potential.

•Ogbeifun wrote in from Lagos.

World.title: Making gas operations safer
World.content:
Nigeria’s ambition to expand the use of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) must be matched by a serious commitment to safety. The Nigerian Association of Liquefied Petroleum Gas Marketers (NALPGAM), at its recent webinar on operational excellence and compliance, warned that rising consumption alone cannot guarantee a sustainable industry. Every facility must be safe, every operator competent, every process compliant and every customer protected.

The warning is timely. LPG offers households and businesses a cleaner alternative to firewood, charcoal and other polluting fuels, but it is highly flammable. Leaking gas, overfilled cylinders, defective valves, poorly maintained equipment and unsafe storage can turn premises into disaster scenes. Illegal decanting and unauthorised propane blending compound these risks, endangering workers, consumers and neighbouring communities. Such practices must not be treated as commercial shortcuts.

NALPGAM’s proposed Standard of Operational Excellence, built around safe facilities, trained personnel, compliant processes and consumer protection, deserves support. But a declaration is not enforcement. The association must translate its aspiration into measurable obligations for members, while the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) must sustain inspections, investigate violations and apply sanctions. Operators should maintain equipment, verify cylinder integrity, provide fire and gas-detection systems, and report incidents promptly. Regulators should publish inspection and enforcement data so the public can judge progress.

Technology can strengthen this effort. Smart filling systems, calibrated load cells, flow meters, automated tank gauges and vehicle tracking can improve measurement, trace product movements and expose losses or suspicious transactions. Digital tools, however, are no substitute for trained staff, independent checks and functioning emergency procedures. Small operators may need affordable training, technical guidance and finance for compliant upgrades; such assistance must never become an excuse to relax minimum safety standards.

Safety also has an economic dimension. Accidents destroy lives, property, investment and public confidence. Consumers who fear explosions or suspect short-changing may avoid cooking gas, frustrating efforts to broaden its use. Reliable cylinder traceability, approved exchange arrangements, accurate measurement and clear consumer information can build trust. Government should involve marketers in LPG penetration and cylinder recirculation programmes, while improving supply and distribution infrastructure to make fuel more accessible and affordable.

The stakes extend beyond individual kitchens. Wider adoption of LPG can reduce household exposure to smoke from solid fuels and ease pressure on forests. A safer, better-regulated market can also attract investment, support certified local cylinder manufacturing, create jobs and deepen Nigeria’s energy economy. The national target of five million tonnes of annual LPG consumption by 2030 will mean little if expansion outpaces safety capacity.

Government, regulators and marketers must turn promises into deadlines, audits, transparent reporting and consequences for negligence. Safety must govern every delivery, filling and transaction. Only then can Nigerians embrace gas with confidence, the environment benefit, and the industry become a pillar of economic diversification.

World.title: When a police officer is caught at crime scene
World.content:
By Owolola Adebola

The sight of a police officer at a crime scene should ordinarily inspire confidence, reassurance and hope. It should signal the arrival of law, the protection of innocent citizens and the beginning of justice for victims. But what happens when the very officer expected to prevent a crime is caught participating in it? What happens when the uniform that should represent honour becomes a disguise for criminality?

At that moment, the incident transcends the conduct of an individual officer. It becomes a test of the integrity of the police institution, the effectiveness of internal supervision and the willingness of the state to hold its own agents accountable.

A police officer caught at a crime scene under suspicious circumstances presents a troubling contradiction. The law enforcement agent who should be chasing criminals may suddenly find himself on the other side of the law. The individual entrusted with protecting lives and property may become a threat to the very people whose safety he has sworn to defend.

Such an incident demands serious investigation, not institutional excuses.

Of course, insanity creeps in when the uniform becomes a shield for criminality because the police uniform carries authority. It commands attention, opens doors and gives its wearer powers that ordinary citizens do not possess. These privileges are granted for public service, not personal enrichment, intimidation or criminal enterprise.

Unfortunately, when an officer abuses that authority, the consequences can be devastating. A police officer involved in robbery, kidnapping, extortion, unlawful possession of weapons or the protection of criminal gangs does more than violate the law. He exploits public confidence and undermines the institution he represents.

The situation becomes even more disturbing when an officer is found at a scene where criminal activities are taking place and credible evidence suggests that he may be involved. Rather than automatically treating the officer as guilty, the authorities must establish what brought him there, what role he played and whether his presence was lawful.

An officer could be at a crime scene to prevent an offence, rescue a victim, investigate an incident or arrest suspects. But where evidence points to complicity, the uniform must offer no protection from investigation.

The badge is not a licence to commit crime. It is a badge of honour and not a badge of horror. The uniform is not immunity from prosecution. And membership of the police force must never become a passport to escape justice.

Public cooperation is indispensable to effective policing. Citizens provide information, identify suspects, report suspicious activities and assist investigations because they expect the police to act in their interest.

But when officers themselves become suspects in criminal investigations, that confidence suffers.

A trader who sees a police officer allegedly collaborating with armed robbers may hesitate before reporting the next suspicious movement. A family whose relative has been victimised by an officer may lose faith in the complaint process. A community that repeatedly encounters alleged police misconduct may begin to regard law enforcement as a source of danger rather than protection.

This erosion of trust gives criminals additional room to operate. Witnesses become reluctant to speak, victims withdraw complaints and valuable intelligence disappears into a climate of suspicion. The damage is not limited to the immediate victims. Honest police officers also pay the price. Their sacrifices, courage and commitment can be overshadowed by the misconduct of colleagues who betray the institution.

It is therefore in the interest of the police themselves to confront criminality within their ranks decisively. Protecting a compromised officer does not protect the institution; it places the reputation of the entire force at risk. In a way, investigation must replace cover-up. Whenever a police officer is apprehended at a crime scene under circumstances suggesting criminal involvement, the first responsibility of the authorities is to establish the facts.

The scene must be secured. Weapons, documents, surveillance footage and other relevant evidence must be preserved. Witnesses should be interviewed without intimidation, and the officer’s movements and communications should be examined where legally authorised.

Where there is credible evidence of wrongdoing, the officer should be subjected to the same lawful investigative process applicable to other suspects. Rank, seniority, political connections and years of service must not determine whether an investigation proceeds. At the same time, fairness requires that allegations be distinguished from proven facts. Being present at a crime scene does not, by itself, establish guilt. The officer must have an opportunity to respond to the allegations, and the investigation must respect due process.

This balance is essential. Accountability without fairness can become persecution, while fairness without accountability can become an excuse for impunity.

The Nigeria Police Force must demonstrate that its disciplinary procedures are effective and that credible allegations of criminal conduct receive prompt, impartial attention. Where the evidence establishes criminal responsibility, administrative discipline alone may be insufficient; criminal prosecution should follow where warranted.

A transfer to another command, quiet retirement or internal reprimand must not become a convenient substitute for justice in a serious criminal case.

Come to Think of It: The Responsibility of Police Leadership

Police leadership has a duty to ensure that officers understand the limits of their authority and the consequences of abusing it. Recruitment, training, supervision and disciplinary systems must reinforce the principle that integrity is as important as operational competence.

Commanders must also be prepared to investigate officers under their supervision without fear or favour. Where a superior officer obstructs an investigation, destroys evidence or shields a colleague from accountability, that conduct must itself attract scrutiny.

Independent oversight, accessible complaint channels and protection for whistle-blowers can help citizens report misconduct without fear of retaliation. Regular audits of police operations, transparent reporting of disciplinary outcomes and effective collaboration with relevant oversight bodies can further strengthen accountability.

In addition, technology also has a role to play. Properly managed body cameras, vehicle tracking systems, digital duty records and evidence-management procedures can help establish where officers were deployed and what occurred during an operation. Such tools must be governed by clear rules to protect privacy, preserve evidence and prevent manipulation.

The objective is not to portray every police officer as a potential criminal. It is to build a system in which honest officers are protected, misconduct is detected and those who abuse their authority cannot easily escape scrutiny.

Justice Must Be Seen to Be Done

When a police officer is caught at a crime scene and credible evidence indicates possible criminal involvement, the public deserves more than official silence. It deserves a credible investigation and, where necessary, prosecution.

The authorities must communicate verified developments responsibly without compromising investigations or prejudicing a fair trial. If the officer is cleared, that outcome should also be acknowledged. Justice must not be manipulated to satisfy public anger, political interests or institutional embarrassment.

Ultimately, the true strength of a police force is not measured by the number of arrests it makes, the weapons it recovers or the criminals it parades before television cameras. Its strength is measured by its willingness to obey the law it enforces.

A police officer who catches a criminal deserves commendation. An officer who becomes involved in crime must face the consequences established by law. There should be no confusion between the two.

Nigeria cannot build a society governed by law if those entrusted with enforcing that law are permitted to stand above it. The police uniform must remain a symbol of service, discipline and courage—not a hiding place for criminal conduct.

When an officer is caught at a crime scene, the decisive question is not whether the institution can protect its reputation by remaining silent. It is whether the institution possesses the courage to protect that reputation by telling the truth, investigating the evidence and allowing justice to take its course.

The uniform may command respect, but only integrity can sustain it. And when the hand entrusted with enforcing the law is suspected of breaking it, the law must be allowed to do its work without fear, favour or compromise.

•Adebola, the State Publicity Secretary of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Ondo State Chapter, wrote in from Akure.

World.title: We never left Egypt, only prodigals need to return home, by Owei Lakemfa
World.content:
President Bola Ahmed Tinubu told Nigerians on October 19, 2026, that they will not return to Egypt. He seems unaware that Egypt is our ancestral home and that we never left and will never leave. This Niger Area is the land of milk and honey we inherited from our fathers and mothers. We were never slaves in this land, will fight any attempt to enslave us; therefore, we never had any reason to flee. We never had any reason to part ways with the sea or for the sea to part ways for us. We never needed to wander in any desert for forty years or more, seeking pathways to freedom or prosperity. This has never been, and will never be, our portion in life.

Ancient Egypt is the origin of modern civilisation. It civilised the Greeks and Romans, who were its pupils before they passed that civilisation to the rest of Europe. The peoples who make up Nigeria were self-sufficient, with viable city-states and empires, and well-schooled in their non-Western education.

One of the natural endowments of this beautiful country is oil. We began producing it in commercial quantities from 1956–57. We were self-sufficient in it, including local refining, with the country running four refineries. As then Head of State Yakubu Gowon said in 1973: “Money is not Nigeria’s problem, but how to spend it.”

What has happened to Nigeria is not that oil has stopped flowing. It is not that the technology to refine sufficient petroleum products for local consumption and export has been lost. Rather, the tragedy we face is that we have had a mainly prodigal leadership since military rule began sixty years ago.

So, in our Egypt, we have sufficient oil reserves that will last at least the next sixty years. There was no fuel subsidy because we did not need to subsidise what we have. It is like asking a rich farmer with fertile soil and bursting barns of yam to subsidise the pounded yam his family will have for supper.

What has happened is that a prodigal political class took over, deliberately ran down the refineries, refused to build new ones and, most criminally, insisted on denominating fuel in inflated dollar accounting. Their paper accounting is based on our country having no drop of oil, which we all know is false, and having to import finished products which are bought by dubious officials from their chosen partners, pay freight, insurance, port fees, demurrage and storage fees. These products are then handed over to a cartel which transports them through deliberately neglected or abandoned roads and sells them to hapless Nigerians at rates imposed by the cartel. In this dubious process is built what is touted as subsidy.

Since the Babangida regime, this dubious subsidy mirage has been factored into our petroleum products. When the latest subsidy removal was touted on May 29, 2023, Nigerians were told the proceeds would be used for development. But what we have experienced is greater misery, multiplication of the hungry, dilapidating infrastructure, a rising number of out-of-school children, lack of mass housing, virtually abandoned basic healthcare and insecurity. Whenever we ask the administration what has been done with the so-called subsidy savings, it points at increasing the revenue allocation to states and local governments. It is aware that most leaders of these tiers are like cats being told to watch over fried fish. Deceptively, it does not point at itself as being the largest recipient of these extra funds, which remain unaccounted for.

When President Tinubu announced that his administration had removed fuel subsidy, the price of a litre of PMS was increased from about N197 to an average N500. Today, it is thrice that price, and the government blames this insanity on the war in Iran. In this, the Tinubu government is behaving like the dirty widow with head lice creeping all over her hair who blames this on mourning her husband by not allowing a drop of water to touch her head since his demise. If the Nigerian government blames the war in Iran for the outrageous price of PMS in the country, why is Iran, which has suffered the catastrophe of having its leadership wiped out, children buried under the rubble of their classrooms, infrastructure and oil facilities bombed and punishing sanctions imposed by the United States, not been similarly affected?

Honourable Victor Afam Oghene, Member, Federal House of Representatives, Ogbaru Constituency of Anambra State, debunked, with verifiable statistics, these childish fairy tales of the Tinubu government. He gave comparative statistics of PMS prices in four oil-producing countries: Iran, which has been at war for years; Libya, which has suffered state collapse since 2011 and had at least three factional governments in Tobruk, Tripoli and Benghazi; Saudi Arabia, which is engaged in war with neighbouring Yemen; and Nigeria, which is not at war. In his statistics, which the increasingly intolerant Tinubu government and its army of internet propagandists have not been able to fault, Honourable Oghene revealed that a litre of PMS in Iran is N38, Libya, N32, Saudi Arabia, N832, and Nigeria, at least N1,300. In contrast, the National Minimum Wage in Iran is N165,000, Libya is N210,000, Saudi Arabia, N1.4 million, and N70,000 in Nigeria! Oghene then analysed these basic statistics in value terms. He showed that the minimum wage in Iran can purchase 4,242 litres of PMS, Libya, 6,562 litres, Saudi Arabia, 1,700, and only 46 litres in Nigeria!

Tragically, despite such sound analysis and the situation in the country, the Tinubu administration appears increasingly irritated, deaf to the cries of Nigerians and incapable of basic thinking. For instance, rather than examine the arguments of various patriots and pro-people activists on the issue of fuel subsidy and the calamitous effects on the populace, it is threatening Nigerians with dire consequences. In its unfathomable scare-mongering, the administration’s Minister of Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, threatened that even an inkling of the administration rethinking the subsidy issue would trigger capital flight. This, he claimed, would lead to the naira, which has already been devalued over fifty per cent by Tinubu, suffering a further sixty per cent devaluation. Oyedele told Nigerians this fable, not based on any analysis, but beliefs. He also claimed that this would raise the price of petrol to at least N2,000 per litre. Even as a product of Yale University and London School of Economics, and an advertised policy expert, the Honourable Minister could not provide the cost component of this his projected N2,000-per-litre PMS.

We Nigerians never left our Egypt, so there is no issue of a return. It is the prodigals of the political class that need to return home, ask for forgiveness and stop suffocating the country.

World.title: Houston’s message to Africa: Innovation must deliver more barrels, lower costs and better returns
World.content:
By Kunle Odusola-Stevenson

The future of Africa’s oil and gas industry will not be determined by the resources beneath its soil alone, but by how effectively it deploys technology, attracts investment and translates policy into commercial results. This was a central takeaway from the Society of Petroleum Engineers’ (SPE) Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition (ATCE) 2026, held in Houston, Texas, from October 21 to 23. Under the theme, “Exploring New Horizons with Innovative Solutions,” the conference brought together energy professionals to examine the technologies, engineering practices and operational strategies shaping the industry’s future. For Nigeria, where increasing production, developing natural gas resources and strengthening indigenous operators remain national priorities, the message was clear: innovation must translate into measurable business performance.

The global energy industry is under pressure to deliver reliable supplies, improve capital efficiency and reduce environmental impacts. For Africa, these demands coincide with a pressing need to expand electricity access, industrialise economies and create productive employment. The challenge is not simply to defend the relevance of hydrocarbons, but to demonstrate that African energy resources can be developed competitively, responsibly and profitably. The lessons from Houston offer a practical starting point. Artificial intelligence, advanced reservoir analytics, predictive maintenance, drilling automation and digital production monitoring are creating opportunities to improve oil recovery, reduce equipment failures, shorten operational delays and strengthen investment decisions. Their significance lies not in technological novelty, but in their potential to improve the economics of producing assets.

Consider Nigeria’s mature oilfields, many of which face declining production, ageing infrastructure, rising water cuts and expensive maintenance requirements. Better integration of geological data, well-performance records and production information can help operators identify underperforming wells, prioritise interventions and determine where additional investment is most likely to recover lost production.

Predictive maintenance can similarly help operators identify early warning signs in pumps, compressors and other critical equipment before failures cause costly shutdowns. Improved drilling analytics can support better well planning, reduce non-productive time and strengthen operational safety. Meanwhile, methane monitoring and flare-management technologies can help operators identify emissions sources, reduce avoidable losses and improve environmental performance. These are practical applications for Nigeria’s oil and gas industry, not automatic outcomes of technology adoption. Results depend on reliable data, competent personnel, appropriate infrastructure and disciplined implementation. Every investment should therefore be assessed against measurable indicators, including incremental production, reduced downtime, lower operating costs, improved recovery and emissions reduction.

This approach is particularly important as Nigeria’s upstream industry undergoes structural change. The transfer of selected onshore and shallow-water assets from international oil companies to indigenous operators has created opportunities for domestic companies to expand their participation and retain more value within the economy. Yet a change of ownership does not automatically produce higher output, stronger profitability or sustainable operations.

Indigenous operators must combine ownership with the technical and financial capacity to manage complex reservoirs, rehabilitate infrastructure, improve recovery and meet environmental obligations. Access to technology, long-term financing, specialised engineering expertise and dependable evacuation systems will be critical to their success. Nigeria’s ambition to achieve three million barrels of crude oil production per day by 2030 must therefore be treated as an execution challenge rather than a statement of intent. New developments, improved recovery from existing fields, reduced production losses, reliable evacuation and sustained investment must work together to deliver the desired outcome.

The leadership transition within the SPE Nigeria Council, from Engr. Francis Nwaochei to Engr. Etta Agbor, also presents an opportunity to strengthen the connection between global technical knowledge and local operating realities. Professional institutions such as SPE can support this process through applied research, technical training, industry collaboration and the development of Nigerian engineering talent capable of evaluating and deploying advanced technologies.

However, technology alone cannot overcome an uncertain investment environment. Regulatory predictability remains fundamental. The Petroleum Industry Act provides an important statutory framework, but investors also require transparent fiscal arrangements, timely approvals, consistent regulatory decisions and clarity over contractual obligations. Effective regulation should protect public interests while enabling commercially viable projects to proceed without avoidable administrative delays.

Security and infrastructure are equally important. Production cannot generate its full economic value if crude oil and gas cannot reach markets reliably. Pipeline disruptions, theft, infrastructure failures and insecurity increase operating costs, undermine revenues and weaken investor confidence. Government institutions, regulators, operators, security agencies and host communities must work together to protect infrastructure and strengthen the reliability of Nigeria’s energy supply chain. Environmental performance is also becoming integral to commercial competitiveness. Methane detection, flare reduction, emissions monitoring and environmental remediation increasingly influence investor assessments and access to international financing. Operators must incorporate these responsibilities into field-development plans and operating budgets rather than treating them as separate sustainability commitments.

Beyond upstream production, Africa’s energy investment proposition extends across the value chain. Gas processing, pipelines, gas-to-power, domestic LNG and LPG distribution can support industrial growth where viable markets and bankable offtake arrangements exist. Refining and petrochemical development can create additional value through domestic processing, fertiliser production, manufacturing and associated logistics. Each opportunity, however, requires commercially realistic assumptions, dependable infrastructure and appropriate risk allocation.

For international investors, the question is no longer simply whether Africa possesses substantial hydrocarbon resources. It is whether specific projects can offer credible returns, transparent governance, manageable risks and reliable access to markets. African governments and operators must make that case through predictable policies, technical competence and consistent delivery. Industry platforms such as the Nigeria International Energy Summit can help connect technology providers, indigenous operators, regulators, policymakers and international financiers. Their value should ultimately be measured by what follows the discussions: capital mobilised, partnerships established, technology deployed, infrastructure completed and production improved.

The message from Houston to Abuja is unmistakable. Africa’s energy future will not be secured by resource abundance alone. It will depend on the disciplined convergence of engineering excellence, investment, reliable infrastructure, environmental responsibility and decisive policy execution.

Nigeria has the resources and entrepreneurial potential to compete more effectively in the global energy economy. The task is to create the conditions that allow those advantages to translate into sustained production, industrial growth and shared prosperity.

Africa must move beyond selling the promise of its resources to demonstrating the strength of its energy business case. Innovation must deliver more barrels, lower costs and better returns. That is how global technology can become local capability, investment can become productive capacity, and energy can become a foundation for lasting economic transformation.

Odusola-Stevenson is CEO of The Legend & Legacy Company Ltd.

World.title: Tinubu: Lion at home, lamb abroad? By Suleiman A. Suleiman
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu

We should begin where we must. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has his virtues. For one, he is not given to petty vindictiveness as former President Obasanjo too often was. Tinubu has not been involved in any open political fights with governors or lawmakers as Obasanjo did. Instead, he appears generally forgiving and conciliatory, having brought several of his fiercest political critics into his government. Also, unlike many of Nigeria’s previous leaders, Tinubu did not come to office by accident, nor was he enthroned by anyone. He arrived in office by sheer personal grit, itself an unusual thing in Nigerian political leadership at that level.

Now, the average Nigerian president is a very powerful person. How they wield that power, however, is the key difference between one president and another. Tinubu is no average Nigerian president. He sits above his party and the nation, in a way that no president has done since 1999. Nigerian ruling parties are characterised by internal dissent, factionalism, and opposition, which serve as a check on a president’s power, often better than can be expected from the official opposition parties. There is no such thing under Tinubu. By removing Senator Abdullahi Adamu as Chairman of the APC within weeks of assuming office, Tinubu made that point clear early on. Now, a personal anthem, “On your mandate we shall stand”, rings out at the mention of his name among officials and party faithful because everyone gets the message.

The President also has an iron grip on his cabinet, the National Assembly, the governors, the security agencies, anti-corruption agencies, and, as the rumours go, the courts, and perhaps INEC too. From 1960 to date, the National Assembly, particularly, has never been this pliant to a president, often passing executive bills in less than 48 hours, even before some members had a chance to read them. By removing officials without cause or notice, he has signalled that even the most favoured appointees can get the sack. He has induced the defection of all but one or two governors to his party, in name or at least in function. Criticism from the media, civil society, or labour has been blunted, if not outright buried, save for a few notable exceptions.

All of this leaves no one in doubt that Tinubu is the lion in Nigeria’s political jungle. Yet, Tinubu’s power is not backed by authority in that specific Weberian sense. Behind this image of an all-powerful president still lies something cosmetic. Obasanjo came to office with the charisma of a former head of state and national hero at multiple points in the country’s history. Buhari was the face of a political movement with more than 10 million loyal votes each election for nearly 20 years. Jonathan came to office by accident, but once there, he commanded the unflinching loyalty of nearly as many Nigerians as Buhari.

Tinubu has none of these. His personal anthem may ring out loud, but it rings hollow still because the President’s political coalition is held together not by popular admiration or ideological belief in his programme, but by the depth of his pocket or the fear of losing one’s job in a Nigeria that has grown much harsher economically for nearly all but those in government. Tinubu is quite possibly the most politically vulnerable president facing re-election since 1999. But the opposition lacks money, and the mass public lacks food. A clear majority of Nigerians may well not be happy with the current conditions in the country, but they lack the energy—or the hope—to put up a sustained fight.

And then there is the not-so-small matter of the incompetence of the government, although in a different sense than Nigerians are used to in their government. Few governments in Nigerian history have initiated as many far-reaching economic reforms from the start as the Tinubu administration: complete fuel subsidy removal, wholesale naira devaluation, free university tuition converted to loans, high electricity tariffs, tax reforms, and so on. Yet, the government clearly appears to lack the capacity to make a genuine success out of its own reforms, and by the end of the first year, all the swagger Tinubu came into office with had gone.

Far-reaching economic reforms generate costs and benefits, and thus, winners and losers. Who are the winners and losers of the fuel subsidy removal policy, for example? How can the policy be tweaked to spread the gains or mitigate the pains? How can we build a genuine political coalition strong enough to sustain the reforms beyond this administration? These are the questions that would engage a more competent reformer, and they would answer them with evidence-based policy adjustment, rather than a shouting match with Catholic bishops. Yet, beyond infographics that have little bearing on reality, you would struggle to find a serious policy paper or further policy actions produced by this government since 2023.

But it is in foreign policy that the real character of the current government is laid bare. Tinubu may be a lion at home, but he is a lamb on the world stage. As Daily Trust reported two weeks ago, Nigeria has agreed to a U.S. “America First Global Health Strategy” framework that effectively amounts to signing off our sovereignty for transactional aid. Under this agreement, Nigeria would provide U.S. companies with our health data on short notice. The companies manufacture drugs and vaccines they will resell back to us at huge profits, effectively turning Nigerian sickness into a cash cow for America. And all of this under a health minister who has talked the most about developing local manufacturing capacity in the healthcare sector.

Mortgaging Nigerian sovereignty—for a pittance or for free—is the norm under this government. Virtually every single foreign policy action this government has taken since 2023 has been either on behalf of or to the benefit of foreign countries, principally France, Britain, the United States, Israel, or Saudi Arabia. Nigeria itself gets almost nothing out of its foreign policy engagements. Under Tinubu, Nigeria has sparred with two neighbours on behalf of France; sold our tax administration to the same country without any receipts; accepted a controversial asylum-seeker deportation deal with Britain; joined a Red Sea Alliance with Saudi Arabia that has no discernible benefit for us; and watched almost helplessly as the United States promotes a narrative that directly threatens our fragile peace.

A bolder government has several countermeasures for each of these foreign policy engagements. France can train our tax officials, rather than hand over our entire system to them. A more strategic government should be capitalising on the current conflict in Europe and the Gulf to do deals that would pump out more of our oil and gas reserves. An Obasanjo or Yar’Adua would have more forcefully rejected the narrative of Christian genocide the U.S. is self-servingly imposing on us to fleece our resources like rare minerals and colonial healthcare deals. A bolder and more sovereignty-inclined Tinubu would at least get the nation to convene an open hearing on this issue, at least to take matters into our own hands.

For Tinubu’s foreign policy, however, the problem is not just the decisions or actions, but the approach and the attitude behind it. The government’s foreign policy actions are almost always conducted in complete secrecy. This means that the President may well be entangling Nigeria in unfavourable or unnecessary foreign arrangements that might be difficult for future leaders to repair. At a time when many countries on the continent are flexing self-determination muscles, the so-called Giant of Africa is crouched on the ground licking foreign what-not. Most disturbing of all, President Tinubu appears to believe that once an idea, policy, or agreement has the approving stamp of a Western government or Western-aligned international institutions like the World Bank and IMF, then such a policy or idea is automatically good for Nigeria. Our government appears unable or unwilling to go against any foreign governments or institutions. This is perhaps the sole reason the government has stuck to a punitive fuel subsidy removal that no one in the administration can point to the gains of with any confidence.

The government may yet be returned in this election. But some things cannot be left unsaid.

World.title: Okonjo-Iweala loses mother, as Tinubu mourns
World.content:
Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala (R) with mother, Prof Kamene Okonjo

‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru

PRESIDENT Bola Tinubu has extended his heartfelt condolences to the Okonjo royal family of Ogwashi-Uku, Delta State, on the passing of Prof. Kamene Okonjo, who died at the age of 96.

Prof. Okonjo was a distinguished scholar, a champion of women’s empowerment, and a revered matriarch.

The President particularly commiserated with her daughter, Dr Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Director-General of the World Trade Organisation, other family members, and the people of Ogwashi-Uku over the loss of their beloved mother, matriarch, and community leader.

President Tinubu described Prof. Okonjo’s passing as the loss of an accomplished academic whose life was defined by intellectual distinction, service to humanity, and an enduring commitment to advancing women and society.

He acknowledged her contributions to scholarship and her inspiring example as a woman who combined professional excellence with dedication to family, community, and the preservation of traditional institutions.

The President prayed that Almighty God will grant the departed eternal rest and comfort the family and all who mourn her passing.

Vanguard reports that Kamene Okonjo, a professor of sociology and advocate for women’s rights, died on Friday, according to reports citing a statement issued by the Umu Obi Obahai royal family of Ogwashi-Uku kingdom in Delta state.

Okonjo-Iweala, in a post on X on Sunday, thanked friends and followers for their messages of condolence and support to her family.

“Today, I have been overwhelmed with messages of condolences and tributes to my wonderful mother.

“I just want to thank all my friends and followers and let you know how appreciative my entire family and I are of your support.

“My mother lived a quality life till the end and we are very grateful we had her for so long. May her soul rest in perfect peace.” She wrote

World.title: ICPC Gets Recognition for Institutional Performance, Accountability, Service Delivery
World.content:
Alex Enumah in Abuja

The Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) has received fresh recognition for its institutional performance in the fight against corruption in the country.

The recognition followed an independent assessment by a Coalition of Civil Society Organisations (CSOs), which identified the Commission and the Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP) among the notable performers in public accountability and service delivery.

A statement by the ICPC noted the assessment, presented at a civil society roundtable in Lagos, examined selected Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs) of the federal government, focusing on transparency, institutional efficiency, accountability and measurable contributions to public service delivery.

The statement referenced a report published by NewsNowOnline on October 24, 2026, wherein ICPC’s contributions to protecting public resources, strengthening institutional safeguards against corruption and promoting integrity within the public service were acknowledged.

“The recognition comes amid ongoing efforts by the Commission, under the leadership of its Chairman, Dr. Musa Adamu Aliyu, SAN, to strengthen the effectiveness of its investigative, preventive and enforcement responsibilities”, the statement read in part.

It observed that beyond investigating allegations of corruption, the Commission has continued to emphasise systemic interventions designed to identify institutional weaknesses, strengthen compliance mechanisms and reduce opportunities for the abuse of public office.

The civil society assessment particularly highlighted the importance of the ICPC’s oversight responsibilities in public procurement, where weak institutional controls and corrupt practices can expose government finances to substantial losses.

The recognition also highlights the Commission’s broader mandate to promote ethical conduct, strengthen accountability, and encourage collaboration among regulatory institutions, law enforcement agencies, and civil society organisations.

Meanwhile, the ICPC under the leadership of its current chairman has maintained its focus on combating corruption through lawful enforcement, preventive interventions and public enlightenment, recognising that sustainable anti-corruption outcomes require more than prosecution alone.

“Significantly, the latest civil society acknowledgement follows the Commission’s performance in the 2026 Transparency and Integrity Index, conducted by the Centre for Fiscal Transparency and Public Integrity, where ICPC recorded 80.13 per cent, up from 78.13 per cent in 2025.

“The separate assessments provide additional perspectives on the Commission’s institutional accountability, transparency and service-delivery responsibilities.

“The Lagos roundtable also underscored the importance of evaluating public institutions beyond policy announcements and routine activities, stressing that institutional effectiveness should ultimately be reflected in measurable outcomes and benefits to citizens”, the statement added.

However, the recognition according to the ICPC, reinforces the importance of sustaining credible investigations, strengthening preventive measures, improving institutional responsiveness and deepening public confidence in the fight against corruption.

It also highlights the continuing responsibility of anti-corruption institutions to demonstrate professionalism, fairness, transparency, and respect for due process in discharging their statutory mandates.

As the Commission continues to pursue its responsibilities, the independent assessment provides an opportunity to consolidate institutional improvements and strengthen collaboration with stakeholders committed to accountability and good governance.

World.title: NDPHC Begins Project to End 15-year Blackout in Kaduna Council
World.content:
Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

The Niger Delta Power Holding Company Limited (NDPHC) has announced the commencement of an electricity infrastructure project aimed at ending a 15-year blackout in Rigasa community, Igabi Local Government Area of Kaduna State.

The project comprises a two-kilometre 11kV line, a 1.5-kilometre 33kV line as well as a 7.5MVA, 33/11kV injection substation designed to strengthen electricity distribution and improve power supply to residents and businesses.

In a statement in Abuja by the General Manager, Corporate Communication and External Relations, NDPHC, Nazo Agim, the company said the project was facilitated by the Bola Ahmed Tinubu Ideological Group (BAT-IG).

According to the NDPHC, the project reached a major milestone at the weekend with a groundbreaking ceremony performed by the Kaduna State Deputy Governor, Dr. Hadiza Balarabe, who represented Governor Uba Sani.

In his remarks, the governor commended NDPHC for the intervention, describing it as a life-saving initiative that would address the community’s long-standing electricity challenges.

Also, the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of NDPHC, Jennifer Adighije, reaffirmed the company’s commitment to improving electricity supply in underserved communities.

Represented by the Executive Director, Networks, Babayo Bello, Adighije said that although the company’s primary mandate was power generation, its interventions extended to transmission and distribution infrastructure to address critical gaps and expand electricity access.

She described the Rigasa project as a worthwhile investment that would ease residents’ hardship and demonstrate the impact of targeted infrastructure development in underserved communities.

In his remarks, NDPHC Executive Director, Strategy and Commercial, Patrick Obahiagbon, appreciated the Kaduna state government and the community for their cooperation and support for the project.

The District Head of Rigasa, Mohammed Aminu Idris, also commended NDPHC’s management for its commitment to expanding electricity access in the community.

Other dignitaries at the groundbreaking ceremony included Senator Shehu Sani, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Kaduna Electricity Distribution Company (KEDC), Umar Abubakar Hashidu, and BAT-IG Convener, Bamidele Atoyebi, alongside government officials, industry stakeholders and community representatives.

NDPHC General Manager, Distribution, Dahiru Muritala Mohammed, whose department is responsible for the project, was also present.

According to the NDPHC, the Rigasa project underscores the company’s commitment to extending critical electricity infrastructure beyond generation to bridge distribution gaps, stimulate socioeconomic development and improve the quality of life in underserved communities across Nigeria.

World.title: Dele Oye: Why FG Must Probe N373bn NELFUND Student Loan Disbursements
World.content:
Says NEC’s 90-day economic recovery plan unachievable without clear targets

Calls for urgent review of multiple taxes, levies

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

Former national President of the Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commerce Industry Mines and Agriculture (NACCIMA), Dele Oye, yesterday called for better clarity and accountability in the administration of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND).

Oye, who is the Chairman of the Alliance for Economic Research and Ethics (AERE), in a commentary on the federal government’s 90-day economic action plan, said this followed the announced disbursement of N372.62 billion in institutional fees and student upkeep allowances.

The past Chairman Organised Private Sector of Nigeria (OPSN), said the scale of the disbursement underscored the need for clear service standards, transparent reporting and effective complaint-resolution mechanisms to ensure that beneficiaries receive the support they need on time.

According to the NELFUND Student Loan Disbursement Report generated on October 3, 2026, he stated that the fund had disbursed N372.62 billion as of September 29, 2026, while processing 1,659,853 applications.

While acknowledging the importance of the scheme, Oye said the amount disbursed should not be treated as the sole measure of its performance, stressing that the government must also demonstrate how efficiently the programme serves students.

He called on NELFUND to publish service standards covering application decisions, institutional payments and upkeep transfers, alongside aggregated data showing approval and rejection rates and payment timelines.

He also advocated a real-time application tracking system that would allow students to monitor the progress of their applications, as well as a transparent complaint-resolution channel with clear response and closure targets.

Oye said the same principles should guide household support programmes, skills financing and small-enterprise credit, insisting that public assistance should be based on verified data, delivered directly to beneficiaries and reported through privacy-protected information.

According to him, publishing measurable results would help Nigerians assess whether government interventions are translating into tangible improvements in their lives rather than remaining as figures in official announcements.

Oye urged NELFUND to publish service standards for application decisions, institutional payments and upkeep transfers; show applicants a real-time status trail; publish aggregated approval, rejection and payment-time data; and operate a visible complaint-resolution channel with response and closure targets

“Accessibility, timely payment, transparent eligibility and swift redress are not side notes. They are the bridge between a scheme on paper and a student who can actually plan a semester,” he explained.

On the National Economic Council (NEC) 90-day economic action plan, Oye said the initiative was a welcome recognition of the country’s cost-of-living crisis but warned that its success would depend on clear targets, defined responsibilities and transparent implementation.

The plan, endorsed by NEC on October 22, 2026, identifies five priority areas: food affordability, tax harmonisation, high-impact projects, investment bottlenecks and regulated household support.

It also provides for a national dashboard to track projects and fuel-subsidy proceeds, while the government has identified reducing headline inflation and interest rates to single digits by 2027 as key policy objectives.

However, Oye noted that the announcement did not provide a delivery matrix, public baselines, named delivery owners, itemised costs or milestone deadlines.

He argued that without these details, Nigerians would struggle to determine what the government intends to achieve within the 90-day period or hold the responsible institutions accountable for missed targets.

He called for a public performance dashboard showing baseline figures, targets, actual results, responsible institutions and the next steps for each commitment.

The proposed dashboard, he said, should track food prices, transport fares, road repairs, regulatory charges, student loan payment performance, completed projects and the use of subsidy-related proceeds.

Oye maintained that the success of the plan should ultimately be measured by improvements in household welfare, including more affordable food, lower transport costs and better conditions for businesses.

The AERE chairman also called for an urgent review of the multiple taxes, fees and levies imposed on businesses by federal and state authorities, warning that overlapping charges and poorly justified regulatory costs could undermine enterprise growth.

He urged federal and state regulators to publish their complete fee and levy schedules within 90 days, including the legal basis for each charge, the agencies authorised to collect them and their annual collection costs.

Oye proposed the establishment of a public Regulatory Cost Register to identify charges that lack a clear legal basis and fees whose collection costs exceed the revenue they generate.

He said such charges should be reviewed, while new levies should expire unless they are reauthorised based on evidence of public benefit.

The objective, he explained, should not be to eliminate legitimate taxation or necessary regulation, but to remove unnecessary costs that place additional pressure on businesses and consumers.

Oye also advocated simpler business registration procedures, a free tax-identification process, a single digital levy notice and an independent channel through which businesses could challenge questionable charges.

He further called for coordinated, risk-based inspections, arguing that small businesses should not be shut down without written reasons and a fair opportunity to seek a review.

He said reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens would help businesses operate more efficiently, support job creation and strengthen the formal economy.

Oye urged the government to complement tax harmonisation with stronger revenue accountability, including the reconciliation of agency remittances, publication of tax waivers and recovery of verified outstanding debts.

He maintained that the government should address revenue leakages and public-sector waste before demanding additional sacrifices from citizens already facing economic hardship.

“A 90-day plan cannot be a motivational speaker in a ministerial folder. It must tell Nigerians what will change, who will make it change, how much it will cost, and what happens if it does not,” he pointed out.

The AERE chief argued that all data must be verified, delivered directly and reported as aggregated, privacy-protected results by state and ward, and not distributed as political theatre, stressing that Nigerians need dignity, not a queue in the sun with a camera at the end of it.

“The same standard belongs in public works. Publish a Sunk Cost Register for abandoned projects: original contract sum, amount paid, physical completion, contractor, remedial path and completion date. Finishing a useful road is generally wiser than launching a new signboard beside an old ruin,” he maintained.

World.title: Tax Ombud Seeks to Ease Compliance Burden, Dispute Costs for Businesses
World.content:
Says proposed NIPOST partnership to usher free complaint-resolution services to market traders, rural taxpayers

Ombud says intervention will improve fairness, compliance without shielding taxpayers from lawful obligations

Transport operators flag overlapping levies, complex tax rules as businesses seek clarity

James Emejo and Precious Ologbondiyan in Abuja

Tax Ombud and Chief Executive, Office of the Tax Ombud, Dr. John Nwabueze, has revealed plans to extend free tax complaint-resolution services to market traders and businesses in rural communities.

Speaking at a town hall meeting in Abuja, over the weekend, he said the move aimed to reduce the cost of resolving disputes with revenue authorities and ease administrative bottlenecks confronting small enterprises.

Acc9rding to him, the initiative, which involves a proposed partnership with the Nigerian Postal Service (NIPOST), is expected to bring the services closer to taxpayers who may otherwise struggle to access formal channels for challenging disputed assessments, procedural irregularities and other grievances arising from tax administration.

This came as representatives of market associations, professional bodies, transport unions, airline operators and other private sector groups highlighted the need for simpler tax procedures and more effective dispute-resolution mechanisms.

Although the proposed collaboration is yet to be formalised, its implementation could provide smaller businesses with a more accessible avenue for addressing tax-related complaints without incurring the costs and delays associated with prolonged disputes.

Nwabueze said the Office was working towards formalising the arrangement with NIPOST to improve access to its services, particularly for taxpayers in underserved locations.

He explained that the tax ombud was established to address operational, procedural and administrative grievances arising from tax and revenue administration through an independent, impartial and non-judicial process.

He said, “Our services, which are offered free of charge, are designed to resolve disputes, mediate complaints, and promote a transparent, fair, and consistent tax administration system.”

No waiver of legitimate tax obligations

Nwabueze stressed that the Office was not established to cancel legitimate tax liabilities or protect taxpayers unwilling to meet their legal obligations.

He said the institution did not formulate tax policy or perform the functions of the courts, but was mandated to facilitate the fair and impartial resolution of eligible complaints within its statutory powers.

The distinction is significant for businesses seeking relief from administrative disputes: the intervention is intended to address unfair processes and grievances, rather than provide a blanket exemption from taxation.

According to him, a fair and predictable tax system is essential to economic growth, investor confidence and improved voluntary compliance among SMEs, traders and the wider business community.

He added that the Office would continue to engage stakeholders and address systemic weaknesses, including inadequate transparency and inefficient grievance-redress mechanisms.

Nwabueze also commended President Bola Tinubu for establishing the Office, while acknowledging the contributions of the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, and other stakeholders to the process.

He said the broader objective was to build confidence between taxpayers and revenue authorities by ensuring that complaints could be considered impartially and resolved through appropriate channels.

The planned NIPOST partnership, if implemented, would widen the geographical reach of that process, potentially helping businesses outside major commercial centres access redress without travelling long distances to reach the relevant office.

However, the extent of the relief businesses would receive would depend on the final terms of the partnership, the accessibility of the proposed service points and the Office’s capacity to resolve complaints efficiently.

The tax ombud reiterated its commitment to protecting taxpayers’ rights while upholding the lawful powers and responsibilities of revenue authorities, maintaining that constructive engagement remained central to a more transparent and taxpayer-friendly revenue system.

Transport operators seek clarity

Contributions at the meeting underscored how uncertainty over tax responsibilities and the multiplicity of collection points can complicate compliance for businesses operating across different jurisdictions.

A representative of the National Union of Road Transport Workers (NURTW) called for stronger collaboration between the tax ombud and transport stakeholders, adding that operators faced difficulties understanding the different tax obligations imposed by government authorities.

Stakeholders raised concerns about the interaction between federal, state and local government revenue responsibilities, particularly in the transport sector, where operators may encounter different levies depending on their activities and locations.

They called for clearer guidelines and better engagement with transport unions to help operators understand their obligations and reduce confusion over payments.

The concerns highlighted the potential economic importance of an accessible complaints mechanism, particularly for businesses that lack the resources to challenge disputed demands through lengthy administrative or legal processes.

Representatives of other stakeholder groups, including the Abuja Market, the National Association of Small and Medium Enterprises (NASME), the Chartered Institute of Taxation of Nigeria and the National Association of Chambers of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture (NACCIMA), also stressed the need for transparent assessment criteria, streamlined procedures and effective channels for resolving complaints.

Essentially, unresolved tax disputes and unclear administrative procedures can add to operating costs, disrupt cash flow and undermine confidence in the tax system for businesses operating on tight margins, particularly market traders and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

The tax ombud seeks to ensure that improved access to redress translates into greater predictab

World.title: MDCN Clears Five Doctors of Prima Facie Misconduct Over Lovelyn John’s Death, Refers One Other to Tribunal
World.content:
Sunday Ehigiator



The Medical and Dental Practitioners Investigation Panel has found no prima facie case of professional misconduct against five doctors linked to the death of Mrs Lovelyn Akudo John at Gynescope Specialist Hospital, while referring another practitioner, Dr Joseph Aliyu Yahaya, to the Medical and Dental Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal.



The development was contained in a recent communication, which outlined the Panel’s findings following its consideration of complaints arising from the circumstances surrounding John’s death.



According to the communication, the five doctors against whom no prima facie case was established are Professor Jude Ehiabhi Okohue, Dr Adeyi Taiwo Olugbenga, Dr Chukwuebuka Igbokwe, Dr Olawale Enigbokan and Dr Owoseni Taiwo.



Professor Okohue, the proprietor of Gynescope Specialist Hospital, was specifically considered by the Panel but was not referred to the Disciplinary Tribunal.



However, the Panel referred Dr Yahaya, who was involved in the management of the deceased patient, to the Tribunal after its preliminary assessment of the allegations against him.



The referral represents a separate regulatory outcome and does not amount to a conviction or a final determination of professional negligence.



It means the allegations against Dr Yahaya will proceed to the appropriate disciplinary stage for further examination and determination in accordance with the applicable procedures.



The distinction between the practitioners’ respective outcomes comes amid public debate over the circumstances surrounding John’s death and the medical care she received.



The controversy has also drawn attention to the need to distinguish preliminary regulatory findings from final decisions on professional misconduct or negligence.



The Panel’s decision not to refer the five doctors indicates that it did not establish a sufficient basis for disciplinary referral against them at that stage. It does not, however, constitute a judicial determination resolving every possible question of liability in other proceedings.



Similarly, Dr Yahaya’s referral does not establish that the allegations against him have been proved, as he remains entitled to present his defence before the Tribunal.



The case is also before the Lagos State Coroner’s Court, where an inquest is ongoing to examine the circumstances surrounding John’s death.



The outcome of the Panel’s preliminary assessment does not, by itself, establish that Gynescope Specialist Hospital has been found legally liable or absolved of every possible claim. Questions concerning institutional liability are distinct from the disciplinary proceedings against individual practitioners and must be considered on the relevant evidence and applicable law.



Likewise, the determination of the medical cause of death does not automatically establish negligence. Any such conclusion would require an assessment of the applicable professional standards, the treatment provided, the clinical evidence and whether an alleged breach caused or materially contributed to the death.



The ongoing inquest is expected to provide a forum for examining relevant evidence and addressing outstanding questions surrounding the circumstances of the incident.



The developments have also renewed calls for the Panel’s findings to be reported in their entirety, rather than focusing exclusively on the referral of one practitioner while overlooking the outcome concerning the other doctors.



The deceased’s family is entitled to seek answers and pursue accountability through lawful channels, while the practitioners concerned are entitled to fair consideration of the allegations against them.



The disciplinary process and coroner’s inquest remain distinct proceedings, and their respective outcomes will be determined through the applicable procedures.

World.title: Nigeria, Cyprus Seek Stronger Economic, Education Ties as Envoy Presents Credentials
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja



Nigeria and Cyprus have pledged to deepen bilateral relations, with particular emphasis on trade, investment, education and political dialogue, following the formal accreditation of Nigeria’s ambassador to the Mediterranean island nation.



The commitment was made at the weekend in Nicosia when Nigeria’s Ambassador to Israel, with concurrent accreditation to Cyprus, Nkechi Linda Ufochukwu, presented her Letters of Credence to the Cypriot President, Nikos Christodoulides, at the Presidential Palace.



The ceremony formally marked the commencement of Ufochukwu’s diplomatic duties in Cyprus and opened a fresh opportunity for both countries to strengthen cooperation in areas of shared interest.
