How much filter is too much filter for kids and teens posting selfies on social media?

That is the question state attorneys general across the country are grappling with following a landmark settlement with Meta this summer. As part of the agreement, the social media giant agreed to block some digital beauty filters for minors — specifically those mimicking extreme transformations like cosmetic procedures or heavy makeup.

Now, the burden falls on state officials to tell Meta where to draw the line. But defining where harmless fun ends and harmful manipulation begins is far from straightforward.

Sponsor Message

Impact on youth body image

For teenagers navigating the digital landscape, the pressure of online perfection is a daily reality. Much of that pressure has been driven by online beauty trends like "Instagram face." Coined in 2019 by The New Yorker writer Jia Tolentino, the phrase refers to a look characterized by a small button nose, high cheekbones and pouty lips. While traditionally only achievable in real life through plastic surgery or extreme makeup, it can be applied instantly online using beauty filters.

Mia Lerner, a 17-year-old high school senior in California and a youth body image activist, knows the toll these digital tools can take. She told NPR experimenting with beauty filters contributed to her eating disorder and left her struggling with her self-image.

"I've even tried to fix my nose with AI," Lerner said. "My face looks a lot better, I think, in [the] photo that I manipulated with these beauty filters. But I'm still living with this nose that I see in the mirror."

Lerner welcomes the aspect of the Meta settlement that aims to restrict beauty filters for minors. "It's a very important step in the right direction," Lerner said.

The problem with 'subtle' editing

However, the agreement reached in August between Meta and 47 U.S. states — plus Washington D.C. and three territories — does not institute a blanket ban on all digital effects.

Sponsor Message

Filters that transform users into playful characters, like elves or puppies, will remain available for young people. But so will filters offering subtle beautification effects — such as smoothing skin tone or adding a slight eye glow.

It is this category of relatively minor editing that particularly concerns Lerner.

"When I see something that has been so obviously AI-generated, it's very easy for me to logically say, 'Well, that's obviously been manipulated so I can't compare myself to that,'" Lerner said. "But when I see these videos of people who are just slightly edited, it's a lot easier for me to go down that comparison path."

Tech guardrails vs. moving targets

Meta has previously implemented measures to manage beauty filters, which are increasingly powered by artificial intelligence.

The tech giant has already banned filters that explicitly promote cosmetic surgery, such as those overlaying pre-surgery marker lines onto skin. It has also shut down its platform for third-party creators of these tools, introduced mandatory labels for AI-generated content, and deployed automated AI detection systems. Despite these systems, harmful aesthetic filters and features that keep children trapped in an endless cycle of scrolling, clicking, and staying online persistently slipped past these guardrails, as a federal judge wrote in a summary judgement denying Meta's defense this summer.

Meta is not the only tech company grappling with teen access to beauty filters. TikTok also restricts users under the age of 18 from using them. Snapchat does not restrict teen access to filters. Neither company responded to NPR's request for comment. YouTube told NPR it does not have any filters. But there's nothing stopping users from posting images or videos made with third party filters to the platform — or onto TikTok and Instagram, for that matter.

Meanwhile, state attorneys general are reaching the end of a two-month window they set themselves to provide Meta with guidance in the form of a letter on what constitutes a bannable filter — and what does not.

Evolving beauty standards

They face a moving target, as digital beauty standards evolve rapidly.

"If the states want to define what is a beauty filter, they should define what is beauty," said Florencia Solari, a creative technologist who has spent years developing AI and augmented reality experiences for global brands.

Sponsor Message

Solari noted that trend cycles move quickly. "Instagram face" is already falling out of favor. "People are starting to move away from that because it's starting to look a bit clownish," Solari said. "Now it's going towards extreme thinness. So that's another problem."

As a result, the tools that are used to achieve the latest look are therefore also changing. So what might be branded by lawmakers as an "extreme" beauty filter in 2026 will likely be different in 2027.

Technological changes

While beauty standards are changing quickly, so is technology.

Instead of sitting in boardrooms debating pixel thresholds for cheekbones, Kelly Frasier, the co-author of a recent study highlighting the negative impacts of social media on body issues in adolescents, said legislators should consider the fact that teens will soon be able to use AI to create entire fake universes around themselves, not just change the way they look. So they should focus on broader AI regulation for minors.

"I think that legislators are asking the wrong question if they're asking where to draw the line for beauty filters," said Frasier. "And to be honest, filters will probably become completely obsolete within the next few years."

Legal and regional challenges

On top of the technological and cultural challenges, legal experts warn that individual states may struggle to reach a consensus on what does and does not constitute what the settlement agreement describes as a "cosmetic procedure filter."

"What we don't really have a sense of is what happens if the states disagree with each other?" said David Greene, senior counsel at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. "What if one state finds, you know, eyebrow lifting to be completely acceptable and another one thinks it's awful?"

NPR reached out to the attorneys general offices in all four plaintiff states that led the trial — California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey — for an update on the guidelines. But officials either declined to comment or did not respond.

Sponsor Message

Beyond the U.S., some international regulators are hoping to avoid discussions around beauty filter definitions entirely.

In Europe, the proposed KIDS Act — designed to regulate youth social media usage — takes a sweeping approach.

In that plan, "Beauty filters – not extreme beauty filters; beauty filters full stop – are forbidden for minors," said European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier. Regnier said EU legislators are closely watching the implementation of the U.S. settlement. "We want child-friendly services for our children. A beauty filter has nothing to do with a child-friendly service," Regnier said.

Teens want to be heard

Meta says that it plans to enforce the ban on "cosmetic procedure filters" by early next year.

For youth activists like Lerner, the hope is that tech companies and regulators will include teens in these discussions. "So often it's just the government or these companies in these conversations," Lerner said. "The company should be asking us for our actual perspectives, like 'Are people actually using these extreme AI filters or is that not going to make a difference?' 'Do we need to target something else?'"

Meta said the company has partnered with teens over the years, but did not respond to NPR's question asking if it is doing so currently.

World.title: Carney's geopolitical ambitions tested in defence industry co-operation with Turkey
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

While in Istanbul this past week, Prime Minister Mark Carney struggled for a moment when asked to describe how he felt about limits that had been placed on Ukraine's access to the Starshield military-grade satellite network.

When he found his voice, he spoke about the "immense human suffering" of missile strikes on Kyiv and elsewhere.

"I search for the right adjective to describe whoever took this decision, or a group of people took this decision, against a country — and it's against a country that is literally fighting for the lives of its citizens against naked aggression."

Carney was, however, quick to turn it into an object lesson for Canadians who are skeptical of warming relations with authoritarian-leaning Turkey.

"We as Canadians do not want to be caught in a situation where we are reliant on one provider that may change their view, or may be forced to change their views, by one nation state that puts Canadians at risk — or compromises our sovereignty, our ability to express our values and live our values.”

WATCH | Carney 'concerned' about Starlink slowdown in Ukraine: Carney says he is 'concerned' about reported Starlink slowdown in Ukraine | Duration closed caption 3:10 Prime Minister Mark Carney says he is concerned about the reported slowdown of SpaceX's Starlink satellite system in Ukraine, which created 'real consequences.' He says Canadians likewise 'do not want to be caught in a situation where we are reliant on one provider that may change their view' and compromise Canadian sovereignty.

Early last week, Ukrainian officials said they had lost some of their access to Starshield, the military version of Starlink, the global satellite communications system owned and operated by Elon Musk's company SpaceX.

Ukraine employs Starshield to both track incoming missiles and jet-powered drones, and to guide interceptor and spy drones, while using Starlink for critical internal communications.

Without mentioning the United States or the Trump administration, Carney's reference was clear: We don't want to find ourselves in the same situation as Ukraine.

Canadian officials have made no secret of wanting to reduce reliance on Starlink in favour of a future Telesat system.

'Middle-power co-ordination'

Much of Carney’s recent whirlwind trip to Istanbul and the Turkish capital, Ankara, was framed through the lens of the contradiction of values-based Canadians cosying up to a regime that shuts down opposition television stations, arrests journalists and attacks 2SLGBTQ+ advocates.

What was mentioned as part of a strategic partnership signed by Carney — but received far less scrutiny — is the burgeoning defence-industrial co-operation between the two countries, which arguably is an early test of Carney's geopolitical ambitions.

"Canada-Turkey defence co-operation is an early test of whether the middle-power co-ordination the prime minister called for at Davos can produce anything more durable than a sequence of transactions,” wrote Tolga Demiryol, an associate professor of political science at Altınbaş University in Istanbul. He was referring to Carney's speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January.

A research paper penned by Demiryol was published on the Canadian Global Affairs Institute website in early October.

WATCH | Carney hails new trade, defence pact with Turkey: Carney hails new trade, defence pact with Turkey | Duration 1:48 Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a new strategic trade and defence partnership between Canada and Turkey, as Ottawa continues its drive to tighten relations with other middle powers and fellow NATO members.

He said both countries now share a similar outlook when it comes to the defence industry as an instrument of national sovereignty.

"Canada is seeking to reduce the concentration of its defence procurement in the United States, while Turkey's industry was built through repeated efforts to escape foreign control over critical components and export permissions," Demiryol wrote.

"Turkey is courted today for two reasons: it has more to offer than it once did; and Canada has more reason than it once had to look beyond the United States."

Demiryol also said Carney is is not searching "for a replacement partner, but rather to reduce Canadian exposure to any single foreign supplier."

Leap of faith

In addition to it being an early test of Carney's middle-power strategy, the defence partnership represents a leap of faith.

Not many years have passed since the events that sent relations between Canada and Turkey into the wilderness.

In 2020, Turkish authorities applied for an exemption related to the importation of target acquisition gear, made by Canadian company Wescam, used in Turkey's Bayraktar drones.

WATCH | 'Engagement is not approval,' PM says of Turkish human rights record: Carney asked about Turkey's record on LGBTQ, human rights: 'Engagement is not approval' | Duration closed caption 4:32 Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking from Turkey during a visit to announce increased economic and defence ties, said he has not met with rights' groups but did raise the issue during his visit, saying there are 'very few countries' that share 'the standards of Canada.'

Documents made public stated that Turkish authorities claimed they were using the cameras for reconnaissance activities related to NATO operations in the north of Syria.

But it was later discovered that the cameras were illegally diverted to Azerbaijan and used during the war in Nagorno-Karabakh.

Human rights groups accused Turkey of lying to the Canadian government.

The de facto arms embargo that resulted was lifted in early 2024 when Canada's Department of Foreign Affairs stopped presumptively denying arms export permits to the Middle Eastern country.

While trust has been restored, Carney made clear following talks with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan that the agreement signed on Thursday does not mean unfettered exports and that permits will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.

"We have standards, we have rules and we will follow them, we will continue to follow them," Carney said.

'A lot of lessons for us'

So what's the attraction of Turkey's defence sector? The short answer is the country's capacity to go from reliance on foreign defence contractors to building its own equipment in a short period of time.

"An important point here, I believe that in Turkey, about 80 per cent of the defence needs of this country are produced here. This is not the case in Canada," Carney said. "So there are a lot of lessons for us on how we can create an industry in our country."

It is also the type of military equipment that Turkey is building that makes it attractive.

A Turkish TB2 drone is seen in Golcuk, Turkey, on Aug. 21. (Burak Kara/Getty Images)

Drones are one example. The TB2, manufactured by Baykar — a private defence and tech company that Carney met with during his stop in Istanbul — proved itself in combat during the opening phase of the war in Ukraine by stopping Russian armoured columns with deadly precision strikes. The country is now manufacturing land and sea drones. It is also developing its own next-generation fighter jet, known as KAAN.

Carney didn't rule out buying Turkish military equipment such as the TB2 but suggested the country's know-how and ability to integrate technologies will be important as Canada expands it own industry.

"We're in a position where we're more in need of Turkish expertise in terms of reinforcing what we need to do to protect Canadians and to serve as a full NATO ally at this stage," Carney said.

Investment in Canada

Mike Ward, executive director of the Canada Turkey Business Council, said direct investment is another attractive aspect for the prime minister.

Last year, four major Turkish defence companies visited the Toronto Global Forum and pitched investment in Canada's aerospace sector, among others.

"They said, 'Look, we want to do business with Canada. And sure ... Canadian companies can invest in Turkey if you'd like. But we really want to invest in Canada,'" Ward said.

WATCH | How are Trump��’s Bombardier threats affecting Canada?: How are Trump’s Bombardier threats affecting Canada? | Duration closed caption 1:47 On Monday, U.S. President Donald Trump declared that Quebec-based aerospace company Bombardier would no longer be able to sell planes in the U.S. Shares in the company fell in early trading, but regained some of those losses later in the day Tuesday. Officials say it's not just Bombardier employees in Canada who could be affected.

"And those companies have been back. So they're looking to invest. They're looking to invest in Ontario. They're looking to invest to Quebec."

In Europe, Baykar finalized the purchase of an Italian aerospace company, Piaggio, in June 2025. It is also in joint partnership with that country's leading aircraft maker, Leonardo, to build drones.

Demiryol, of Altınbaş University, said he sees shared production and joint rights as a possible way ahead for Canada and Turkey in this new relationship.

But he said transparency will be key to making it work and avoiding the issues that led to the breakdown in relations.

World.title: Danielle Smith scores slim majority on immigration questions, Albertans reject constitutional changes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Most Albertan voters have sided with the province on its questions relating to immigration, but have rejected constitutional reforms in a controversial referendum this week.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative government asked citizens nine questions, outside the one related to separation, with all five immigration-related questions getting majority approval from voters.

Elections Alberta said in a Sunday afternoon statement that the count had been completed Saturday night, about three days later than the agency had aimed to complete the count and publish the results in order to meet the 48-hour deadline set under Alberta's referendum regulations.

Elections Alberta said it had hand-counted 20,574,612 ballots, which the agency said was the highest number of ballots ever counted by hand in any Canadian electoral event.

Results, including the number of Albertans who cast ballots, will be made official on Oct. 29.

The question with the highest “yes” vote share was Question 5 — requiring proof of citizenship to vote in provincial elections — which garnered 58 per cent support.

Results show about 55 per cent of voters said yes to Alberta’s pitch to take greater control of immigration, in part to decrease the number of newcomers.

The three questions that suggest different methods for limiting public and social services to some non-permanent residents garnered 52.6-, 53- and 52 per cent support.

Smith says she will 'proceed with caution'

As results were still trickling in on Wednesday, Smith told reporters she will prioritize adjusting Alberta’s approach on economic migrants. On the rest of the immigration questions, she said the province will “proceed with caution.”

“I think that people who came here and had certain expectations under one set of rules, it's always very difficult if you change things midstream. So I want to be very cautious about that and try to interpret a little bit of the result that we got back.”

WATCH | A rural-urban divide for 'the 9' in Alberta referendum: A rural-urban divide for 'the 9' in Alberta referendum | Duration closed caption 2:12 Elections Alberta is finalizing the count of referendum ballots, but so far, results suggest rural voters seem to hold different views on immigration and constitutional fights than those in urban areas. CBC’s Nicole Healey has the details.

Lori Williams, Mount Royal University political scientist, doesn’t believe these results are the strong mandate Smith wanted. The government ran a $4-million advertising campaign advocating for Albertans to vote “yes” to the other nine questions.

“The fact that she has … got the results that she does on the nine questions is, I think, a bit of a problem,” Williams said.

“It doesn't give her the mandate she wanted. It doesn't give her the authority to move forward and sort of detract from the issues that were raised by separatists because we have this very close division on all of the questions.”

With the referendum questions being less popular in Calgary and Edmonton, Smith told The Calgary Eyeopener’s Loren McGinnis on Thursday that conservatism across the country needs to figure out how to appeal to urban voters.

‘I think that’s something all conservative leaders are going to have to be thoughtful about,” she said. “The bread and butter conservative issues that matter in rural Alberta are just different than the ones that matter in urban centres.

LISTEN | Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on the province's path forward: Calgary Eyeopener 13:16 Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on the province's path forward We're still learning about how Albertans are responding to nine of the province's referendum questions. As a picture begins to emerge, Alberta Premier, Danielle Smith, joined us to discuss how her government will act upon the results.

All 5 immigration questions pass

The five questions concerning immigration included proposals for the province taking more control over immigration from Ottawa, requiring residents to have an “Alberta-approved immigration status” to be eligible for public and social services, and showing proof of citizenship before voting in elections.

If all five of the successful proposals become law, Alberta could require some temporary residents — such as international students or temporary foreign workers — to have lived in the province for at least 12 months before they can qualify for some provincial social supports such as childcare subsidies, and charge a “reasonable fee or premium” for their use of the public health care and education systems.

Smith has floated the idea of charging temporary residents a $1,900 fee for access to public health care, akin to a premium charged by the United Kingdom.

WATCH | Alberta's referendum questions on immigration, explained: Alberta's referendum questions on immigration, explained | Duration closed caption 14:53 There are five referendum questions for Albertans to consider on immigration. CBC's Rukhsar Ali breaks down each one to look at what happens if you vote 'yes' or 'no.'

Calgarian Camille Katigbak, who owns the marketing agency Katigbak Technologies, is one of the more than half of voters who supported immigration changes. She is also the daughter of immigrants from the Philippines.

To her, the proposed changes make sense. She worries about too many people putting pressure on the system.

“I think if we just limit and kind of pre-qualify, we make sure okay, these people are here for the right reasons, I think that would really help our system be more streamlined and we're not overwhelmed,” she said.

“I do know that we have to help our neighbours too. Like we have to think about helping others, but at what cost, right?”

The question about requiring proof of Canadian citizenship to vote in provincial elections was also something she supported.

WATCH | Why Alberta's fight with Ottawa over immigration won't end soon: Why Alberta's fight with Ottawa over immigration won't end soon | Duration closed caption 3:21 Albertans may have overwhelmingly rejected separating from Canada, but referendum results show significant support for more provincial control over immigration. CBC's Lyndsay Duncombe examines what that means for relations with Ottawa, and the concerns it raises for newcomers in the province.

But not everyone feels as positively about the results as Katigbak does.

Calgarian Dozie Anyaegbunam, who came to Canada from Nigeria in 2021, has been critical of the referendum and had hoped the immigration questions would fail.

While they did pass, the host of The Newcomers podcast said he’s encouraged by how many people voted against them.

“I think it's good to kind of see that it is not an overwhelming majority,” he said. “Even if the government says they have a mandate, they don't have a full mandate. And that gives me some hope in terms of how we move forward from here as a community.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Tuesday that he and Smith had discussed "other priorities" facing Canadians, namely, immigration.

"Constitutional change is difficult, it's long," Carney said. "I believe, for example, on the issue of immigration and co-operation between the federal government and the provinces for sustainable immigration … that we can accomplish that without constitutional change."

Voters reject all 4 constitutional questions

All four Constitution-related questions were rejected, including the proposals relating to the province selecting its own judges for certain courts, abolishing the federal Senate , opting out of some federal programs , and prioritizing provincial laws over federal laws in some areas where they conflict.

Gerard Kennedy, University of Alberta constitutional law professor, said getting the public interested in constitutional amendment has never been easy, and this referendum has not proved to be an exception.

But on the matter of selecting judges, Smith isn’t the only premier who has shown interest in a constitutional change.

Saskatchewan, Quebec and Ontario also have an appetite for selecting their own judges, but Kennedy said the odds of a constitutional amendment “I would think are very, very low.”

“What we could have is agreements from the federal government to change the system to give the provinces more of a weight, but it will ultimately be the decision of the federal government to decide whom to appoint.”

Campaigning less noticeable on the other 9 questions

Amongst third-party advertisers, campaigning on the nine non-separation questions was noticeably less prominent in much of the referendum conversation.

Perhaps the most notable, “No to the Nine” became a memorable slogan on the federalist side, based on signs erected by longtime political strategist Stephen Carter’s campaign Alberta’s Voice.

As early results came in, Carter said he still considered his campaign a success, though the five immigration questions being passed was “a significant blow.”

“Immigrants come to Alberta to do two things: create jobs and do jobs,” he said. “They don't come to take advantage of our healthcare system, they don't come to take advantage of our education system.”

On the flipside, the separatist group Alberta Prosperity Project recently encouraged supporters to “decline” marking an answer on the other nine questions, writing on social media it “would not lend its name to bogus referendum questions.”

A lesser-known group called Alberta Women for Independence was one of the few organizations whose blue pro-separation signs also encouraged yes votes for the nine questions.

When could changes happen?

On Friday, the United Conservative Party laid out its plans for legislation in the upcoming fall sitting, but said Albertans shouldn’t expect to see new laws tied to how they voted in the referendum.

When it comes to new immigration policies, Evan Menzies, vice president at Crestview Strategy, suspects some policies, like requiring non-permanent residents to pay for social services, could take longer to implement.

“That could be too disruptive too fast, there might need to be some sort of transition phase,” said Menzies, who was also formerly a political staffer with the UCP.

“And especially considering that there’s an election 12 months away, I don’t know how much the province has an appetite to push too hard too fast with that respect.”

World.title: Who is B.C.'s new premier Lorne Doerkson?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson struck political gold Saturday night.

The former small-town newspaper publisher delivered a stunning defeat to David Eby's NDP and led the B.C. Conservatives to a commanding majority government.

Early Sunday morning, Doerkson's Conservatives were leading in 64 ridings, reducing the NDP to just 27 seats and toppling several cabinet ministers.

It's a remarkable turnaround for a political party that was in disarray just five weeks ago, days before a snap election was called.

But where his political opponents may have seen weakness, Doerkson said British Columbians chose instead to seize an opportunity.

"For a very long time, a lot of British Columbians have felt like Victoria forgot about them, like the map maybe stopped at Hope," Doerkson told a throng of more than 1,000 supporters at the Rocky Mountaineer Station in Vancouver.

"But tonight the whole map counts."

WATCH | Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson gives victory speech: FULL SPEECH: Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson's victory speech | Duration closed caption 17:01

Rodeos to newspapers to politics

Born in New Westminster, Doerkson grew up in Surrey and the B.C. Interior, before settling in Williams Lake, where he raised a family.

He spent 20 years publishing community newspapers and volunteering with local business and community service groups before entering politics.

"That was a very good education for me," he told supporters. "You learn what’s really going on in a town: who’s hiring, who’s closing, who’s hoping."

Doerkson was first elected in Cariboo-Chilcotin as a B.C. Liberal in 2020, and later joined John Rustad's fledgling Conservative caucus.

His victory makes him the first premier from B.C.'s Interior since Bill Bennett left office in 1986.

Doerkson was on his way home from South Africa last month when he learned his Conservative caucus colleagues wanted him to take over the party as interim leader.

Kerry-Lynne Findlay had just resigned after months of scandals that led to the departure or expulsion of more than a dozen MLAs.

Doerkson admitted he needed convincing.

"Of course, it was a little bit of a short notice," he said in a pre-election interview with CBC News.

Lorne Doerkson speaks to supporters in the crowd during provincial election night Saturday. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

Promises to cut income taxes, red tape

Doerkson spent his victory speech Saturday night introducing himself to British Columbians at the same time as celebrating the "trailblazers" who came to the province searching for gold and a better life.

It's a spirit he told supporters that still animates the province, where people want to build something big, from resource communities through to the big metro areas.

"That is the trailblazing spirit of British Columbia and it never left, it just needs government that’s on its side," he said.

WATCH | CBC News projects a Conservative government: CBC News projects a B.C. Conservative majority government | Duration closed caption 1:59

Doerkson reiterated promises to cut red tape "like it’s never been cut before," speed up forestry and mining permits, and triple natural gas production by 2035.

"A province only works if all of it works," he said.

"A mill running in Quesnel keeps a trucker working in Surrey. A mine opening in the north keeps the port busy in Delta. It’s one economy and it runs through every town on our map."

Doerkson also pledged no new taxes and health care that is "fully and publicly funded."

Still, questions remain about how he'll pay for everything, including a promise to cut income taxes by $1,000 a year.

The province is already on track to see a $13.8-billion deficit in 2026-27.

The NDP spent their campaign warning that the Conservatives' platform could mean cuts to health care and education.

Speaking in Vancouver Saturday, Doerkson reiterated election promises, including to cut red tape 'like it’s never been cut before.' (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

Overcoming divisions

As premier-designate, Doerkson now faces the challenge of not only governing but keeping together a coalition that includes social conservatives and more centrist, fiscal conservatives.

And though he has promised to repeal B.C.’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People’s Act, he appealed to First Nations communities as partners in the province’s development.

"This future is one we build together as partners with the certainty that all of us need," he said.

One source of division Doerkson won't need to deal with immediately will be the NDP.

With preliminary results showing New Democrats reduced to fewer than 30 seats, the Official Opposition's first priority will be choosing a new leader to replace David Eby who announced Saturday that he will step down.

World.title: Trump critic Lula narrowly wins re-election in Brazil presidential vote
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of U.S. President Donald Trump, was re-elected on Sunday in a result that keeps some distance between Latin America's biggest economy and Washington.

With 100 per cent of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula held an unassailable lead.

The announcement capped an evening of chaos at polling places across Brazil, following a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours.

That decision by a Supreme Court justice may trigger legal action by opponent Flávio Bolsonaro.

More to come

World.title: Serbia's longtime strongman Vucic concedes election defeat to student-led opposition
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Serbia's Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Sunday that ends his long grip on power ​and heralds a new political era in the ​Balkan country.

Vucic, a populist and nationalist, has dominated ‌Serbian politics as prime minister or president since 2014.

But he called a snap election in September after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against ⁠perceived corruption and creeping ⁠authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of ‌16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024.

"It is clear that ​we have lost these elections, the Student List has won,' Vucic said in a televised speech.

Within moments of his announcement, the streets of the capital, Belgrade, erupted in celebration after Vucic's announcement, with cars honking and students shouting "victory" and "he's done."

PHOTOS | Serbs celebrate Vucic election defeat:

The students' win marks a profound political shift in the country of some six million people and is reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary's Viktor Orbán in April.

It may also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the ​streets in recent weeks to protest — in some cases violently — against poor education standards and a lack of prospects.

Vucic said the students would ⁠have between 135 and 140 seats in the ⁠250-seat parliament and that his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) will have 105, based on preliminary results.

"Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard," said Radomir Sajcic, a professor at ⁠Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. "Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future."

Record turnout

Lines of unprecedented length had snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country earlier in the day, and even Vucic waited for nearly two hours to vote in Belgrade. Pollsters and the election commission put ⁠turnout at close to 70 per cent, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.

"[The turnout] did not surprise me because there was a large and strong mass that has formed throughout the past two years," voter Katarina Petrovic said.

People line up outside a polling station in Belgrade on Sunday. (Armin Durgut/The Associated Press)

Vucic, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, was a strong incumbent, and few in the student protest movement dared ‌believe that he would concede so fast.

Supporters credit him with modernizing Serbia's economy and building new highways, railways, schools and hospitals.

"Some businessmen, some people will leave us, but our structure is firm, we are very united, very strong, we are used to being in the opposition," Vucic said.

New leadership not yet clear

Much remains unclear about how the student-backed candidates will fare.

Their list of 250 largely unknown personalities includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija ​Srdanovic, although it is still unclear who will be prime minister.

The students' domestic agenda aims to root out graft and improve schooling. Political analysts predict some kind of purge of Vucic allies in the police, security services and ministries. But the ⁠students have been quieter on their international ambitions.

As Vucic did for years, they will have to juggle relations with China, a major investor; Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal ⁠supplier of natural gas; and the European Union, Serbia's largest trading partner.

'People have been waiting for this'

The student-led street protests, sparked by the station disaster, started small but quickly became ⁠the biggest ⁠in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups ​and activists say repression has worsened in the period since.

"For decades the people have been waiting for this time, something to bring hope that we can live freely and by ​the rules of democracy," actor Jelena Stupljanin, 48, ⁠said at a Belgrade polling station.

A voter casts a ballot into a box at a polling station in Belgrade on Sunday. (Marko Djurica/Reuters)

Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He said the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss.

Meanwhile, on the streets of Belgrade, a traditional brass band struck up, and a group including a man in a "students are champions" jumper floated balloons in the shape of the number 3, representing the number of the students' list of candidates.

"We will drink a beer to celebrate, we will get drunk, we are so happy, I have no words ⁠to describe how much," said Andjela, a student who was ‌with a group of friends.

World.title: Is this Quebec-developed fruit the 'apple of the future'?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Orléans apple — developed on Île d’Orléans, Que. — is hitting grocery store shelves this fall, but has been in the works for nearly 25 years.

Beginning back in 2002, producers handpicked pollen from Honeycrisps and Empire apple flowers, and then spent years crossbreeding them until they arrived at the bright red and crisp Orléans. While it has been available in Quebec orchards for about two years, it's only now hitting grocery store shelves.

"I have some clients coming here asking especially for that kind," says Karen Morin. She thinks it just might be "the apple of the future."

The co-owner of the Verger du Roy in Portneuf grows 57 different types of apples, but Morin says the Orléans is growing more and more popular this year with apple pickers.

"It's a mix of Honeycrisp and Empire, so these two together, it's like a bomb. It's really, really good, so sweet [and] still really crispy," says Morin. "In the future, our children, it won't be the Honeycrisp anymore that will be the top one, it will be the Orléans."

Morin says that, while apple preferences can vary from generation to generation, people are always looking for apples that stay crisper longer. She believes that's why the Orléans apple is increasing in popularity.

Karen Morin says the Orléans apple has been growing in popularity for the past two years with apple pickers, but many people still aren't aware of the latest apple varieties coming to the market. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)

"It's like on the top of the list for firmness, and it's almost top of the list for sugar content," says

Benoit Caron, the owner of La Maison de la Pomme. Caron planted 20,000 Orléans trees at his orchard in Frelighsburg about five years ago.

"It's not the first apple created in Quebec, but it's the first one that we can supply at least 10 months a year because of [its] conservation," says Caron.

He adds that this particular variety is great as a snack, "but it's also a really good apple for cooking. It will hold itself together. So if you do apple custard or apple pie, you will have the nice apple slice that will stay together."

More supply and more demand for Quebec produce

Jérôme-Antoine Brunelle, the executive director of the Producteurs de pommes du Québec, says it's good to have new varieties to appeal to all the different types of consumers, but that the demand for Quebec produce has also been growing recently.

"If these new varieties can help us gain market shares from imported apples and that we can source more of Quebec-grown apples to consumers, it's a win for everyone," he says.

Brunelle says recent tensions with the U.S. and tariff woes did have an impact. "Consumers had more of an interest in locally sourced food," he says, and apples were no exception.

There’s been a bigger interest for locally sourced apples for the past two years, "and it doesn't seem to be slowing down," says the executive director of the Producteurs de pommes du Québec, Jérôme-Antoine Brunelle. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)

"That interest for locally sourced fruit helps us out, and we see that Quebec consumers are more conscientious of where their food comes from," says Brunelle.

He says he is aware, however, that producers and grocery stores must make sure Quebec apples are clearly identified as such in produce aisles to attract more consumers .

Different regions, different apples, different ciders

Claude Jolicoeur, an author who's published three books about apples and cider production, wants to increase the number of apple varieties in Quebec, specifically for cider. "And eventually maybe to have an appellation ‘regional cider,'" he says.

Jolicoeur says this could bring Quebec cider production to another level, similar to wine production in Italy — where different grape varieties, grown in different regions, produce different types of wines, with distinct flavours.

Morin, for instance, says Quebec-grown apples can also taste like other fruits, such as bananas, pineapples, strawberries, and even chestnuts.

"You can compare apples with apples, but they're different," she says.

Regardless of their provenance or flavour, cider apples would not be the same ones as those picked in orchards, or bought at the grocery store, however. "When you want to sell apples in a grocery store, that apple has to be beautiful," says Jolicoeur.

In the cider context, however, he notes, "no one is going to see the apple, so what it looks like is not important at all."

Jolicoeur hopes Quebec cider and apple producers will grow more and more Quebec apple varieties in the coming years.

However, apple producers reiterate, in the meantime, several apple varieties are already available year round, not only in the fall — including the brand new Orléans.

World.title: Funeral mourners recall friendship, dedication of sergeant killed in CFB Wainwright fire
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A funeral home in central Edmonton was full Sunday morning, with most in attendance wearing poppies over their hearts to honour the sergeant who died last weekend at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, in central Alberta.

Eight service members carried the casket of Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, draped in the Maple Leaf, to the front of the room as bagpipes played him in.

The flag was later replaced with a yellow descendants’ blanket — a traditional Chinese textile used during funerals — before a shrine, featuring a framed photo of Wong, fruit, rice and flowers, was placed in front of the casket and other Buddhist funeral customs were performed.

“Each one of us has our own special memories of Morgan, and I hope holding onto those memories will remind us to live our lives with courage and integrity, like he did,” his sister, Megan, said in a speech during the service.

“He was too young when he left us,” she said. “But I hope his life will be a reminder for each of us to use the time we have to achieve a life we would be proud of.”

WATCH | Sgt. Morgan Wong's funeral in Edmonton on Sunday: Funeral held for sergeant who died at CFB Wainwright | Duration closed caption 1:46 Soldiers, family and friends gathered Sunday for the funeral for sergeant Morgan Wong, one of the four soldiers who died at CFB Wainwright this month. CBC’s Nicole Healey has more from outside the funeral home.

Megan described her brother as brave, warm and hilarious, a loyal friend and dedicated soldier. She added that Wong was close to their mother — and that now they’re together again.

The family also offered their condolences to the other soldiers who died and were injured at CFB Wainwright.

A fire at CFB Wainwright on Oct. 17, resulting from a training exercise, was first reported in the base's grenade launcher range — a "permanent danger area" that base firefighters couldn't enter. Strong winds in the region that day spread the flames quickly, overwhelming service members and eventually burning beyond the base.

The fire caused dozens of casualties and killed four service members including Wong, a member from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment who served with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

Canadian Armed Forces members arrive at the memorial service for Sgt. Morgan Wong, held Sunday in Edmonton. The funeral home was full during the ceremony. (James Maclennan/The Canadian Press)

“The love that Canadians have shown for Sgt. Wong means more to all of us than we could ever explain. We will always remember him, and his family will forever be part of our family,” Lt.-Col. Bryn Wright, commanding officer of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, said in a written statement to journalists Sunday.

In a statement issued earlier this week, Wong's family expressed their love for him and how proud he had made them. They said he joined the military in 2017 and was training at CFB Wainwright last weekend to prepare for a second deployment to Europe.

During Sunday's service, Wright, who knew Wong throughout the sergeant's military career, shared three stories that spoke to Wong's dedication to service and discipline to hold trainees to the highest standard.

"Passionate, professional, committed to excellence — that was Sgt. Morgan Wong," he said, later adding that every service member in attendance Sunday will carry his example with them.

Some fellow service members and Wong’s longtime friends also shared stories during the ceremony that highlighted similar traits: humour, integrity, generosity and a willingness to help out however he could. Each expressed gratitude for knowing him.

One of Wong's longtime, childhood friends, shown here before Sunday's memorial service, shared multiple anecdotes during the ceremony about the man's humour, their shared disdain for the Kansas City Chiefs and Wong's love for boneless chicken wings at Boston Pizza. (James Maclennan/The Canadian Press)

Since the news of his death, friends and people Wong volunteered with described him as a passionate volunteer and a mentor.

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack and some city councillors attended Sunday’s service. Afterward, Knack told reporters he was happy the community was able to come together to celebrate Wong’s life and his impact on people across the country.

“This is somebody who, no matter who you were, was there to support you,” he said. “It’s impossible to replace someone like that, who’s given so much.

Knack added he hopes Canadians can practise the level of care Wong showed for others moving forward.

World.title: Ukraine says its military did not violate Starlink terms, disputing Elon Musk claim
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian officials have disputed claims by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk that the country's military violated Starlink's terms of service by using the civilian satellite internet network for offensive drone strikes.

Serhii Beskrestnov, a defence technology adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said long-standing restrictions on the civilian system in Ukraine made such offensive use impossible.

"It's very strange that Elon Musk doesn't know about the restrictions on Starlink's operation in Ukraine," he wrote in an online post.

SpaceX's Starlink and its military-focused Starshield service are critical to Ukraine's wartime connectivity. Earlier this month, Ukrainian drones connected to Starshield lost connectivity at high speeds, disrupting air defences during daily Russian air attacks. Officials said the so-called speed caps were lifted on Saturday, and the service was restored.

Still, questions have persisted about who ordered the interruptions to satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks .

Writing on Telegram, Beskrestnov said that drones operated via the civilian Starlink system had a speed restriction of 70 to 90 km/h within Ukraine and did not work in Russia.

Serhii Beskrestnov, also known as Flash, an adviser to Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says it would not be possible for Ukraine's military to use Starlink for offensive drone strikes. (Efrem Lukatsky/The Associated Press)

"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes or medium-range strikes," he said.

Musk acknowledged on Saturday that SpaceX had throttled Starlink in Ukraine.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

But he maintained that the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication.

U.S. President Donald Trump has maintained that he didn't make that call, while Vice-President JD Vance has hinted at White House co-ordination with Musk.

Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the Ukrainian military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.

They also added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by Trump's reported deal with Moscow to import diesel from Russia that Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.

New push to end the war

The restoration of Starlink service followed a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month.

On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by efforts from both first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy on Sunday said Russia had launched nearly 2,300 drones targeting Ukrainian cities over the past week, renewing his call on Western allies to speed up deliveries of interceptors.

He said the attacks — many of them deadly — had affected nine regions of the country, damaging power plants, grain stores, civilian homes and commercial facilities.

WATCH | Mark Carney on consequences of Starlink slowdown: Carney says he is 'concerned' about reported Starlink slowdown in Ukraine | Duration closed caption 3:10 Prime Minister Mark Carney says he is concerned about the reported slowdown of SpaceX's Starlink satellite system in Ukraine, which created 'real consequences.' He says Canadians likewise 'do not want to be caught in a situation where we are reliant on one provider that may change their view' and compromise Canadian sovereignty.

More civilian deaths

Russia launched more than 20 attacks on Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region overnight into Sunday, using drones and an aerial bomb, according to local authorities. Three people died at the scene and a fourth man later died in hospital, regional military administration head Oleksandr Hanzha reported, while over a dozen people were injured.

In Vinnytsia, a city in central Ukraine, at least six people were injured when a Russian drone struck a residential building, according to the state emergency service. The attack also damaged a nearby care home, with emergency crews evacuating 15 elderly residents, the service said.

Also according to the emergency service, consecutive Russian strikes on a shopping centre in Kharkiv injured four people late on Saturday, including three rescue workers. Ukraine has long accused Russia of so-called double-tap strikes, in which an initial attack is followed by another once rescuers arrive on the scene.

Firefighters work at the site of the shopping mall missile strike in Kharkiv on Saturday. (Sofiia Gatilova/Reuters)

Russia's Defence Ministry on Sunday claimed its forces targeted multiple sites in and around Kharkiv, including a shopping and logistics centre that it said had stored dual-use goods meant for the Ukrainian military.

In Russia, two people were killed and 13 others injured in Belgorod, a city 40 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, following "mass" nighttime drone strikes by Kyiv, regional Gov. Alexander Shuvayev reported on Sunday.

In the Russian city of Oryol, body of a fourth victim was pulled from the rubble the day after a Ukrainian strike on an industrial plant, local Gov. Andrey Klychkov reported. On Saturday, local authorities said three people had been killed in the attack.

Ukraine's general staff that day said its forces hit an electronics plant in Oryol that makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities.
