World.title: Full speed ahead: The 39th Carrera Panamericana lives up to its billing
World.content:
“Mexico is the only place in the world where you can pass the police while going 180 mph, and they’ll smile and wave at you,” said Jan Bednar, a professional race car driver who made his debut in Mexico. “I love it. I’m having the best time.”

A few days prior, Bednar had arrived in Mexico from Czechia to compete in the legendary La Carrera Panamericana, or the Pan-American Race.

The Czech driver brought a restored 1969 BMW 3.0 CS that once competed in the Pan-Am over a decade ago. He even gathered the original team that had once raced in Mexico with the same vehicle — a classic German speedster that he said he found collecting dust in a forlorn garage in Eastern Europe. He was inspired when, after asking around, he found out about its former days in the Pan-Am.

Bednar was one of many international motorists from 15 countries to have saved up enough resources — upwards of $75,000 — to race in the 39th edition of La Carrera Panamericana.

A deadly origin story on the open highway

The race has developed a notorious reputation as one of the most dangerous, even deadly, open-road endurance rallies in the world. It launched in 1950 as part of an initiative from the Mexican government to highlight its completion of the Pan-American Highway.

The highway itself, which spans 19,000 miles, was proposed by the United States as a railroad in 1889. In 1923, that idea evolved into an automobile thoroughfare and was revisited at the International Conference of American States in Santiago, Chile.

It took 13 years for the 21 involved nations to sign on to build their respective sections, a sprawling agreement finalized at the Convention on the Pan-American Highway in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

In 1936, the highway — heralded as an international diplomatic success — announced the completion of its first section from Laredo, Texas, to Mexico City. Eventually, Mexico became the first country to finish its border-to-border commitment, prompting the idea for the inaugural Pan-Am race.

The race has since had a controversial, albeit exhilarating, history that brings professional racers, amateurs and hobbyists to Mexico for the landmark event. Known for its high death toll, with more than 30 fatalities in the first five years of its existence, the race was canceled in 1955 and remained dormant until 1988, when it returned in a modernized and regulated format.

A modern course winding through mountain passes

Today, the course extends from Chiapas to Chihuahua, covering eight states and nearly 2,400 miles for a seven-day haul across Mexico’s public roads. It is sectioned into timed portions and various classifications.

While Mexican road conditions have significantly improved since the 1950s, the race is still seen as a perilous task and offers a highly coveted trophy.

After kicking off on Friday, Oct. 16, in Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the 50 registered crews and their vehicles — mostly vintage Porsches, Fords, Studebakers and Chevrolets — flock northward along the coast of Veracruz and up to the state’s port city before banking inland and ascending up the rainy highway into the Sierra Madre mountains toward Puebla.

The 100 drivers made a colorful pit stop in Xalapa, where hundreds of local fans gathered in the parking lot of a science museum to cheer on the competitors, who drove through the city’s avenues as a caravan. Many drivers got out to mingle with supporters and took a smoke break before blazing off in an impressive procession of throttling engines.

The loudest applause came when Xalapa’s first local team, Don Justo, made its anticipated debut. Its two Mexican drivers, Iván Martínez and Salvador Aburto, received a hero’s welcome on their home turf.

Local fandom and international drivers unite

Fans of all ages gathered to witness La Carrera Panamericana in person, which has only passed through Veracruz a handful of times because the route continuously shifts with each edition.

“Motorsports have had a major boom in Mexico since Checo Pérez (debuted in Formula One in 2013),” said Arturo Ibáñez Gómez, a fan from Xalapa. “But it’s not common to always see these racers up close, especially in smaller cities.”

Despite a busy work schedule, Ibáñez Gómez said he wouldn’t miss the rare chance to see the race cars up close, even braving the scattered rain and high winds that morning.

He certainly wasn’t alone in his dedicated fandom. Ramsés López and his father, Alejandro, were in attendance among hundreds of others as car enthusiasts and vintage collectors. For them, having the race in their hometown was a blessing.

For others, being in Xalapa — let alone Mexico — was an unlikely yet thrilling moment. Carter Fournier of Dallas, Texas, entered the race with his 1970 Porsche 911. Like many participants, it was his first time racing south of the U.S. border.

“This is the last road race like this of its kind in the world. It’s special,” Fournier said. “There’s nothing like it left. This is the best of the best. It doesn’t get any better.”

A timeless tradition in North American racing

Notable racers included former Production World Rally Championship champion Benito Guerra Jr., a Mexican legend who was swarmed by fans in his 1983 Porsche 911. His small but muscular car was tailored with RSR specs built specifically for tarmac rally racing.

Though the race has lost some of its universal fame over the decades, it still evokes a sense of romantic timelessness from a renegade era of Mexican motorsports.

For those in the know, it’s a holy grail event in North American racing lore — and worth standing around in inclement weather as part of a large crowd just to give a driver a thumbs-up (trust me, they’ll always give you one back).

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: From the archive: What’s inside that piñata? A guide to Mexican candy
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in June 2025 — is a humorous yet informative look at the candies waiting to be liberated inside Mexico’s iconic piñatas.

If you’ve been in Mexico for a while, chances are you’ve been invited to — and perhaps attended — a few children’s parties.

Whether or not you know the child being celebrated is truly irrelevant. A party is something their parents throw, and they get a big say in who attends. This is only right because parties are expensive.

Sure, at least some of the kid’s friends will be there too. But you’d be forgiven for peeking into a salón de fiesta and wondering why a bunch of beer-drinking grown-ups rented a bouncy house.

A central feature of the Mexican kid’s party — and Christmas party, and New Year’s party — is, of course, the piñata.

Piñatas, as you might guess, have been around for quite a while. Before the papier-mâché varieties of today, for example, piñatas were literally clay pots. (For an informative read on the history of piñatas, check out MND’s excellent article on the subject.)

As a parent, I have watched as my daughter and other guests take turns trying to smash many a piñata to smithereens. My voice has gone hoarse from singing the “dale dale” song; thankfully, I usually have a beer to soothe it. And of course, my heart has stopped many times as I watched particularly enthusiastic children swing with all their might, even as others rushed toward them, one or two pieces of candy on the ground already.

Piñata candy-collecting is not a sport for the weak. You either rush in there and scoop up candy as fast as you can — or you don’t get candy. My daughter, whom I’ve infected with some of my gringa sensibilities, tends to hang back and grab stragglers, often sharing with smaller kids. This is kind, yes, but it’s also safe: She knows she’ll get a gift bag at the end of the party too. Under no circumstances will she go without.

You might think that once your kids get candy, you’ll get candy. This is true. There’s usually plenty to go around, along with — thank goodness — a big supply of local dentists.

Some of the candy is what we’re already familiar with, like chocolate. There are paletas (suckers) too, of course, and the little pieces of hard candy called caramelos.

But, oh, the variety. Everyone seems to love these things around here, so let’s have a look at what some of the less-familiar ones are!

Miguelitos

I have not met a Mexican who does not love miguelitos. My daughter loves them too. I, myself, would rather eat paint chips.

What are miguelitos, you may ask? Well, they’re little paper or plastic packets of powder that, since they’re sold as candy, you would think would be sweet. Basically, it’s a chamoy-flavored powder.

And what is chamoy, you may ask? It’s the stuff on the rim of your glass if you have a michelada, for one. It’s sweet, sour, salty and spicy all at the same time, and Mexicans go nuts for it. In powder or sauce, it goes on fruit, candy, popcorn, the rims of glasses or straight into the mouth. For a fascinating history of chamoy in Mexico, check out this video.

Pelón Pelo Rico

This is another favorite of pretty much every kid I know, including my daughter, and is in the tamarind candy category. Its presentation is silly: it’s a push-up goo made to look like a little green fellow’s red hair. It’s tangy and spicy, and also a little … salty? Not my bag, but it doesn’t have to be: It’s got tons of fans.

Tamarind is the featured flavor in a few other popular Mexican candies as well, like Pulparindo, which my partner calls his personal favorite. This one is just a bit heavier on the spiciness and saltiness — and it’s chewy, like a fruit roll-up. Salty fruit roll-ups, anyone? There’s also a kind of tamarind pulp sold in an actual plastic spoon to lick off!

Mazapán

Now that we’ve talked about some of the many things they put salt and chile in, let’s move on to something, in my opinion, much tastier. Mazapán — De la Rosa is the brand — is a round disk of ground peanuts and sugar pressed together. It’s technically a solid, but it has a way of both breaking off and then melting in your mouth that’s just so satisfying.

Obleas

I was very confused the first time someone handed me one of these. “Are these two body-of-Christ wafers with caramel in the middle?” That’s exactly what they are.

The cream in the middle is cajeta, a gooey caramel made from goat’s milk (the similar dulce de leche is made from cow’s milk). There are also cajeta suckers, which are delicious, and rollos de guayaba filled with cajeta, which are also worth seeking out, though they can’t typically be found in a piñata. I just wanted to mention them because I love them.

Paleta payaso

If you’re lucky, there will be a few of these in the piñata. The paleta payaso is a chocolate-covered marshmallow on a stick with a candied smiley face.

Unwrapping one is always a comical event, because the face is always misshapen. I remember frowning for a good five seconds the first time someone handed me one. But it’s pretty good.

Which Mexican candies do you like?

This article isn’t a complete list — obviously. I tried to stick mostly to things that might seem foreign to … well, foreigners.

Even after 23 years, there are some of these candies that I just don’t like: chile and salt with sweet and sour, for example, will never be okay in my book. But most candies, I do like.

So come on, out with it: What are your Mexican faves?

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Trade optimism holds despite a CIA-linked treason case
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico and the United States were “very close” to a trade deal, both presidents said this week — but lower tariffs were still a negotiating goal, not an agreement. Meanwhile, the arrest of Chihuahua’s former attorney general over alleged unauthorized CIA involvement in a drug raid sharpened the dispute over foreign agents operating in Mexico.

At home, Sheinbaum acknowledged that fuel seized in a much-publicized bust was not stolen, while Guadalajara residents continued to march for clean water. Water is on the mind of many outside Jalisco as well, as recent rains have proven insufficient to ease drought across areas of the country. Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Tariff talks and sovereignty

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said Monday that Mexico hoped for U.S. tariff reductions before year-end. Steel and aluminum face 50% duties, while vehicle tariffs include exemptions for U.S. content. USMCA remains in effect despite Washington’s July decision not to extend it another 16 years.

On Tuesday, Sheinbaum outlined the remaining obstacles to a trade agreement: Washington was offering tariff reductions in exchange for concessions Mexico had not fully accepted. She said Mexico would not accept terms that run contrary to its laws or that damage the economy or jobs.

Meanwhile, former Chihuahua Attorney General César Jáuregui was arrested for treason over allegations he authorized CIA participation in an April drug-lab raid without federal approval. On Friday, Sheinbaum recounted how Chihuahua Gov. Maru Campos denied authorizing foreign agents, accusing Jáuregui during a tense private meeting in September.

Mexico also announced plans to file a complaint over Emiliano Andrade Covarrubias’ death in ICE custody. The Foreign Ministry counted 18 Mexican deaths in custody or during immigration operations since Trump’s second term began. At the same time, U.S. authorization to test a heat ray along the Mexico-U.S. border raised concerns about possible burn injuries to targets on both sides of the border.

Security claims under scrutiny

On Tuesday, the U.N. Committee on Enforced Disappearances’ chairman urged General Assembly consideration of Mexico’s disappearances crisis. Mexico rejects the committee’s crimes-against-humanity characterization.

Wednesday brought official figures of 2,539 fuel-related arrests since October 2024, but also a qualification: Sheinbaum said 59 million liters confiscated in Guanajuato were not stolen or illegally imported. The company from which the fuel was confiscated had produced documentation establishing the facility’s legal operation, while the federal prosecutor in Guanajuato was fired and placed under investigation over irregularities in the bust.

Friday’s urban security survey found 58.1% of adults in surveyed cities felt unsafe, the lowest proportion in the series begun in 2013.

Water protests and persistent drought

Guadalajara’s contaminated-water crisis drew another mass protest a week after a similar protest ended with arrests and accusations of police brutality. This past Sunday, some 10,000 people marched. Participants blamed masked infiltrators for violence along the route, but their affiliations remained unestablished. Residents’ demands for clean tap water remained unresolved.

Nationally, rainfall had not erased accumulated drought deficits. Moderate-to-severe drought covered 12.7% of Mexico on Oct. 15, compared with 7.5% a year earlier. Rain helped some northern areas but failed to reverse earlier shortfalls in the south and southeast.

Economy and labor

The peso closed Thursday at 18.71 per dollar, depreciating 9.7% since Sept. 4. A narrower Mexico-U.S. interest-rate gap and trade uncertainty contributed to the slide.

Also on Thursday, the government announced 20 additional industrial parks, bringing Plan México’s operating total to 40.

In labor news, healthcare workers’ protests appear to be winding down after the union representing IMSS workers negotiated a new pay agreement. The package combines 4% more base pay with 4% in housing assistance, below the requested 10% base-pay increase; demonstrators also demanded medicines and better conditions. While protesters have promised to keep pressing for a better deal, attendance at the most recent marches dwindled following the improved pay offer.

Healthcare was not the only public service under examination: MND’s education deep dive found that more young adults are completing upper secondary education, even as education spending as a share of GDP and student test scores declined over the periods reviewed.

Politics and legislation

The Morena party’s dominance in Mexican politics appears to be holding strong, with early polling showing Morena as the overwhelming favorite in next year’s 2027 midterm elections. The party is preferred by 46% of Mexicans, although 31% expressed no preference and party preferences for gubernatorial contests were more varied.

Senators approved legislation that would allow the Finance Ministry to require digital payments in designated sectors, with gas stations and highway tollbooths expected to be among the first affected. Supporters say the measure would combat tax evasion; opponents warn it could exclude people who rely on cash

Congress also approved the so-called “anti-meme law,” penalizing misuse of official government logos. Supporters say it targets fraud; opponents warn ambiguous wording could threaten satire and political criticism.

Culture

In San Cristóbal de las Casas, a new textile conservation laboratory will repair damaged garments and protect the Maya World Textile Center’s 3,400-piece collection from insects and fungi. Other traditions found an audience onstage: 12 delegations brought music and masked dances to Oaxaca’s first Afro Guelaguetza, a dedicated celebration of Afro-Mexican heritage in Chacahua Isla. Further afield, Ballet Folklórico will celebrate its 75th anniversary with a 24-city U.S. tour, featuring regional dances and live music.

Other news from across Mexico

Looking ahead

The week ends with tariff relief still unresolved and new payments legislation awaiting promulgation. The Federal Reserve’s Oct. 27–28 meeting, followed by Banxico’s Nov. 5 decision, will put interest rates back in focus after the peso’s recent slide. Businesses and consumers will also be watching for Hacienda’s designation of sectors facing cash-payment restrictions once the legislation takes effect. Meanwhile, across Mexico, families and communities are preparing to remember their dead on Nov. 1–2.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Brazil Vote Dispute: Claims and Facts
World.content:
Brazil votes on electronic machines run by the electoral court, which also registers every published opinion poll. (Photo: "Urna eletrônica brasileira UE2020" by TSE - Tribunal Superior Eleitoral, via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.)

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS

Published Sunday, 25 October, 8:15 p.m. ET (00:15 Monday, Lisbon) · Source: TSE data, court statements, party and official statements

Key Facts The count With all polling stations counted, Lula has 51.77% of valid votes against 48.23% for Flávio Bolsonaro.

The trigger A Supreme Court order extended voting two hours; the right calls it interference, Lula’s allies say buses failed.

The mood The right attacks the court order; Lula’s side says the right is preparing to contest.

The status The TSE’s formal declaration follows; no winner is declared until then.

Prediction markets · who wins the runoff Implied chance of winning Brazil’s presidency on 25 October, from traders’ prices. Polymarket Flávio Bolsonaro 0.1% · Lula 99.9% (US$238 million traded) Kalshi (regulated in the US by the CFTC) Flávio Bolsonaro 0.4% · Lula 99.8% As of 25 October, 8:20 pm ET (00:20 Lisbon), updated every 20 minutes. Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them. Want prediction market reports on Brazil? Get yours free, right after you confirm →

The Mood Tonight

Brazil went to bed on Sunday with a shock. Nearly every final poll, and the prediction markets until Sunday afternoon, had Flávio Bolsonaro ahead; the count now shows Lula leading, 51.77% to 48.23%, with all polling stations counted.

Brazil Election Data Room Runoff poll average: Flávio Bolsonaro 51.0 %, Lula 49.0 % 45 national polls from 21 pollsters since 4 October, updated hourly. Every poll, free to download. Open the Data Room · Download the CSV · Embed the chart

The spark was a Supreme Court order. Justice Cristiano Zanin extended voting nationwide to 7 p.m. Brasília time after both campaigns complained, and the electoral court, the TSE, paused results for about two hours.

How the Right Talks

File photo

Opposition lawmakers, among them members of Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL), say Zanin trampled the TSE’s authority and helped only Lula. Marcel van Hattem called the order an “absurdity” and an attempt to win “in the courtroom,” and said he would seek impeachment of justices who abused their power.

WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Nikolas Ferreira, a PL deputy, said the extension helped “only one team,” and Bia Kicis said she could smell “a PT coup in the air.” Flávio Bolsonaro, after voting, said Brazil cannot take four more years as it is; he had not contested the count in public by 00:40 in Lisbon.

How the Left Talks

Lula’s coalition says it asked for more time because mayors had cut bus fleets in Bahia and São Paulo, leaving voters stranded. Lula said he would accept the result whoever wins.

Lula’s allies describe the right as preparing a challenge in advance. A Goldman Sachs analysis had warned that a margin below one point could raise the risk of a contested result.

The Institutions Speak

TSE president Kassio Nunes Marques said no polling station needed paper ballots and that criticism of the court is welcome. Judges at the electoral court, speaking privately, were reported to see Zanin’s order as stepping on their turf while ruling out a “third round.”

Tereza Cristina, a senator, said the episode will leave marks on the electoral system. Senate president Davi Alcolumbre asked everyone to accept the ballot result, and São Paulo governor Tarcísio de Freitas had said before the count that Flávio would “pacify” the country.

What Is Being Whispered

Rumour one: the extension was meant to prepare the annulment of the runoff. Sebastião Coelho, a retired judge, said in a video that “we are facing the preparation to annul this second round” and called it “a great fraud”; his followers point to the timing of Lula’s request and Zanin’s order.

Rumour two: the machines can be rigged because they print no vote for the voter to check. Flávio Bolsonaro said in July that Brazil’s machines share an origin with those of the company Smartmatic, and his supporters point to the missing paper trail.

Rumour three: poll watchers should be policed. Flávio urged supporters on voting day to go to polling places after 5 p.m. to watch whether election workers registered votes for absent voters; opponents called that a recipe for intimidation.

Rumour four, from the other side: the right is laying the ground for a coup narrative. Left commentators point to Ferreira’s own warning that the extension could feed one, and to Jair Bolsonaro’s years of attacks on the machines.

The Questions People Are Asking

Why did the polls miss? The final polls gave Flávio 50.7% to 51% of valid votes, our own average 51%, against about 48.2% in the count, a gap of nearly three points; in the first round the polls had Lula ahead and Flávio won 47.03% to 45.16%.

Who sits where? Zanin was Lula’s personal lawyer and joined the Supreme Court in 2023 on Lula’s appointment.

Nunes Marques, the TSE president, and André Mendonça, its vice president, were appointed to the Supreme Court by Jair Bolsonaro.What about the machines?Brazil’s voting machines give voters no paper receipt, and each prints a result bulletin (boletim de urna) at closing, published by polling section.

In the United States, President Donald Trump wrote on 4 October that Detroit and Philadelphia “will often take weeks to Rig,” and he has said Washington is “watching.”

What Happens Next

The TSE will formally declare the winner, and challenges must be filed with the electoral courts within legal deadlines. The president-elect takes office on 5 January 2027.

World.title: Serbia’s Socialists Miss Parliament Cutoff
World.content:
File photo: Ivica Dačić in 2011. Photo: Medija centar Beograd, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Published Sunday, 25 October, 8:10 p.m. ET · Source: CeSID, Ipsos, Socialist Party of Serbia, Kalshi

Key Facts Projection: CeSID, a Belgrade election-monitoring group, and Ipsos, a polling firm, give the protest-backed Student List 52.9% and Vučić’s list 38.8%.

Socialists: The Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) fell below the 3% entry threshold, with about 2% in projections.

Leader: Ivica Dačić, the SPS chief, said the party missed the threshold and congratulated the Student List.

Prediction markets: Kalshi, a US prediction market, prices the Student List 96% to win, Vučić’s list 1%, 8:02 p.m. ET.

Serbia’s Socialist Party, a long-time coalition partner of the ruling camp led by Aleksandar Vučić, has missed the 3% threshold needed to enter parliament, projections showed on Sunday 25 October. Its leader, Ivica Dačić, accepted the outcome and congratulated the winning Student List, the list backed by the student protest movement.

The Socialists have been part of Serbian politics since the 1990s, when the party was led by Slobodan Milošević, Serbia’s strongman of that decade. For readers abroad, their exit shows how far the vote moved against the old governing coalition, as our earlier report on Vučić’s concession described.

Socialists Fall Below the Entry Line

CeSID, the Center for Free Elections and Democracy, and Ipsos project 52.9% for the Student List and 38.8% for the list headed by Vučić, “Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia”. The Socialist list, called “Ivica Dačić – Factor of Stability”, stood at about 2%, below the 3% line a list needs to win seats.

The threshold does not apply to lists of ethnic minorities, which have separate rules. Lists that clear the line share the 250 seats in proportion to their votes.

Projections gave the Student List between 138 and 140 of the 250 seats in the National Assembly, Serbia’s parliament. A majority needs 126 seats, as our projection report explained.

Dačić Concedes but Vows to Fight On

Dačić told a press conference that the party had tried to claim political space in what he called a “referendum atmosphere”. He said that atmosphere “is unbeatable” and that “we did not manage to achieve the result we wanted”.

He thanked about 100,000 people who voted for the list and called it “one lost battle”. He congratulated the winners, including the Student List, and said the party would keep fighting for Serbia.

File photo: Serbian flags at a night protest in central Belgrade.

A Vote Shaped by Student Protests

The early election, called on 9 September 2026, followed nearly two years of student-led protests against Vučić’s governing system. Many analysts treated the vote as a referendum on that system, which is the frame Dačić himself used.

The Student List, campaigning under the slogan “Students Win”, grew out of those protests. Its main rival, Vučić’s list, has said it lost, and our election-day report set out how the contest was framed.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Kalshi, the Student List was priced at 96% to win the Serbian parliamentary election and the Vučić-led list at 1%, at 8:02 p.m. ET on 25 October. The market had traded 143,637 contracts, and Polymarket, another prediction market, priced the Student List at 99.2% to win.

A separate Kalshi market priced the Student List at 96% to win at least 46% of the vote and 86% to win at least 50%. Kalshi is regulated in the US by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), and its prices are bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

If the projections hold, Serbia’s next parliament will contain far fewer of the parties that ran the country for years. Investors, diplomats and travellers watching the Western Balkans should expect the Student List to lead coalition talks, with the pace set by the official count.

The Socialists’ fall also shows the cost of sharing power with a camp voters rejected. That pattern, a junior partner hit harder than the leader, is worth watching in other elections where voters turn on an incumbent.

What Is Not Known

The official result of the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), the state body that runs the vote, is not yet published. It has up to 96 hours after polls close, so the exact Socialist share and the final seat split may still change.

It is also unknown whether Dačić will stay on as party leader, and which minority lists will win seats. We will update the Serbia coverage when RIK publishes figures.

World.content:
Aerial view of the National Congress and the Esplanada dos Ministérios in Brasília, file photo. (Photo: Agência Brasil archive, CC BY 3.0 BR)

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS · PREDICTION MARKETS

Published Sunday, 25 October 2026, 7:30 p.m. ET · Source: Superior Electoral Court (TSE, Brazil’s official vote counter) count, Polymarket and Kalshi market data

Key Facts — Prediction markets Polymarket: President Lula wins by under 4 points, 83%, up 67 points in 24 hours (7:29 p.m. ET).

— Second exchange Kalshi, a US exchange regulated by the CFTC (the US derivatives regulator): Lula by 3–6 points, 57%.

— Count Lula leads by 0.74 point with 55.56% of polling sections counted (7:30 p.m. ET).

Prediction-market traders now put the chance of a Lula win at 91%, and most of that money expects a close finish. On Polymarket, a crypto-based exchange, the contract for the winner of the runoff stands at 91% for President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and 9% for Flávio Bolsonaro (7:20 p.m. ET), and Kalshi agrees at 91%.

On Polymarket, a crypto-based exchange, the price for “Lula wins by under 4 points” rose about 67 points in 24 hours to 83%.It matters to US readers because Brazil is Latin America’s largest economy, and a razor-thin result can keep investors in Brazilian stocks, bonds and the real waiting.

The move coincided with the start of the official count, which shows the two candidates close together.

In Plain English Runoff: a second vote between the top two candidates, held because nobody won more than half of the valid votes on 4 October. Margin of victory: how many percentage points the winner finishes ahead of the loser. TSE: the Superior Electoral Court, Brazil’s official vote counter. An 83% price: traders pay about 83 cents for a contract that pays US$1 if that outcome happens.

What Prediction Markets Say

Two exchanges list margin-of-victory markets for the runoff between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro, a conservative senator and the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Polymarket uses four-point bands.

Kalshi uses three-point bands.

Polymarket, Lula by under 4 points: 83%, up about 67 points in 24 hours and 65 in a week.

The bands are cut differently, so Polymarket’s and Kalshi’s prices cannot be compared one to one. Kalshi’s last trades also jump around, as the wide gap between bids and asks shows.

Polymarket’s margin market has traded about US$9.2 million in all, including about US$3.0 million in the past 24 hours. Kalshi’s eight bands saw about 240,000 contracts traded in 24 hours, so both are actively traded tonight.

On Polymarket’s main winner market, Lula is at about 94% and Flávio at about 6%; Lula’s contract alone has traded about US$39 million. Prices were read on 25 October 2026 at 7:29 p.m. ET; they are bets, not polls.

Why the Odds Moved

Polls closed at 5 p.m. Brasília time (4 p.m. ET). At 8:28 p.m. Brasília time (7:28 p.m. ET), the TSE had counted 51.35% of polling sections.

Lula: 31,754,986 votes, 50.15%.

No single cause for the move was confirmed. It came in the hours when polls closed and the count began, and the narrow-win bands for both candidates drew heavy trading.

A finish this close could keep Brazilian markets uncertain until the TSE publishes a final tally. That matters for US investors in Brazilian stocks, bonds and the real, including through US-listed shares of Brazilian companies.

Our

runoff guide explains the vote, and our Brazil hub tracks the economy and politics around it. More odds sit on our Latin America odds page.

It is not known which candidate will finish ahead, because the count is still under way and the gap is only 0.30 point. We do not know which regions are still to report.

We also could not confirm exactly how each platform measures the margin, whether in valid votes or all votes. Only the TSE’s final count will settle it.

What do prediction markets say about Brazil’s runoff margin?

Polymarket gives 83% to Lula winning by under 4 points. Kalshi’s last trades put Lula by 3–6 points at 57% and by 0–3 points at 30% (25 October, 7:29 p.m. ET).

How big was the move?

On Polymarket, the “Lula by under 4 points” price rose about 67 points in 24 hours, from roughly 15.5% to 83%. Flávio Bolsonaro’s matching price fell from about 45% to 6.5%.

Why did the odds move?

No single cause was confirmed. The move came as the official count by the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) began, and Lula led by 0.30 point with 51.35% of sections counted.

No. They are real-money bets, not polls and not a forecast by this newsroom. Kalshi is regulated in the US by the CFTC, and prices can reverse quickly as the count moves.

Published Sunday, 25 October, 7:28 p.m. ET · Updated 8:38 p.m. ET · Source: Superior Electoral Court (TSE), Brazil’s election authority, results feed; Kalshi, a prediction market

Lula, Brazil’s president, leads the almost complete official count of the runoff, the second-round vote between the top two candidates, in the Brazil election 2026 with 51.77% of valid votes (votes for a candidate, excluding blank and spoiled ballots). Flávio Bolsonaro, senator for Rio de Janeiro and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, has 48.23%, with 99.9% of polling stations counted at 8:38 p.m. ET.

That is 64,172,678 votes to 59,790,616, a gap of 4,382,062, according to the electoral court (TSE). The TSE has not yet formally declared the winner. Our live map on the Brazil election results page shows each state’s counted share and both candidates’ percentages as you hover over it.

The gap Lula leads by 4,382,062 votes; the TSE has not yet formally declared the winner.

Big states São Paulo is 99.99% counted, Rio de Janeiro 99.99% and Minas Gerais (the second-largest state) 99.69%; together they hold about 40% of voters.

Prediction markets Kalshi, a prediction market regulated in the US by the CFTC, the federal derivatives regulator, priced a Lula margin of victory of at least 3 percentage points at 99% (8:36 p.m. ET).

Where the Count Stands

Lula leads by 4,382,062 at 99.9% counted; 482 of 499,248 polling stations (0.10%) are still outstanding, far too few votes to close that gap.

Lula leads in all nine states of the Northeast, Brazil’s poorer region, including Bahia and Pernambuco, two of its largest. Flávio leads in Paraná and Rio Grande do Sul.

Why the Big States Matter

São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro hold about 40% of Brazil’s 158.7 million registered voters. They came into the count late: São Paulo is now 99.99% counted, Rio de Janeiro 99.99% and Minas Gerais 99.69%.

Flávio leads in São Paulo (53.85%) and in Rio (53.10%). With all three states almost fully counted, the remaining votes are too few to change the national picture, but the TSE has not yet issued its formal declaration.

Minas Gerais

Minas Gerais, the second-largest state, holds about 10% of Brazil’s voters and is 99.69% counted. Lula leads there by 98,717 votes, or 50.39% to 49.61%, so it is effectively level.

Lula won the state with 50.2% in the 2022 runoff. In this year’s first round, Flávio took 48.2% there and Lula 43.3%.

By camp, the 14 states and the Federal District (the capital region) that Flávio won in the first round hold 66.3% of voters and are 99.9% counted; he leads in 14 of those 15 areas. The 12 states Lula won hold 33.7% of voters and are 99.8% counted; Lula leads in 12 of the 12.

What Else Is Happening

Voting ran until 6 p.m. ET (7 p.m. in Brasília, the capital) after Cristiano Zanin, a justice of the Supreme Federal Court (STF), ordered an extension nationwide, as we reported earlier.

We have no ruling on any challenge to the vote.

Votes cast abroad are almost fully counted: with 1,310 of 1,351 overseas sections counted (96.97%), Lula has 53.63% and Flávio 46.37%, according to the TSE.

What Prediction Markets Say

Kalshi, a prediction market regulated in the US by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), priced a Lula margin of victory of at least 3 percentage points at 99% at 8:36 p.m. ET. The prices are bets, not polls, and they move as each state reports. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Our Brazil election odds page follows the prices live.

What It Means for US Readers

Brazil’s stock exchange opens on Monday, 26 October, at 9 a.m. ET, before the New York open. US investors who hold Brazilian shares through American depositary receipts (ADRs), US-listed certificates of foreign stocks, can see early moves in pre-market trading.

What Is Not Known

The TSE has not said when it will formally declare the winner and certify the result. We do not know how the last 482 uncounted sections will split, or whether any challenge will be filed.

What Happens Next

The TSE must still finish the count and formally declare the winner. We have no confirmed date for that declaration or for the inauguration.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who leads Brazil’s runoff count?

At 8:38 p.m. ET, with 99.9% of polling stations counted, Lula had 51.77% of valid votes and Flávio 48.23%, according to the TSE results feed. The TSE has not yet formally declared the winner.

Who declares the winner of Brazil’s runoff?

The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) publishes the official results. Early counts and prediction-market prices are not official outcomes.

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS

Published Sunday, 25 October, 7:04 p.m. ET · Source: Superior Electoral Court (TSE) results feed; Polymarket, a prediction market

Flávio Bolsonaro, senator for Rio de Janeiro and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, leads the official count in the Brazil election 2026 with 50.51% of valid votes (votes for a candidate, excluding blank and spoiled ballots). Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, has 49.49%, with 25.19% of polling stations counted at 7:03 p.m. ET.

That is 15,716,679 votes to 15,399,270, a gap of 317,409, according to the electoral court (TSE). Our Brazil election results page tracks every update.

The gap Flávio’s lead is 317,409 votes, up from 36,775 at 15% counted; the TSE, Brazil’s electoral court, has not called the race.

Still to come Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Bahia, Pernambuco and Ceará are barely counted.

Where the Count Stands

Flávio Bolsonaro has moved ahead since our last count report. At 15.38% counted his lead was 36,775 votes; it is now 317,409.

Lula led the first returns, at 11.39% counted, before Flávio overtook him. His lead is widening as Brasília, Paraná and other conservative-leaning states report.

Which Regions Are Counted

The count is lopsided. The Federal District (Brasília) is about 90%, Tocantins 85% and Paraíba 79% counted, while Paraná and Mato Grosso do Sul are about 64% and 76% in.

Rio de Janeiro is 0.95% counted and São Paulo 4.32%, both states where Flávio leads so far. Lula leads every Northeast state reporting, but Bahia (8%), Pernambuco (12%) and Ceará (15%) are largely uncounted.

Minas Gerais, the swing state with the second-largest electorate, is 19% counted and split almost exactly evenly, with Lula at 49.96%. Bahia, Pernambuco and Ceará, all led by Lula, have most of their votes to report.

What Else Is Happening

Voting hours were extended earlier on Sunday by order of a justice of the electoral court, and the national count was paused until polls closed, as we reported.The TSE resumed its national count after the extended voting ended, and its feed now updates every minute.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a prediction market where traders bet real money on outcomes, priced a Lula win at 79.0% and a Flávio Bolsonaro win at 20.7% at 7:03 p.m. ET. More than US$211 million has been traded on that market. A separate Polymarket market on the margin of victory priced a Lula win by less than 4 points at 73.0%. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Traders are pricing the uncounted Northeast and the large states ahead, not today’s tally. Our Brazil election odds page follows the prices live.

What It Means for US Readers

Brazilian markets are closed on Sunday and reopen on Monday, 26 October. US investors who hold Brazilian shares through American depositary receipts (ADRs), US-listed certificates of foreign stocks, will see the first reaction in New York trading hours.

The real, Brazil’s currency, and the interest-rate outlook depend on who wins, so the final count matters more than any early reading.

What Is Not Known

The TSE has not said when it expects to publish a result. We do not know how the uncounted Rio, São Paulo and Northeast votes will split.

Our next report follows the TSE’s next counting step.

Lula leads in all nine states of the Northeast, Brazil’s poorer region, including Bahia and Pernambuco, two of its largest. Flávio leads in Paraná and Rio Grande do Sul.

Lula, Brazil’s president, photographed on 9 July 2026. File photo. (Photo: Lula Oficial, the president’s official photo account, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Why the Big States Matter

São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro hold about 40% of Brazil’s 158.7 million registered voters. They came into the count late: São Paulo is now 99.99% counted, Rio de Janeiro 99.99% and Minas Gerais 99.69%.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 75.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Flávio leads in São Paulo (53.85%) and in Rio (53.10%). With all three states almost fully counted, the remaining votes are too few to change the national picture, but the TSE has not yet issued its formal declaration.

Minas Gerais

Minas Gerais, the second-largest state, holds about 10% of Brazil’s voters and is 99.69% counted. Lula leads there by 98,717 votes, or 50.39% to 49.61%, so it is effectively level.

Lula won the state with 50.2% in the 2022 runoff. In this year’s first round, Flávio took 48.2% there and Lula 43.3%.

By camp, the 14 states and the Federal District (the capital region) that Flávio won in the first round hold 66.3% of voters and are 99.9% counted; he leads in 14 of those 15 areas. The 12 states Lula won hold 33.7% of voters and are 99.8% counted; Lula leads in 12 of the 12.

What Else Is Happening

Voting ran until 6 p.m. ET (7 p.m. in Brasília, the capital) after Cristiano Zanin, a justice of the Supreme Federal Court (STF), ordered an extension nationwide, as we reported earlier.

We have no ruling on any challenge to the vote.

Votes cast abroad are almost fully counted: with 1,310 of 1,351 overseas sections counted (96.97%), Lula has 53.63% and Flávio 46.37%, according to the TSE.

What Prediction Markets Say

Kalshi, a prediction market regulated in the US by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), priced a Lula margin of victory of at least 3 percentage points at 99% at 8:36 p.m. ET. The prices are bets, not polls, and they move as each state reports. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Our Brazil election odds page follows the prices live.

What It Means for US Readers

Brazil’s stock exchange opens on Monday, 26 October, at 9 a.m. ET, before the New York open. US investors who hold Brazilian shares through American depositary receipts (ADRs), US-listed certificates of foreign stocks, can see early moves in pre-market trading.

What Is Not Known

The TSE has not said when it will formally declare the winner and certify the result. We do not know how the last 482 uncounted sections will split, or whether any challenge will be filed.

What Happens Next

The TSE must still finish the count and formally declare the winner. We have no confirmed date for that declaration or for the inauguration.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who leads Brazil’s runoff count?

At 8:38 p.m. ET, with 99.9% of polling stations counted, Lula had 51.77% of valid votes and Flávio 48.23%, according to the TSE results feed. The TSE has not yet formally declared the winner.

Who declares the winner of Brazil’s runoff?

The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) publishes the official results. Early counts and prediction-market prices are not official outcomes.

World.title: Brazil’s Early Count Leaves Big Regions Out
World.content:
The JK Bridge over Lake Paranoá at dusk, photographed in April 2014. Runners cross the bridge between about km 7 and km 11. Photo: Gisele Pasquali / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

Published Sunday, 25 October 2026, 6:47 p.m. ET · Source: Superior Electoral Court (TSE) official results file, data as of 6:47 p.m. ET

Brazil’s electoral court (TSE) had counted 15.4% of polling sections in the presidential runoff at 7:47 p.m. Brasília time (6:47 p.m. ET) on Sunday 25 October. Flávio Bolsonaro had 50.10% and Lula 49.90%, a gap of 36,775 votes, and the lead has already changed hands tonight.

Key Facts — Count Flávio Bolsonaro 50.10%, Lula 49.90%, 36,775 votes apart, with 15.4% of sections counted.

— Missing Only 4.7% of Southeast sections are counted; the region holds about 41% of all sections.

— Why Early counts follow which regions report first, so this snapshot is not a forecast.

— Prediction markets Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 35% and Kalshi at 33% (Lula: 66% and 67% ), as of 25 October, 6:40 pm ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

Live results Brazil Election Data Room Runoff poll average: Flávio Bolsonaro 51.0 %, Lula 49.0 % 45 national polls from 21 pollsters since 4 October, updated hourly. Every poll, free to download. The Brazil election 2026 runoff is tight so far. Lula led by about 64,000 votes in the TSE file at 7:43 p.m. in Brasília, and Flávio Bolsonaro led by about 37,000 votes at 7:47 p.m., so the order can switch within minutes.

Our Brazil election results page updates with every official file. Our Brazil election polls tracker shows the survey picture.

In Plain English Runoff: the second round between the top two candidates, held because nobody passed 50% on 4 October.

the second round between the top two candidates, held because nobody passed 50% on 4 October. Polling section: one group of voting machines; the TSE counts progress in sections, not in voters.

one group of voting machines; the TSE counts progress in sections, not in voters. Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is the left-wing president seeking another term; Flávio Bolsonaro is a conservative senator and the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Which Regions Are Counted So Far

The count is uneven. The Southeast (São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo) holds about 41% of Brazil’s polling sections but only 4.7% of them were counted.

What the First Round and 2022 Show

In the first round on 4 October, Flávio Bolsonaro finished first with 47.03% and Lula second with 45.16%, according to the TSE. Lula led in all nine Northeast states then, while Flávio led in all four Southeast states, all three Southern states and all four Centre-West units, including the Federal District, the federal unit that contains the capital Brasília.

In the 2022 runoff, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro 50.90% to 49.10%, the TSE’s final result. A close finish is therefore not new, but early numbers have little to say about the late ones.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, traders put Lula’s chance of winning the presidency at 63.5% at 6:49 p.m. ET on Sunday 25 October, with about US$208.6 million traded. Another Polymarket market priced Lula winning by less than 4 points at 55.0%.

What It Means for US Readers

Brazil is a large market for US investors and exporters, and the result could affect trade and tariff talks with Washington. Markets in both countries are closed on Sunday, so the first price reaction comes on Monday 26 October.

Treat tonight’s numbers as a live snapshot. Check the live results page before drawing a conclusion.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how the Southeast and the Northeast will split once their sections are counted. The TSE had not declared a winner at the time of this snapshot.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is ahead in Brazil’s runoff count?

Flávio Bolsonaro had 50.10% and Lula 49.90% at 6:47 p.m. ET, with 15.4% of sections counted. The TSE had declared no winner.

Why can an early count mislead?

Regions report at different speeds, and each leans differently. A lead built on the regions that report first can shrink or grow as the rest arrive.
