World.title: Eldeniz and Sanan Make History in Astana
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 25. The World Wrestling Championships are underway in Astana, the capital of Kazakhstan.

On the second day of the competition, two of our wrestlers were crowned world champions.

According to the Azerbaijan Wrestling Federation, Eldeniz Azizli (55 kg) has added another title to his collection. Azizli defeated Iran’s Payam Balutaki 3–1 in the final to become a five-time world champion. With this achievement, the decorated wrestler set a new personal record in Azerbaijani wrestling.

Sanan Suleymanov (77 kg), meanwhile, faced Moldova’s Alexandrin Gutu in the decisive bout. Defeating his opponent 8–3, Sanan became a senior world champion for the first time.

Sanan also ended a 15-year wait. Suleymanov became the first Azerbaijani male wrestler since 2011 to win a world title in an Olympic weight category.

World.title: Olive Festival concludes at Baku Boulevard (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 25. The three-day Olive Festival at Baku’s Seaside National Park concluded on October 25, with the final day featuring local products, music and entertainment.

Held during the olive harvest season, the festival showcased olives and olive products from various producers. The pavilions set up along Baku Boulevard gave visitors an opportunity to explore the product range, speak directly with producers and make purchases.

The festival aimed to promote Azerbaijan’s olive-growing traditions, raise the profile of local producers and support them, as well as contribute to the development of a national brand in the sector.

The festival’s music and entertainment program also attracted considerable interest over the three days.

At the closing evening concert, Azad Shabanov and Zamig Huseynov performed their popular songs. The performance by People’s Artist Aygun Kazimova brought the festival’s musical program to a close.

Despite the rainy weather, Baku residents and visitors continued to arrive at the festival grounds on the final day. They watched the concerts, danced to the music and spent time with family and friends.

The Olive Festival was organized with the support of the State Tourism Agency and the Seaside Boulevard Administration, with olive product producers Absheron Olive Gardens and Olivea as sponsors.

World.title: Melbourne Market board quits over appointment of former Demons chief Paul Guerra
World.content:
The full board of the Melbourne Market Authority (MMA) has quit over the appointment of former Melbourne Football Club chief executive Paul Guerra as boss.

Mr Guerra was chosen by the Victorian government to be the new chair of the statutory authority, which oversees the Victorian government-owned Epping-based fruit and vegetable wholesale market.

Angie Bradbury had been acting chair since May this year, and told the ABC she applied to be appointed to the three-year chair role after serving on the board since 2022.

She has now resigned from the board after being overlooked for the top job.

"I was not prepared to step aside and go back to the board table when I have been an effective leader," Ms Bradbury said.

"This is not about Paul Guerra, I don't understand how the decision has been made, the value it offers and what issue it is [the government] think they are solving," she said.

Ms Bradbury, along with other board members Margaret Burdeu and former Victorian Farmers Federation president Emma Germano, resigned effective October 29.

Acting chief executive and executive director Keith Louie has given his one month notice of resignation.

A letter from two board members prior to the announcement, seen by the ABC, asked Victorian Agriculture Minister Michaela Settle to reconsider the decision.

In the letter, the two board members threatened to resign unless Ms Bradbury was appointed as chair instead.

"We are unwilling to lend our professional standing, governance experience and statutory accountability to an appointment that we consider presents foreseeable and unacceptable risks to the Authority," the letter said.

Ms Settle has been contacted for comment.

Market future hinges on Victorian election

Mr Guerra was removed as the Melbourne Football Club chief in April, seven months into his term, and has begun proceedings against the club in the Federal Court for breach of contract.

The first case management hearing for his case will be heard in court on October 30, the same day he is due to start the three-year term as market authority chairman.

Mr Guerra has been contacted for comment.

The market authority is the statutory authority responsible for overseeing the Melbourne Market at Epping, Australia's largest wholesale fruit, vegetable and flower market.

Earlier this week the Victorian Coalition pledged to sell the Melbourne Market if it won next month's state election, while Labor said it would stay in government hands if Labor won.

Mr Guerra was previously the chief executive of the Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, and of the Royal Agricultural Society of Victoria.

He also was the executive chair of the Queen Victoria Market.

The Victorian government statement regarding his appointment said Mr Guerra brought "significant commercial, governance and stakeholder engagement experience to the role".

Melbourne's wholesale fruit, vegetable and flower market is in Epping. (ABC News: Cath McAloon)

"The Melbourne Market is a significant part of Victoria's fresh produce industry, and I am committed to supporting the market and its users in my role as chair of the Melbourne Market Authority,'" Mr Guerra said in the government statement.

A Victorian government spokesperson declined to comment on Mr Guerra's salary, but said renumeration for such a role ranged from $21,941 to $61,750.

There has also been instability at the executive level of the authority.

Rob Clayton, who was appointed as chief executive of the market authority in March, quit after three months.

He had been appointed after former head of the organisation Mark Maskiell stepped down after almost 14 years.

Matt Elliott will take up the role of chief executive in January. Mr Louie is the acting chief executive.

World.title: Breaking: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva set to reclaim Brazilian presidency
World.content:
Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will win the country's presidential election, defeating right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a run-off to secure a fourth non-consecutive term.

The electoral court confirmed Lula's win, as did leading pollster Datafolha.

The shock result defied polls, precedent, and global anti-incumbent sentiment, putting the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America.

With just over 78 per cent of ballots counted, Lula led Senator Bolsonaro, son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, with 51.21 per cent to Senator Bolsonaro's 48.79 per cent.

It was a chaotic day for voters in the presidential election.

Polls were initially set to close at 5pm, local time, but were extended by two hours after Supreme Justice Cristiano Zanin accepted a request by Lula's campaign to extend voting, pointing to public transportation issues in three cities in the state of Bahia.

Lula started strongly, and although Senator Bolsonaro overtook him, Lula retook the lead with about half of the votes counted around 8:30 pm local time.

Win for 'democratic processes', expert says

Dr Flavia Bellieni Zimmermann, an international political analyst from Deakin University, said Lula's win would result in "the consolidation of an attempt to have political matters sorted through the democratic process, through the rule of law, through the institutional framework".

Dr Bellieni Zimmermann said the Bolsonaro family represented the right-wing side of Brazil's political spectrum.

"They also represent political forces which have been very much consolidated during the military dictatorship," she said.

"His [Senator Flávio Bolsonaro's] father, Jair Bolsonaro, he is a former military man, and is currently in home arrest because during the 2023 presidential elections, when he lost his re–election bid, there was an attempt of a coup d'etat in Brazil."

She said Senator Bolsonaro was very aligned with US leadership.

Loading

AP/Reuters

World.title: Victorian Liberals to ban 'globalise the intifada' chant if elected
World.content:
Victorian Liberal Leader Jess Wilson is pledging to follow Queensland's lead and outlaw the phrase "globalise the intifada" if her party wins the state election.

Ms Wilson said her party will expand incitement of violence laws to include the phrase, which has been used at pro-Palestine protests in Melbourne.

The meaning of "globalise the intifada" is contested.

The word "intifada" means "shaking off" in Arabic and has been used to refer to two periods of violent Palestinian protest against Israel.

Many in the Jewish community argue use of the term is hateful and a call for violence.

Ms Wilson said the phrase will be banned if her party wins government.

Jess Wilson says the phrase is regularly used by pro-Palestinian protesters in Melbourne. (ABC News: James Oaten)

"When I see these protests on the streets of Melbourne, I see these people yelling 'globalise the intifada', that is inciting violence against our Jewish community," she told 774 ABC Melbourne.

" We need to take the temperature down, and that's exactly why, if we are elected, we will change the law. "

Ms Wilson said there was no justification for using the phrase during demonstrations.

"We have families not wanting to come into the CBD on weekends, we have the Jewish community not coming into the CBD on the weekend," she said.

"Enough is enough."

The Queensland Liberal government passed legislation earlier this year to ban the phrases "globalise the intifada" and "from the river to the sea", deeming the phrases antisemitic.

A group of pro-Palestinian protesters mounted a High Court challenge to the laws after more than 20 people were charged under Queensland laws.

Former Australian of the Year, Grace Tame, faced criticism from Jewish leaders, as well as federal MPs and the NSW premier, for leading chants of the phrase at a rally in Sydney in February.

World.title: Antonelli is two points away from the F1 title, and can win it next week
World.content:
With his ninth grand prix win of the season on Monday morning (AEDT), Italian Kimi Antonelli put himself on the cusp of winning his maiden Formula 1 drivers' championship.

The 20-year-old Mercedes pilot has been a class above the rest in 2026, and could have sealed the championship with his victory in Texas on Monday, but other results meant he had to wait at least one more week before popping the champagne.

Next weekend's Mexican Grand Prix shapes up to be the coronation of Antonelli as an F1 champion. Here is how he can seal the world title.

Antonelli needs just two more points

Heading into Monday's United States Grand Prix, there were still five drivers who could mathematically catch Kimi Antonelli in the race for the title.

Kimi Antonelli is in just his second season of Formula 1. (Getty Images: LAT Images/Simon Galloway)

But Antonelli's win reduced his challenges to teammate George Russell and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.

Drivers' championship standings

1: 365 — Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

2: 242 — George Russell, Mercedes (-123)

3: 241 — Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari (-124)

With just five grands prix left to run, there is a maximum of 125 points a driver can achieve by winning every race.

Antonelli has 365 points, 123 ahead of Russell and 124 over Hamilton.

The maximum total Russell and Hamilton can end the season with is 367 and 366 points, respectively.

That means Antonelli needs to win just one more point to eliminate Hamilton from the title race, and two points to eliminate Russell.

Antonelli can achieve that in Mexico City by finishing ninth or higher.

He would also win the title if neither Russell or Hamilton win the race.

Even if Russell or Hamilton finish exactly 100 points adrift of Antonelli at the end of the race in Mexico, with 100 points still available, the Italian would be crowned champion, as his nine grand prix wins cannot be topped by either rival.

'Very excited' Antonelli wants to win in style

Antonelli has held the lead of the drivers' championship since his victory at the Japanese Grand Prix in round three.

Despite leading since March, Antonelli has dismissed any and all notions of thinking about winning the drivers' championship in just his second season.

But with the championship all but won, he has finally been able to acknowledge that only the most calamitous set of circumstances would deny him becoming champion.

Speaking after his tremendous win in Texas, Antonelli said his mindset for the rest of the 2026 season is to continue pushing and scoring as many points as possible.

"I am very excited. We would love to clinch the title in style with a great result," Antonelli said about his impending title win.

"That's always the mindset, and that is going to be the mindset from now until the end of the season.

"Just going to try and enjoy every moment, because these we'll always remember."

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the F1 Mexican Grand Prix on Monday, November 2, with the race beginning at 7am AEDT.

World.title: Passenger says 'double check' after landing at wrong Sydney airport
World.content:
Sydney's new status as a two-airport city is already causing confusion for some travellers.

Julie Lundmark, from Sweden, headed to Melbourne for the weekend from Sydney Airport but was surprised to discover her return flight landed at the brand new Western Sydney International Airport (WSI).

The airport, which has been decades in the making, began operating passenger flights on Sunday.

Ms Lundmark and her friend were on Jetstar flight JQ373 when they realised the mistake.

"We landed here and looked out of the window and had no idea where we were," she said.

"And we looked down the map and we thought to ourselves, we are a little bit lost."

The first international flight departed this morning. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

She said she had checked the name of the airport on her boarding pass a few days ago.

"The funny thing is we googled because we didn't recognise the name 'west airport' that was on the boarding pass, and we googled it and it took us to the normal Sydney airport."

Ms Lundmark said they were left looking for ways to get back to Sydney Airport.

"We have our car parked at the other airport," she told 702 ABC Sydney.

"We are stuck in Western Sydney."

A metro service from St Marys to WSI was not completed before the airport opened, with buses and a free shuttle operating to and from the station being the main public transport options until the rail link opens.

However, Ms Lundmark said given it would take her two hours to get to Sydney Airport, she hoped a friend with a car would help out.

"We've made some panic calls to the city and hopefully someone will pick us up," she said.

"Double check, everyone, on your tickets before."

'I'm meant to be in Perth'

Ms Lundmark was not the only confused traveller at WSI this morning.

One holiday-maker found out he booked a ticket to the wrong airport. (ABC News)

One man who disembarked flight NZ165 from Auckland said he thought he was travelling to Western Australia.

"I got confused, I saw Western Sydney," he said.

"I thought it was Western Australia, and I'm meant to be in Perth, but look, it's still pretty fun, so we'll make the best of it.

"I realised by the time I got on the flight that that's not where it was going, but we'll figure it out.

"I'm on holiday, so it's not the worst thing."

Weighing up if a trip from Sydney's new airport is for you The doors to Western Sydney International Airport are set to soon welcome commercial passengers.

Some of the first passengers to travel through WSI have praised the new $5.6 billion airport terminal's layout and operation.

Three domestic Jetstar flights are scheduled for today, with Air New Zealand flights this morning marking the first international departure and arrivals.

Seven carriers have signed up to operate out of WSI.

Flights to Singapore are scheduled to start soon, with other destinations including Nadi in Fiji, Ho Chi Minh City and Doha to follow.

World.title: Women take bushfire preparation into their own hands
World.content:
For Gemma Woodmore, a flurry of phone calls and messages from worried friends during a bushfire in Western Australia's Midwest highlighted the need for more disaster education for women.

The coastal town of Dongara, 350 kilometres north of Perth, is prone to bushfires, with multiple Emergency Warning level blazes in recent years.

Ms Woodmore said she had helped several friends evacuate.

She said some were single, while others had partners who worked away or were out fighting the blaze.

"The girls ended up calling me going, 'I don't know what to do,'" Ms Woodmore said.

It led the beautician to spearhead plans for a comprehensive fire preparation day specifically for women titled "her safety, her plan".

Lives and homes were threatened in the Dongara area in March. (ABC News: Chris Lewis)

Ms Woodmore said firefighting spaces were frequently male-dominated and women could feel intimated to join, therefore missing out on crucial advice.

"Women just lack the knowledge most men know because they [men] go to the fire meetings and they're told, 'OK, you need to do this,'" she said.

" Women aren't really told that. "

Ms Woodmore has since joined the volunteer fire brigade.

"Sometimes going into a male-dominated field can be a bit scary but they've welcomed me with open arms, so it's just been amazing."

The workshop in Dongara was aimed at empowering women during emergencies. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chloe Henville)

Lessons hit home

Irwin local Freya Smyth, who attended the workshop, said she had a wake-up call in 2024 when a blaze came just 300 metres from her house.

Ms Smyth was with her family interstate when she received a call from a friend watching the property and her horses.

A fire came dangerously close to Freya Smyth's home in 2024. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chloe Henville)

"We didn't really have an action plan," she said.

"It was quite harrowing."

Ms Smyth said the friend was "quite experienced" and moved the horses to safety, but the situation showed she was vulnerable.

She said she joined the workshop to gain practical skills and knowledge to help her family in the future.

"Coming into this summer, I will be teaching my kids how to evacuate, where to meet, what they should do if they get cut off in the house … that sort of thing," Ms Smyth said.

Filling knowledge gaps

Local community emergency services manager Mick Antony helped coordinate and run the event.

"We've tried to make it a safe environment," he said.

Mick Antony says he tried to make it a safe space for women. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chloe Henville)

Mr Antony said most people had the bare bones of an emergency plan but missed the finer details that become crucial when under pressure.

"We have over 900 fires a year in people's homes and people don't think about this," he said.

"We have muster points at work but we don't have a muster point at home."

Mr Antony said the workshop was wide-ranging, from home preparedness and evacuation plans, to practical training on how and when to use a fire extinguisher.

Gemma Woodmore demonstrates how to use a fire blanket. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chloe Henville)

He said other local governments were looking at hosting similar events.

Mr Antony said the knowledge also translated to a variety of emergencies.

"If we had a cyclone, a flood, very bad storms, things like this need to be done," he said.

Key takeaways

Mr Antony's core advice was simple: form a solid plan, with multiple back-ups, before it was too late.

How your phone could help save your life Anyone could be caught in a disaster — and most of us carry something in our pocket that could help us stay safe, or even alive, when it strikes.

"Think about an escape route out of your area, how to get yourself to a safe place," he said.

He explained how to pack an emergency kit, including a reminder to bring some form of identification if you evacuate.

"I was part of the Wooroloo fires [in 2021] and a lot of people left home, because the fire was so intense and so fast, without having ID," Mr Antony said.

"So prepare your ID maybe digitally and store it somewhere."

Mr Antony said the Emergency WA app was the "one source of truth" during a fire.

World.title: Youth boxing program fights off negativity, provides positive role models
World.content:
Encouraging young boys to put on gloves and fight each other inside a boxing ring may not seem like the most obvious way to keep them out of trouble at first glance.

But those behind this weekend's amateur Gloves of Hope challenge in Darwin would argue the sport is helping do just that, and much more, for young people in the Northern Territory.

The event is an initiative of local grassroots organisation Hoops 4 Health — an Aboriginal-led service behind several sport programs designed to support struggling youth, including some inside NT detention centres.

The sold-out event saw boxers from across the region compete at Marrara Stadium. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

The free Gloves of Hope program aims to give young men and women a chance to learn boxing skills from professional coaches while building resilience, discipline and a support network in their community.

"We try to improve their mental health, but also guide them with integrity about how they live their lives," social impact director Matthew Bonson said.

Mr Bonson said the program was based on evidence-backed models of therapy which use patterned, rhythmic exercise to help trauma-affected youth regulate their emotions.

Matthew Bonson says the patterned, rhythmic exercise has been shown to help with emotional regulation. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"Through sport and the structures around good coaches, you can help these young men stay cool longer and also help young women get more confidence about who they are," he said.

As the NT grapples with some of the highest youth incarceration rates in the country, particularly among First Nations boys aged 10 to 14, Mr Bonson said providing young people with positive role models was a key part of the program's success.

While the program is "not a magic-wand solution", Mr Bonson says it exposes the young boxers to positive role models. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"Particularly with young men, if you put the right older men in front of them — who they know are trying to help them — they do want to listen," Mr Bonson said.

" It's not a magic-wand solution, but we're trying our best to give [young people] positive examples. "

Territory boxing talent on show

On Saturday, Gloves of Hope teamed up with Boxing NT to host one of Darwin's biggest amateur boxing events of the last decade.

The sold-out event at Marrara Stadium brought together boxing clubs from across Darwin and Alice Springs, with one team even travelling from Kununurra in Western Australia.

Declan Unwin-Walker was one of the fighters competing for the title belt on Saturday and said he was "keen, excited, nervous — but ready to go".

Declan Unwin-Walker says Gloves of Hope is all about supporting each other and encouraging fellow boxers to continue showing up. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

Mr Unwin-Walker trained with Gloves of Hope for more than a year in the lead-up to the event and said the sport had been rewarding, physically and mentally.

"We all push each other and show up every day and its definitely about pushing each other and just yeah — keep showing up," he said.

Jerrel O'Riley from the Kununurra Warriors Boxing Club said it was exciting to compete on a big stage.

Jerrel O'Riley and his team were visiting from Kununurra in Western Australia, with plenty of representation from rural Darwin clubs in attendance too. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"I was pretty surprised to hear there was 1,000 people coming," he told the ABC ahead of the sold-out event.

" That's the main thing I'm worried about, getting knocked out in front of 1,000 people. "

Richard Garling, who has coached the sport for more than four decades, was there on behalf of the Humpty Doo Boxing Club.

Mr Garling said pathways into boxing that helped kids from rural areas compete were essential to fostering NT talent.

Mr Garling hopes events like this will encourage young boxers to continue on their journey, going on to compete in even bigger competitions over time. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"There's a lot of potential in the Territory," he said.

" Hopefully all these kids tonight can continue their journey somewhere higher — state titles, national titles or Golden Gloves. "

The event also featured a half-time performance by NT music star Yung Milla, fresh from his triumph on reality music competition show The Voice Australia.

The funds raised from ticket sales were donated to help the Gloves of Hope initiative, with organisers hopeful the event will return next year.

World.title: Fowler's City draw to end winning start
World.content:
Manchester United striker Elisabeth Terland scored a late equaliser to knock visitors Manchester City off top spot in the Women's Super League table on Sunday evening as a hotly contested derby finished 1-1 at the Leigh Sports Ground.

Matildas star Mary Fowler slid the ball to Bunny Shaw to open the scoring for the champions in the 66th minute.

Making her 100th WSL appearance, Shaw brushed off the challenge of Dominique Janssen and powered a shot into the far corner to break the deadlock and silence the home fans, who booed and heckled her throughout.

However, Norway international Terland was on hand to blast the ball into the net to grab a point for her side in the 89th minute of the game.

It was the first time that City has dropped points this season, allowing Ellie Carpenter's Chelsea to go top on goal difference after it came back from a goal down to beat Crystal Palace 3-1 earlier in the day.

Ellie Carpenter had to battle hard for Chelsea. (Getty Images: WSL/Tom Dulat)

Chelsea and City both have 19 points, with London City Lionesses third on 16 and Manchester United fourth on 11.

On Merseyside, Liverpool's Jana Fernandez Velasco struck deep into stoppage time to snatch a 2-2 draw at home to London City.

Aston Villa raced out to a 3-0 lead over Everton by the 50th minute with Amalie Vangsgaard scoring twice, but the home side scored twice late on to ensure a nervous finish as Villa held on for a 3-2 win.

Charlton Athletic's miserable run continued as it slumped to its seventh straight defeat.

Substitute Wilma Leidhammar scored the only goal of the game for Birmingham City in the 68th minute to leave Charlton, who counts Matildas veteran Emily van Egmond among its ranks, still firmly rooted to the bottom of the table and searching for its first point of the season.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: The Monday meeting that could seal Sam Walker’s future at Bondi
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 The Monday meeting that could seal Sam Walker’s future at Bondi Christian Nicolussi October 26, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Sam Walker is meeting with his management team on Monday in the hope of finally brokering a new deal that will keep him at the Sydney Roosters. Walker achieved a childhood dream of playing for Australia against Fiji on Sunday night in a 36-22 win that included him scoring a try. Loading Time will tell if Kangaroos’ coach Kevin Walters backs Walker or Tom Dearden to partner Cameron Munster in the halves for the remainder of the World Cup following the injury suffered by Mitchell Moses in Australia’s first opening cup match against New Zealand. As he celebrated the win and his first Test in the sheds with family, Walker gave a quick update on his playing future with the Roosters, with the Bondi club eager to know by Monday if he was ready to accept their three-year extension, worth around $1.4m a season, which would keep him at Bondi until at least the end of 2030.



The 24-year-old was happy to park all talks in the back half of the regular NRL season, then made it clear last week he wanted all the focus on his Kangaroos’ debut. “I’ve spent this week not worrying about [the contract] and letting my manager do his job in the background,” Walker said. Sam Walker on his Kangaroos debut on Sunday night. Bradley Kanaris/Getty Images “My job was to go out and play football. I’m sure on Monday I’ll have a conversation with him, and we’ll sit down and hopefully get something sorted. “I’m sure I’ll have time over the next couple of days to [go through it].



“It’s nice to be wanted. I’m going to make a decision soon on my future. But right now, my focus was completely on making sure I got the win for Australia.” Walker has made it clear he has little appetite for going to the open market, with all players off contract at the end of 2027 open to fielding offers from rival clubs from November 1. Sam Walker and Angus Crichton after winning the grand final with the Roosters. Getty Images The Roosters won the premiership but lost Daly Cherry-Evans (Hull FC), Mark Nawaqanitawase and Angus Crichton to rugby, Spencer Leniu to Parramatta, Connor Watson to St George Illawarra, while Daniel Tupou retired. Locking down Walker has become a priority. The club has also been linked to Dolphins’ centre Herbie Farnworth and Melbourne prop Stefano Utoikamanu, who family is eager for a return home to Sydney.



Walker, Hugo Savala and Toby Rodwell are viewed as the Roosters’ future halves players. Related Article Rugby League World Cup November 1 is looming. But Sam Walker is keeping his contract talks on hold The on-field chemistry Walker has with James Tedesco, who has indicated he is eager to play on for one final year in 2028, was one of the few positives for the Roos on Sunday night. The team will need to improve quickly if they are to defend their World Cup, starting with Saturday’s trip to Townsville to face the Cook Islands. Sunday’s win was clunky, with the forwards out-enthused and Walker and Dearden both solid without being dominant. “I’m sure once we get the job done, I’ll have a bit of time to sit back and reflect on the whole year,” Walker said of a year that also included him making his Origin debut for Queensland.



“We’re all here to make sure we put Australia first and do a job for them; whatever role I’ve got – whether it’s starting, coming off the bench, or helping out at training – it doesn’t matter. I’ll make sure I do my best and help out where I can. “It’s special to play with [Tedesco], and I’m very lucky to be captained by him. The way he leads, it’s not just with his voice but also his actions, which is really cool, and I’m able to follow off the back of him. “You just have to keep pushing around him because you know something’s going to happen.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: ‘We don’t play games’: Trump’s threats have markets nervous
World.content:
BusinessMarketsOil Opinion ‘We don’t play games’: Trump’s threats have markets nervous Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist October 26, 2026 — 11:58am

October 26, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz has returned to something close to pre-war levels. So why has the price surged again to near six-month highs? After trading below $US100 a barrel last month, the price climbed to just under $US117 a barrel last week, with pricing in the futures market suggesting it could still be trading above $US100 a barrel well into next year. With the elections just over a week away, Trump’s rhetoric has hardened. AP Photo/Alex Brandon That’s despite shipments from the Middle East running close to their pre-war levels as the volume of oil mon tankers being escorted through the strait by the US navy – and some tankers that appear to be paying Iranian fees for safe passage – have rebounded. Flows through Saudi Arabia’s pipeline to the Red Sea have also picked up, despite Houthi attacks on the pipeline and the port of Yanbu.



The flows are holding up despite recent escalation of Iranian attacks on ships in the strait and Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure, oil fields and the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Related Article Analysis

Global economy The prince’s bet on Trump is blowing up in his face Last week the UK’s Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) reported 11 confirmed attacks in the strait last week, although the real number is probably higher, given that the UKMTO says most targeted ships don’t report the attacks. Other authorities claim there have been at least 28 incidents so far this month. If the oil is flowing, why has the price taken off again? Part of the explanation may be that while more oil might be reaching the global market, the cost of getting it there has exploded.



The cost of chartering a tanker to carry oil through the strait is about 12 times what it was pre-war; the cost of insuring the cargo more than three times what it was. Ships captains are being paid nearly six times what they were being paid, plus bonuses in the tens of thousands of dollars, and crews two or three times their pre-war salaries, as incentives for taking the risk of being attacked. The way oil is being moved out of the strait – vessels are shuttling into and out of it and transferring their cargoes to other ships waiting outside the strait – adds to the cost and time and has created a global shortage, not of ships, but of tanker capacity because of the extra vessels tied up in the Middle East trade. The other dimension to the spike in prices is Donald Trump.



Trump stopped attacking Iran in late July in the hope that would take some of the heat out of the oil prices – and US gasoline and diesel prices – in the lead up to the US midterm elections. Related Article US midterms Long lines, late nights, adulation: What it’s really like inside Trump’s midterm election rallies He has subsequently done everything he can – convincing the G7 to release strategic reserves of diesel, allowing tax-exempt diesel in the US (normally reserved for off-road usages) to be used on public roads and controversially (and probably illegally) lifting sanctions on Russia and striking a deal with Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel to the US. While none of those attempts to lower US domestic gasoline and diesel prices have had any material effect – gasoline prices are still 40 per cent higher than a year ago, diesel prices about 74 per cent higher and Trump’s poll numbers have plumbed new lows – Trump has maintained the moratorium on attacks. With the elections just over a week away, Trump’s rhetoric has hardened. On Thursday, he told reporters that “something one way or the other” would happen “fairly soon” with Iran. Then on Sunday, he said it was “getting to be decision time” on whether to strike a deal with Iran or re-start the attacks.



“I have a decision to make. Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal?” he said on Fox News. “That’s all. We don’t play games.” “Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job’ Iran emerged even stronger”: Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is not backing down from Trump. AP The US has been moving diplomats and military staff out of the region and sending more military resources to the Middle East in preparation for an escalation of hostilities. The Iranians have vowed to retaliate if the US does resume its attacks.



“Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job’ Iran emerged even stronger,” its foreign affairs minister posted on social media. “Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs, too,” Abbas Araghchi wrote. ‘I have a decision to make. Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal?’ Donald Trump on Fox News It’s that prospect of renewed conflict that seems to be the major influence over the surge in oil prices. There are, broadly, two markets that price oil. One is the futures market, which prices oil for delivery at some point in future, and the other, “Dated Brent,” is for physical delivery in the near term.



Dated Brent, which normally trades at a relatively modest premium – less than $US2 a barrel – to the futures price, was trading around $US125 a barrel late last week after a sudden jump late in the week, which might suggest a sudden urgency from buyers to get their hands on oil before a new round of violence erupts. The futures prices, in turn, might be surging in anticipation of the disruption that a renewed conflict will have to supply from the Middle East. Whatever the explanation, it would appear clear that traders believe there is both a significant probability that the war will flare up again and that flows through the strait and through the Saudi pipeline could be materially impacted despite Trump’s confidence that he can “finish it (the war) off” quickly. Loading He has, of course, expressed similar confidence since the US and Israel launched their attacks on February 28. Nearly eight months later, you’d have to say that confidence was misplaced.



The futures market pricing would suggest that traders, too, have little confidence that Trump and his “Department of War” can do in the near term what he has consistently failed to deliver over nearly eight months. Related Article Opinion

Oil As Trump’s Iran war drags on, we’re facing the next oil crunch Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The other dimension to the conflict and its impact on gasoline/petrol and diesel prices is that there has been significant damage to Middle Eastern oil refineries, while Ukraine’s very successful targeting of Russia’s refineries has also taken significant Russian supply out of the global market. Even if flows of oil from the Middle East could be sustained through renewed hostilities, flows of refined products will continue to be less than what they were before the two wars. No-one pumps crude oil into their cars or trucks, so the impact of the conflict where it hurts US and other consumers and companies will persist for some times beyond the end of the war, whenever – if ever – it ends. World.title: ‘Make sure you don’t talk’: Recorded conversations with Lamarre-Condon played in court
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWLamarre-Condon trial ‘Make sure you don’t talk’: Recorded conversations with Lamarre-Condon played in court Michaela Whitbourn October 26, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Accused killer Lamarre-Condon was captured in a recorded call from prison telling a friend that he “should make sure you don’t talk to people”. Lamarre-Condon’s Supreme Court trial heard recordings of a series of conversations between the accused and his friend in 2024 and 2025, after the former NSW police officer was arrested over the alleged murder of Sydney couple of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies. Footage released by the court of Beau Lamarre-Condon buying a surfboard bag with a friend. The friend, whose identity cannot be reported due to a court order, gave evidence on Monday in Lamarre-Condon’s Supreme Court murder trial about the contents of the conversations while the accused was in prison. In one call, on April 8, 2024, Lamarre-Condon said to his friend: “Make sure you don’t talk to people about stuff, you know what I mean?”



“I don’t know what you’re talking about, bro,” the friend replied. Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, put to the friend on Monday that he was “putting on a bit of a voice” in the call. “Sounds like it, yes,” the friend replied. Beau Lamarre-Condon is accused of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies. The court heard that by this date the friend had provided statements to police on February 23 and 24 and March 12. He has given evidence in court about Lamarre-Condon buying a surfboard cover shortly before the alleged murders, and telling him later that he had killed two people. Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the shooting deaths of Baird, 26, a former Network Ten producer and presenter, and Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, on February 19, 2024. The bodies of Baird and Davies were found in Bungonia, near Goulburn, in two layers of surfboard bags on February 27, 2024.



In a later call, more than a year later on December 14, 2025, Lamarre-Condon refers to the men being due to speak to each other in person later that day and tells him to “bring your big boy diapers”. Asked by the prosecution what he believed the accused meant, the friend said: “We were going to have a conversation that might not make me feel too good.” Luke Davies and Jesse Baird were allegedly murdered by Lamarre-Condon. NSW Supreme Court Lamarre-Condon told the man in a further recorded conversation that day, during the friends’ face-to-face meeting, that he had been suicidal from late 2023 because of trauma from work. The accused told his friend that this was why he took him on a drive to the Royal National Park in Sydney’s south in early 2024, where he used police training bullets to shoot his service pistol twice into bushland and asked his friend how loud the gunshots were.



Lamarre-Condon said he was planning to return to that location alone and take his own life. “If they think I’m a missing person, perfect,” he said of his thinking at the time. The accused told his friend that he was “upset like anyone is” after Baird ended their casual relationship in November 2023, but “it’s normal”. He said that within two or three weeks he “didn’t really give a f---king shit about him” and was “dating someone new in February”. Lamarre-Condon said that he entered Baird’s Paddington share house to “get my shit back” after their breakup and was “not doing anything wrong”. The accused also told his friend that “you cannot put a silencer on a police-issued f---ing firearm”. The friend told the court on Friday that Lamarre-Condon had been trying to buy a silencer in December 2023 or February 2024.



Lamarre-Condon told his friend that he was a police officer by the time he was 21 and “you’re not fully self-aware in the way that I am”. Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial ‘Pew, pew’: Lamarre-Condon allegedly confessed to friend about double murder The friend said during the conversation that he was getting frustrated and was close to leaving. “What you’re telling me might not be the truth,” the man said. “I’m really trying to stay calm.” The friend said of Lamarre-Condon entering Baird’s home on the day of the alleged murders: “How is it not break and enter?”



The accused replied: “He got a key cut for me. It’s technically not. He gave consent. It actually doesn’t meet the definition. It’s trespass. “Normal people do this on an everyday basis [retrieving belongings from an ex-partner’s home].” Lamarre-Condon told his friend earlier in the conversation: “I fully take accountability that you’re involved because of me now.” The friend has given evidence that Lamarre-Condon told him he killed two people and the second person was killed to eliminate a witness. The accused told his friend he had never said this. “Don’t you dare switch up,” the friend replied. Lamarre-Condon suggested to him that he was wrong in his recollection of events.



The Crown case is that Lamarre-Condon had his police-issued Glock pistol with him for a work shift on Sunday, February 18, the day before the alleged murders, and pretended to return it to a police gun safe at Balmain, near his home, later that day. “He retained it despite having no authorised reason to do so,” Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, said in his opening address to the jury. The Crown alleges Lamarre-Condon pretended to retrieve the pistol from Balmain on February 20, before he returned the weapon that was already in his possession to Miranda police station, where he was based. The trial continues. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491 or Lifeline on 13 11 14.

World.title: Family pays $220,000 above reserve for Stanmore ‘renovators delight’
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Family pays $220,000 above reserve for Stanmore ‘renovators delight’ Carmen Forward October 26, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

Key points A five-bedroom house in Epping sold just below the top of its guide for $3,419,168.

Experts say buyers and sellers in Sydney are holding back, which is reflected in the clearance rate.

In Allambie Heights, a three-bedroom mid-century home sold just below its reserve for $2 million.

A family from Newtown paid $220,000 above the reserve for a four-bedroom renovator’s delight in Stanmore, which sold under the hammer for $2.52 million on Saturday. The two-storey terrace home at 106 Cavendish Street, which was considered unlivable had remained unrenovated for decades, was guided at $2.2 million. The home had five registered bidders and three active during the auction, all looking to upsize into western Sydney. The Stanmore property was one of 885 auctions scheduled in Sydney last week. By evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 45 per cent from 490 reported results, while 184 auctions were withdrawn.



Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Bidding in Stanmore opened at $2.1 million with offers of $50,000, $20,000 and $10,000 increments following. The property needed a lot of work done. Gerber Properties The price reached its reserve of $2.3 million and continued to climb until it was called three times at $2.52 million where it sold under the hammer. Gerber Properties’ Nicole Gerber said the property would cost at least $1 million to make it livable.



“I think it’s very interesting that such a property that is actually not livable… in this market and these conditions actually sold,” Gerber said. “I think people sort of fell in love with the dream of what it can be.” The vendor, who was thrilled with the result, grew up in the home which had been in the family since the 1950s. In Epping, a five-bedroom house at 17 George Street with a $3.2 million to $3.5 million guide, sold for the unusually precise number of $3,419,168 to an upsizer from Castle Hill. Five bidders registered and three competed for the grand family home.



Bidding opened at $2.8 million and rose in $100,000, $50,000, and $1000 increments. When the price reached $3.4 million the $3.5 million reserve was adjusted down by $100,000, and it was put on the market. After forty or so minutes from start to finish the home sold for $3,419,168. Related Article Auctions Maroubra ‘blank canvas opportunity’ goes for $7 million Uniland Real Estate’s Andy Lin said the interested buyers had upsized to Epping. “The market is still tough,” Lin said. “Agents are finding it much harder to sell a property at auction, and only property with a good location and good land can still sell, but they also drop in price compared to last year [by] around seven to 10 per cent.” The vendor is downsizing to the Hills area, with the house last trading for $480,000 in 2002, records show.



In Allambie Heights a three-bedroom house at 22 Kirra Road sold at its guide price of $2 million, but below the $2.05 million reserve. It last sold in 2020 for $1,235,000 records show. Four bidders registered for the renovated mid-century property with butterfly roofline, but only two competed, with the buyer from Camperdown becoming the new owner. Bidding opened at $1.8 million and quickly jumped in $50,000, $20,000 and $10,000 increments until it sold under the hammer. “People loved that the quality was high, of the rebuild in 2021,” McGrath Manly’s Tim Cullen said. “There was nothing to do. It was move-in ready, ready to go.”



Related Article Sydney house prices ‘The downturn’s broadened’: Sydney’s median house price falls to $1.66m It also offered a good opportunity for the vendor to upsize, he said. “It’s the best climate I’ve ever seen to trade up,” Cullen said. “So when people say, ‘Is it a good market or a bad market?’,” It depends on your current situation.” LJ Hooker’s head of research and business intelligence Mathew Tiller said Sydney’s clearance rate of 45 per cent meant buyers and sellers were sitting on the fence. “There is still a lot of price pressures in the economy at the moment, which I think will probably lean the RBA more to [interest rate] hiking than holding,” Tiller said. “So that will obviously affect confidence again. “Given we’re in the spring selling season, and it’s meant to be the height of confidence for the property market, we’re just not seeing that come through this spring.”

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has defended a cartoon showing independent Senator Lidia Thorpe being run over by a bus, just days after independent MP Helen Haines was rammed by a car. Hanson’s unapologetic stance in a Monday morning interview with radio station 2GB prompted Thorpe to accuse One Nation of leaving death threats against her unmoderated on its platforms for months. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson in the Senate. Alex Ellinghausen On Sunday, AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett urged politicians to speak carefully as she drew a direct link between inflamed rhetoric and the rise in violent threats. She indicated, when asked about a One Nation clip of cartoon character Bluey driving down Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and former Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews, that there was a reaction when “examples like that” were produced. But Hanson is determined not to take down two cartoons showing politicians being run over, posting on X Sunday night that “they will not be going anywhere” and telling 2GB on Monday she would not apologise to Thorpe for the 2023 episode, Under the Bus.



“Look, this woman’s on the floor of parliament … You should see the hatred coming out of her mouth,” Hanson said. “So don’t tell me about my cartoons because they’re satirical … And besides, that last episode happened years ago in the cartoon,” Hanson said. Victorian senator Lidia Thorpe. Dominic Lorrimer The One Nation leader accused Barrett of deflecting responsibility for protecting Australians. “You’ve got kids out there on streets with ‘kill Pauline Hanson’. ‘I hate Pauline Hanson’, ‘shoot Pauline Hanson’. What does the commissioner do about that? Absolutely nothing,” Hanson said.



“So don’t tell me about the cartoons because this is passing the buck where you haven’t been able to do your job, [to] make it safe for the same people.” Related Article Haines attack Hanson hits back at AFP chief’s cartoon claims as MPs urged to sign civility pledge Thorpe said on Monday that Hanson should “think carefully about the example she is setting”. “Making light of violence, particularly against women in this country, is a problem. It’s not something anyone should be joking about,” the senator told this masthead. Thorpe added that she had reported a number of death threats posted by users on Hanson’s social media pages that had been left unmoderated by her team for months.



“If her supporters are making death threats against other politicians, that should be a red flag, and she should reflect on what sort of leadership qualities she is showing, and what sorts of things she is making light of. We can disagree fiercely about politics, we can have a laugh at each other, but making jokes about violence is not on.” Hanson last week apologised for a separate cartoon mocking Tasmanian senator Jacquie Lambie for her battle with vaginal prolapse, and One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce did offer an apology last month to Coalition frontbencher Andrew Hastie, who was labelled a traitor in another clip for testifying in the defamation case Ben Roberts-Smith has brought against Nine. Monday’s clash comes on the same day parliament pays tribute to independent MP Helen Haines, who remains in hospital recovering from an attack last Monday afternoon in the Victorian town of Wangaratta. Speaker of the House Milton Dick. Dominic Lorrimer Speaker of the House Milton Dick told parliament on Monday that politicians had a responsibility to lead by example.

World.title: An inscribed bullet on the windscreen: The mafia-style ‘death threat’ against a Victorian minister
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEmergency services An inscribed bullet on the windscreen: The mafia-style ‘death threat’ against a Victorian minister Alexander Darling Updated October 26, 2026 — 11:50am ,first published October 26, 2026 — 10:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

By the time Paul Edbrooke found the inscribed bullet on the windshield of his car in Frankston late last week, he was no stranger to threats and abuse. The emergency services minister had been the target of scorn for months, as the government remained locked in a series of disputes with the United Firefighters Union. Only a day earlier, union secretary Peter Marshall had said Edbrooke and Premier Ben Carroll were “in the gun” ahead of the November election. A bullet left on the windscreen of Paul Edbrooke’s car over the weekend. But when Edbrooke peered closer at the menacing object, his blood ran cold: The word “RAT” was etched into the gold metal casing. Even more chilling was an inscription on the other side: His five-digit ID number from when he was a firefighter, a personal detail known to only a small number of people. As his mind began to race, he suspected immediately where this “death threat” had come from.



“My kids drive this car, and you know, you start thinking: ‘Am I being followed? Who knows I’m here? Am I being surveilled?’,” he recalled to ABC radio on Monday. “It’s not subtle… that’s a death threat.” Coming mere days after federal MP Helen Haines was allegedly deliberately mowed down by a vehicle outside her Wangaratta office on Monday, Edbrooke told Premier Carroll over the phone that he was making a report to police. He also had to explain what had happened to his family, including three young adult children, showing them the bullet. Emergency Services Minister Paul Edbrooke has taken aim at the UFU after finding the engraved bullet. The Age “I could see the terror, and I didn’t want to traumatise them. I think they took it in their stride, but at the same time, this is an escalation they’ve never seen. Just seeing the look in their eyes made me really sad.”



The matter, now with police, is the latest example of violence and intimidation towards elected officials that has dominated the national conversation since the alleged attack on Haines. Haines remains serious but stable in the Alfred hospital, having had both legs amputated to save her life. The driver, Brendan Nugent, is now behind bars, charged with several offences. Edbrooke worked as a firefighter in Frankston for 14 years, during which he served as the station’s workplace representative for the UFU and fought the Black Saturday bushfires in Marysville and Kinglake. He was also a long-time teacher before turning to politics. Edbrooke had been out in the community meeting his constituents face-to-face the day he walked back to his car to find the bullet. “I’m not sure how long it had been there. It could have just been put there, possibly. I’m waiting for the police to investigate that.”



He points the finger at the same union he once worked for because very few people knew his five-digit ID number. “The only people I’m really getting aggressive threats from at the moment are members of that union,” he said. “This is a new low in a pattern of threatening behaviour against politicians.” Related Article Exclusive

Industrial relations Firefighters shocked after union sends them debt recovery letters “There is a small minority in the UFU who think threats and intimidation are acceptable - this does not represent our firefighters.” “It’s one thing to be an armchair critic and say what you want from behind a computer. It’s another thing to follow somebody and put something on their car like a bullet.” He added that the small group of UFU members he was referring to “believe everything they are told by the leadership and think that by someone intimidating or bullying me, I will support them and give them a taxpayer-funded slush fund for the union. It ain’t gonna happen”.



Edbrooke clarified that there was an issue with an income protection scheme going to the UFU, when he believed it should go to firefighters directly. “That’s what this is about. It’s not about firefighter safety or staffing. There is no threat to that from the state government.” He urged candidates from other parties to stop campaigning with the UFU. “The message I’d like to get out there to all [election] candidates is: if you enjoy our democracy, the standard you walk past in the standard you accept,” he said.



Opposition leader Jess Wilson said her thoughts were with Edbrooke. “I can’t imagine how upsetting it is for him and for his family,” she said. “There’s just no place for these sort of threats and intimidation in Victoria or this country.” Edbrooke has also recently been the target of a fresh campaign by the UFU: Since Wednesday, it has been running televised ads urging people to put Labor last in next month’s state election, angry that the government wants to end enforceable minimum staffing for firefighters. “Firefighters beat these arguments in court when a Liberal government ran them. Now a Labor government is running the Liberals’ case against its own firefighters,” said UFU Secretary Peter Marshall in a statement announcing the ad blitz. “Minister Edbrooke can end this with the stroke of a pen. Until he does, firefighters will tell voters the truth.”



Marshall also addressed union members on Friday, saying Edbrooke and Premier Ben Carroll would be “in the gun” if they affected his members. On Monday, Marshall clarified this comment. “I meant at the ballot box and anyone there, or seeing the video, would know that,” he said. “Threatening anyone, including a minister we strongly disagree with, is the opposite of everything this union stands for. I condemn it without qualification.” Marshall said whoever had planted the bullet did not act for his union or for firefighters more generally, and that he hoped police found the culprit. The union has also been locked in a years-long pay dispute with the government, which remains before the Fair Work Commission. In August, Fire Rescue Victoria firefighters urged the government to intervene, alleging Marshall was stalling the negotiations.



“We stand ready to give firefighters the pay rise they want, but we won’t be including any kind of slush fund in that agreement,” Edbrooke said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Lost in the arena: Lily Allen’s intimate theatrical drama falls flat plus other big shows this week
World.content:
TikTok Entertainment Centre, October 25, also October 26

In her brutal narrative album of marital discord and disaster, West End Girl, Lily Allen has the perfect vehicle to merge several elements of her career and appeal into something new.

There’s the frank feminist who bridged aspiring-cynic teens with seasoned-cynic adults and the hook-tastic pop singer who made that sound like a hoot; the hedonist-who-tried-it-all and the romantic-despite-it-all; the latter-day stage actor of other people’s words and the life-long diarist who will share her truth.

Lily Allen did not speak between songs, performing the show as more of a theatrical piece. Emma Louise Smith

So turning last year’s record firstly into a small theatre creation and then into this year’s arena pop show – to which you can add a solid bit of sisterhood bonding over male treachery, with women near me regularly yelling out affirmations (“you’re too good for him … get him Lils”) and condemnations (“he’s a c---” and, to the marital interloper Madeline, “f--- you bitch”) – didn’t just make sense, it was excitingly different for an artist who has not always found live performance a particularly interesting exercise.

World.title: The Monday meeting that could seal Sam Walker’s future at Bondi
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 The Monday meeting that could seal Sam Walker’s future at Bondi Christian Nicolussi October 26, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Sam Walker is meeting with his management team on Monday in the hope of finally brokering a new deal that will keep him at the Sydney Roosters. Walker achieved a childhood dream of playing for Australia against Fiji on Sunday night in a 36-22 win that included him scoring a try. Loading Time will tell if Kangaroos’ coach Kevin Walters backs Walker or Tom Dearden to partner Cameron Munster in the halves for the remainder of the World Cup following the injury suffered by Mitchell Moses in Australia’s first opening cup match against New Zealand. As he celebrated the win and his first Test in the sheds with family, Walker gave a quick update on his playing future with the Roosters, with the Bondi club eager to know by Monday if he was ready to accept their three-year extension, worth around $1.4m a season, which would keep him at Bondi until at least the end of 2030.



The 24-year-old was happy to park all talks in the back half of the regular NRL season, then made it clear last week he wanted all the focus on his Kangaroos’ debut. “I’ve spent this week not worrying about [the contract] and letting my manager do his job in the background,” Walker said. Sam Walker on his Kangaroos debut on Sunday night. Bradley Kanaris/Getty Images “My job was to go out and play football. I’m sure on Monday I’ll have a conversation with him, and we’ll sit down and hopefully get something sorted. “I’m sure I’ll have time over the next couple of days to [go through it].



“It’s nice to be wanted. I’m going to make a decision soon on my future. But right now, my focus was completely on making sure I got the win for Australia.” Walker has made it clear he has little appetite for going to the open market, with all players off contract at the end of 2027 open to fielding offers from rival clubs from November 1. Sam Walker and Angus Crichton after winning the grand final with the Roosters. Getty Images The Roosters won the premiership but lost Daly Cherry-Evans (Hull FC), Mark Nawaqanitawase and Angus Crichton to rugby, Spencer Leniu to Parramatta, Connor Watson to St George Illawarra, while Daniel Tupou retired. Locking down Walker has become a priority. The club has also been linked to Dolphins’ centre Herbie Farnworth and Melbourne prop Stefano Utoikamanu, who family is eager for a return home to Sydney.



Walker, Hugo Savala and Toby Rodwell are viewed as the Roosters’ future halves players. Related Article Rugby League World Cup November 1 is looming. But Sam Walker is keeping his contract talks on hold The on-field chemistry Walker has with James Tedesco, who has indicated he is eager to play on for one final year in 2028, was one of the few positives for the Roos on Sunday night. The team will need to improve quickly if they are to defend their World Cup, starting with Saturday’s trip to Townsville to face the Cook Islands. Sunday’s win was clunky, with the forwards out-enthused and Walker and Dearden both solid without being dominant. “I’m sure once we get the job done, I’ll have a bit of time to sit back and reflect on the whole year,” Walker said of a year that also included him making his Origin debut for Queensland.



“We’re all here to make sure we put Australia first and do a job for them; whatever role I’ve got – whether it’s starting, coming off the bench, or helping out at training – it doesn’t matter. I’ll make sure I do my best and help out where I can. “It’s special to play with [Tedesco], and I’m very lucky to be captained by him. The way he leads, it’s not just with his voice but also his actions, which is really cool, and I’m able to follow off the back of him. “You just have to keep pushing around him because you know something’s going to happen.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: ‘We don’t play games’: Trump’s threats have markets nervous
World.content:
BusinessMarketsOil Opinion ‘We don’t play games’: Trump’s threats have markets nervous Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist October 26, 2026 — 11:58am

October 26, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz has returned to something close to pre-war levels. So why has the price surged again to near six-month highs? After trading below $US100 a barrel last month, the price climbed to just under $US117 a barrel last week, with pricing in the futures market suggesting it could still be trading above $US100 a barrel well into next year. With the elections just over a week away, Trump’s rhetoric has hardened. AP Photo/Alex Brandon That’s despite shipments from the Middle East running close to their pre-war levels as the volume of oil mon tankers being escorted through the strait by the US navy – and some tankers that appear to be paying Iranian fees for safe passage – have rebounded. Flows through Saudi Arabia’s pipeline to the Red Sea have also picked up, despite Houthi attacks on the pipeline and the port of Yanbu.



The flows are holding up despite recent escalation of Iranian attacks on ships in the strait and Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure, oil fields and the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Related Article Analysis

Global economy The prince’s bet on Trump is blowing up in his face Last week the UK’s Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) reported 11 confirmed attacks in the strait last week, although the real number is probably higher, given that the UKMTO says most targeted ships don’t report the attacks. Other authorities claim there have been at least 28 incidents so far this month. If the oil is flowing, why has the price taken off again? Part of the explanation may be that while more oil might be reaching the global market, the cost of getting it there has exploded.



The cost of chartering a tanker to carry oil through the strait is about 12 times what it was pre-war; the cost of insuring the cargo more than three times what it was. Ships captains are being paid nearly six times what they were being paid, plus bonuses in the tens of thousands of dollars, and crews two or three times their pre-war salaries, as incentives for taking the risk of being attacked. The way oil is being moved out of the strait – vessels are shuttling into and out of it and transferring their cargoes to other ships waiting outside the strait – adds to the cost and time and has created a global shortage, not of ships, but of tanker capacity because of the extra vessels tied up in the Middle East trade. The other dimension to the spike in prices is Donald Trump.



Trump stopped attacking Iran in late July in the hope that would take some of the heat out of the oil prices – and US gasoline and diesel prices – in the lead up to the US midterm elections. Related Article US midterms Long lines, late nights, adulation: What it’s really like inside Trump’s midterm election rallies He has subsequently done everything he can – convincing the G7 to release strategic reserves of diesel, allowing tax-exempt diesel in the US (normally reserved for off-road usages) to be used on public roads and controversially (and probably illegally) lifting sanctions on Russia and striking a deal with Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel to the US. While none of those attempts to lower US domestic gasoline and diesel prices have had any material effect – gasoline prices are still 40 per cent higher than a year ago, diesel prices about 74 per cent higher and Trump’s poll numbers have plumbed new lows – Trump has maintained the moratorium on attacks. With the elections just over a week away, Trump’s rhetoric has hardened. On Thursday, he told reporters that “something one way or the other” would happen “fairly soon” with Iran. Then on Sunday, he said it was “getting to be decision time” on whether to strike a deal with Iran or re-start the attacks.



“I have a decision to make. Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal?” he said on Fox News. “That’s all. We don’t play games.” “Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job’ Iran emerged even stronger”: Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is not backing down from Trump. AP The US has been moving diplomats and military staff out of the region and sending more military resources to the Middle East in preparation for an escalation of hostilities. The Iranians have vowed to retaliate if the US does resume its attacks.



“Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job’ Iran emerged even stronger,” its foreign affairs minister posted on social media. “Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs, too,” Abbas Araghchi wrote. ‘I have a decision to make. Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal?’ Donald Trump on Fox News It’s that prospect of renewed conflict that seems to be the major influence over the surge in oil prices. There are, broadly, two markets that price oil. One is the futures market, which prices oil for delivery at some point in future, and the other, “Dated Brent,” is for physical delivery in the near term.



Dated Brent, which normally trades at a relatively modest premium – less than $US2 a barrel – to the futures price, was trading around $US125 a barrel late last week after a sudden jump late in the week, which might suggest a sudden urgency from buyers to get their hands on oil before a new round of violence erupts. The futures prices, in turn, might be surging in anticipation of the disruption that a renewed conflict will have to supply from the Middle East. Whatever the explanation, it would appear clear that traders believe there is both a significant probability that the war will flare up again and that flows through the strait and through the Saudi pipeline could be materially impacted despite Trump’s confidence that he can “finish it (the war) off” quickly. Loading He has, of course, expressed similar confidence since the US and Israel launched their attacks on February 28. Nearly eight months later, you’d have to say that confidence was misplaced.



The futures market pricing would suggest that traders, too, have little confidence that Trump and his “Department of War” can do in the near term what he has consistently failed to deliver over nearly eight months. Related Article Opinion

Oil As Trump’s Iran war drags on, we’re facing the next oil crunch Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The other dimension to the conflict and its impact on gasoline/petrol and diesel prices is that there has been significant damage to Middle Eastern oil refineries, while Ukraine’s very successful targeting of Russia’s refineries has also taken significant Russian supply out of the global market. Even if flows of oil from the Middle East could be sustained through renewed hostilities, flows of refined products will continue to be less than what they were before the two wars. No-one pumps crude oil into their cars or trucks, so the impact of the conflict where it hurts US and other consumers and companies will persist for some times beyond the end of the war, whenever – if ever – it ends. World.title: ‘Make sure you don’t talk’: Recorded conversations with Lamarre-Condon played in court
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWLamarre-Condon trial ‘Make sure you don’t talk’: Recorded conversations with Lamarre-Condon played in court Michaela Whitbourn October 26, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Accused killer Lamarre-Condon was captured in a recorded call from prison telling a friend that he “should make sure you don’t talk to people”. Lamarre-Condon’s Supreme Court trial heard recordings of a series of conversations between the accused and his friend in 2024 and 2025, after the former NSW police officer was arrested over the alleged murder of Sydney couple of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies. Footage released by the court of Beau Lamarre-Condon buying a surfboard bag with a friend. The friend, whose identity cannot be reported due to a court order, gave evidence on Monday in Lamarre-Condon’s Supreme Court murder trial about the contents of the conversations while the accused was in prison. In one call, on April 8, 2024, Lamarre-Condon said to his friend: “Make sure you don’t talk to people about stuff, you know what I mean?”



“I don’t know what you’re talking about, bro,” the friend replied. Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, put to the friend on Monday that he was “putting on a bit of a voice” in the call. “Sounds like it, yes,” the friend replied. Beau Lamarre-Condon is accused of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies. The court heard that by this date the friend had provided statements to police on February 23 and 24 and March 12. He has given evidence in court about Lamarre-Condon buying a surfboard cover shortly before the alleged murders, and telling him later that he had killed two people. Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the shooting deaths of Baird, 26, a former Network Ten producer and presenter, and Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, on February 19, 2024. The bodies of Baird and Davies were found in Bungonia, near Goulburn, in two layers of surfboard bags on February 27, 2024.



In a later call, more than a year later on December 14, 2025, Lamarre-Condon refers to the men being due to speak to each other in person later that day and tells him to “bring your big boy diapers”. Asked by the prosecution what he believed the accused meant, the friend said: “We were going to have a conversation that might not make me feel too good.” Luke Davies and Jesse Baird were allegedly murdered by Lamarre-Condon. NSW Supreme Court Lamarre-Condon told the man in a further recorded conversation that day, during the friends’ face-to-face meeting, that he had been suicidal from late 2023 because of trauma from work. The accused told his friend that this was why he took him on a drive to the Royal National Park in Sydney’s south in early 2024, where he used police training bullets to shoot his service pistol twice into bushland and asked his friend how loud the gunshots were.



Lamarre-Condon said he was planning to return to that location alone and take his own life. “If they think I’m a missing person, perfect,” he said of his thinking at the time. The accused told his friend that he was “upset like anyone is” after Baird ended their casual relationship in November 2023, but “it’s normal”. He said that within two or three weeks he “didn’t really give a f---king shit about him” and was “dating someone new in February”. Lamarre-Condon said that he entered Baird’s Paddington share house to “get my shit back” after their breakup and was “not doing anything wrong”. The accused also told his friend that “you cannot put a silencer on a police-issued f---ing firearm”. The friend told the court on Friday that Lamarre-Condon had been trying to buy a silencer in December 2023 or February 2024.



Lamarre-Condon told his friend that he was a police officer by the time he was 21 and “you’re not fully self-aware in the way that I am”. Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial ‘Pew, pew’: Lamarre-Condon allegedly confessed to friend about double murder The friend said during the conversation that he was getting frustrated and was close to leaving. “What you’re telling me might not be the truth,” the man said. “I’m really trying to stay calm.” The friend said of Lamarre-Condon entering Baird’s home on the day of the alleged murders: “How is it not break and enter?”



The accused replied: “He got a key cut for me. It’s technically not. He gave consent. It actually doesn’t meet the definition. It’s trespass. “Normal people do this on an everyday basis [retrieving belongings from an ex-partner’s home].” Lamarre-Condon told his friend earlier in the conversation: “I fully take accountability that you’re involved because of me now.” The friend has given evidence that Lamarre-Condon told him he killed two people and the second person was killed to eliminate a witness. The accused told his friend he had never said this. “Don’t you dare switch up,” the friend replied. Lamarre-Condon suggested to him that he was wrong in his recollection of events.



The Crown case is that Lamarre-Condon had his police-issued Glock pistol with him for a work shift on Sunday, February 18, the day before the alleged murders, and pretended to return it to a police gun safe at Balmain, near his home, later that day. “He retained it despite having no authorised reason to do so,” Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, said in his opening address to the jury. The Crown alleges Lamarre-Condon pretended to retrieve the pistol from Balmain on February 20, before he returned the weapon that was already in his possession to Miranda police station, where he was based. The trial continues. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491 or Lifeline on 13 11 14.
